**arXiv:2501.19386v1 [stat.ME] 31 Jan 2025**  
**Multi-Frame Blind Manifold Deconvolution for Rotating Synthetic Aperture Imaging**  
Daolin Li and Jian Zhang  
School of Mathematics, Statistics and Actuarial Science, University of Kent  
Martin Benning  
Department of Computer Science, University College London  
February 3, 2025  

**Abstract**  
The rotating synthetic aperture (RSA) imaging system captures images of the target scene at various rotational angles by moving a rectangular aperture. Deblurring the collected RSA images is vital for reconstructing a clear latent image of the scene. Over the last ten years, the introduction of blind convolution technologies has significantly impacted this area by successfully modeling complex features from captured images. Many existing approaches to resolving this ill-posed inverse problem focus on maximizing a posterior. However, there has been minimal exploration of the low-dimensional manifold structures of the latent image within a higher-dimensional ambient space. In this paper, we introduce a novel technique for processing RSA images through manifold fitting and penalization within multi-frame blind convolution. We also present efficient algorithms for executing the proposed method. Simulation results illustrate that the manifold-based deconvolution exceeds traditional deconvolution techniques concerning sharper estimates of pixel intensities and enhanced structural detail preservation.  
**Keywords:** Rotating synthetic aperture imaging, multi-frame blind deconvolution, manifold fitting, latent image reconstruction  

---

**1 Introduction**  
The compactness and light weight of contemporary satellites limit the use of large telescopes required for high-resolution Earth imaging. The rotating synthetic aperture (RSA) imaging system, pioneered by Rafanelli and Rehfield (1993), captures images by rotating a rectangular aperture at varying angles over time. RSA has the potential to improve the resolution of all acquired imagery, optimizing the functionality of these restricted platforms. Due to the aperture’s configuration, images typically demonstrate lower resolution along the shorter axis than the longer axis, resulting in spatial asymmetry in the underlying point-spread function (PSF)—or blur kernel in deconvolution terminology—which evolves over time as the mirror rotates (Sun et al., 2023). The directional variability during rotation allows images taken at various angles to capture unique scene features along the longer axis (Zhi et al., 2021). Consequently, implementing an effective image fusion technique to synthesize information across the image sequence due to mirror rotation into a single high-resolution outcome is paramount. The synthesized results could match or surpass the resolution of traditional circular apertures, presenting a cost-efficient and straightforward method (Monreal et al., 2018). In contrast, circular apertures produce images characterized by a uniform PSF, leading to a consistent degradation of quality across all angles, limiting the capture of angle-dependent features in the image sequence. To achieve high resolution with circular apertures, larger lenses are necessary, which come with significant production costs (Stepp et al., 2003). Recent optical remote sensing research has highlighted the RSA’s capacity to minimize payload size and weight issues commonly linked with conventional large-aperture systems (Sun et al., 2024; Lv et al., 2021). To fully capitalize on the RSA's capabilities, sophisticated image fusion methods are essential for reconstructing a high-resolution image from multiple frames collected by the strip aperture imaging sensor. Standard fusion strategies, like principal component analysis (Kwarteng and Chavez, 1989; Jelenek et al., 2016), wavelet transforms (Li et al., 1995; Amolins et al., 2007), and wavelet decomposition (Cheng et al., 2015), often fall short due to inadequate adaptation to the unique degradation features of RSA. Current fusion software mainly relies on integrating multiple PSFs across different angles (Zackay et al., 2016), leading to images that may degrade because of the rectangular aperture. Furthermore, satellite vibrations during orbit can blur the acquired images and compromise RSA's effectiveness. Both non-blind (Gregson et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2011) and blind deconvolution techniques (Kotera et al., 2013; Sroubek and Milanfar, 2011) have been suggested for RSA image reconstruction. Non-blind deconvolution uses a known PSF to clarify the acquired image set, whereas blind deconvolution seeks to recover a sharp image from blurred images obtained via RSA when the PSFs are unknown. This constitutes an ill-posed inverse challenge, making most blind deconvolution algorithms depend heavily on regularization. A prevalent approach is based on maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) methods with pre-selected priors (Satish et al., 2020). MAP allows for versatile integration of suitable priors for both the image and blur kernel at various stages, aiming to alleviate the ill-posed aspects of the deconvolution dilemma and guide the algorithm toward accurately reconstructing images (Levin et al., 2019). MAP methods can be segregated into two primary categories (Levin et al., 2019): (a) the MAP(x,k) method, which estimates the latent image and PSFs concurrently; (b) the marginal posterior model, which first estimates the PSFs by using their marginal posterior followed by applying non-blind deconvolution algorithms to recover the latent image (Babacan et al., 2008; Wipf and Zhang, 2014). In both instances, prior selection remains crucial. Researchers have examined a variety of priors, such as hyper-Laplacian prior (Krishnan and Fergus, 2009), indicative of gradient sparsity in natural images (Miskin and Mackay, 2000); L0-norm prior applicable in deblurring text images (Pan et al., 2016); total variation (TV) prior (Chan and Wong, 1998); L1 L2-norm prior (Krishnan et al., 2011); low-rank prior (Gu et al., 2014); and dark channel prior (He et al., 2010). Rameshan et al. (2012) indicated that many blur kernels are not uniformly distributed and often display distinct configurations, such as radial or lateral symmetry. Common priors employed for blur kernel estimation encompass L1-norm prior (Dong et al., 2012), L2-norm prior for a steady estimate (Ren et al., 2016), Lp-norm within a gradient-domain (Rameshan et al., 2012), and specialized priors that encapsulate how blurred images relate to the sharp counterpart (Liu et al., 2014). In an RSA imaging scenario, multiple images of a specific target are captured from various angles, aiding in mitigating the ill-posed nature of the blind deconvolution problem. Studies on multi-frame blind deconvolution can be found in works by Sroubek and Milanfar (2011), Dong et al. (2012), and Delbracio and Sapiro (2015). Most existing deconvolution algorithms operate iteratively, where each iteration refines the estimates for the PSFs and the latent image. Techniques such as MAP and expectation-maximization serve as iterative methods. Despite the enhanced image quality achieved through these advanced algorithms, vibrations during RSA operation can still diminish the imaging outcomes due to unknown scene structures. In light of these challenges, we present a manifold fitting approach, utilizing a sparsity prior, to ameliorate noise in the captured images. Manifold fitting has established applications in dimensionality reduction (Weinberger and Saul, 2006), predicated on the manifold hypothesis (Fefferman et al., 2016), suggesting that high-dimensional data typically resides close to a low-dimensional manifold within the surrounding ambient space. The blurry images from an RSA system are embedded within a high-dimensional ambient space, often exhibiting a low-dimensional manifold structure (Osher et al., 2017; Gong et al., 2010). This motivates our endeavor to estimate a low-dimensional manifold that encapsulates the latent image, into which we project the acquired multi-frame images. By leveraging the manifold structures, we can significantly enhance the quality of the captured images. Our methodology unfolds in three stages: (1) deconvoluting the captured images and enforcing sparsity in the super-resolution images through an L1-norm penalty; (2) employing manifold fitting to further enhance image resolution; (3) synthesizing these refined images to construct a high-resolution representation of the scene. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:  
• A multi-frame blind manifold convolution model is proposed, accompanied by an advanced algorithm to minimize the bias of manifold deconvolution on each acquired image, thus bolstering the ensuing manifold fitting efficacy.  
• Expedient algorithms are developed to address the related optimization problems.  
• Comprehensive simulation studies reveal that merging blind deconvolution with manifold fitting surpasses both direct manifold modeling and straightforward blind convolution of the original captured images. In comparison with existing methodologies, our proposed technique yields sharper, high-quality images from the collected RSA images concerning precise pixel intensities and structural details. The ensuing sections of this document are organized as follows: Section 2 details the proposed procedure's description and implementation. Section 3 assesses the effectiveness of the proposed method using simulated datasets. Section 4 concludes the paper with suggestions for future enhancements. Throughout the document, symbols Yi, Ki, X, Ni denote random variables, while the lowercase letters yi, ki, x, ni signify their associated specific values. The vectorization of a multidimensional array by column stacking is denoted by vec(·). The operator ∗ indicates a two-dimensional discrete convolution applied to each channel independently, as defined in Appendix A.  

---

**2 Methodology**   
The imaging process within the RSA system can be modeled as a multi-frame blind convolution of blur kernels (i.e., PSFs) with a high-resolution image captured from various angles, plus additive noise, expressed as  
Yi = Ki ∗X + Ni, where i = 1, · · · , n.  

Here, Ki, Yi, X, Ni ∈ RC×a×b represent the unknown blur kernel, acquired blurred image, latent high-resolution image, and additive noise from angle i, respectively. The noise is typically assumed to be Gaussian. For simplicity, we consider that the blur kernels {Ki}n i=1 share the same known dimensionality s << min{a, b}, such that Ki ∈ Rs×s lies on the probability simplex, indicating a finite number of pixels supported. Ki signifies a non-negative light distribution, summing to one, thereby retaining overall brightness within the image. We assume independence between X and Ki. Convoluting equation (2.1) with Gh and Gv gives us a model for gradient images, represented as  
∇jYi = Ki ∗∇jX + ∇jNi, for i = 1, ..., n; with j ∈ {h, v},  

where Gh = [1, −1] and Gv = [1, −1]T, and for an image x, vec(∇hx) = Gh∗x and vec(∇vx) = Gv ∗x denote the horizontal and vertical differences, respectively, across channels and pixels. Determining an object's boundaries within a scene is termed edge detection. For natural images, edges are identified via local intensity variations, typically assessed by intensity gradients using differentiation operators. As previously noted, multi-frame blind deconvolution enables the recovery of the latent image from a set of blurred images amidst unknown kernels, i.e., estimating X using captured images (Yi) for i ranging from 1 to n when (Ki) for i = 1 to n remain unavailable. This amounts to a severely ill-posed inverse challenge, given that infinite pairs of (x, k) could satisfy equations (2.1) and (2.2). Strong priors are therefore necessary for both the sharp image and the blur kernels to regularize the solution space effectively.  
To elucidate a sparse prior on the blur kernels, we introduce Qi ∈ Rs×s as generalized blur kernels with specific values denoted as qi’s. We can reformulate Ki by projecting Qi onto the probability simplex as follows:  
Ki = arg min{||K −Qi||2 F : K ∈ Rs×s, K is in the probability simplex}.  

**2.1 MAP blind deconvolution: XK-procedure**   
An important insight into blind deconvolution highlighted by Levin et al. (2009) relates to the conventional MAP approach's limitations. Their research underscored the advantages of isolating kernel estimation relative to simultaneous estimation of both the image and kernel. Recent findings reveal that utilizing gradient images and marginalization surpass conventional MAP performance. While prior specifications may differ, the improved MAP primarily involves estimating x and ki through iterative optimization in two phases (Zhou et al., 2021), relying on the multi-frame images y = (y1, · · · , yn) captured by RSA.   
X-Step: Maintaining the value of k = (k1, ..., kn), we maximize the penalized least squares function defined as:  
l(x|y, k) = λ1 n ∑ i=1 ||yi −ki ∗x||2 - log pX(x),  

where pX(x) indicates the prior density function of X. Intense gradients in sharp natural images often exhibit sparsity (Miskin and Mackay, 2000); consequently, such gradients predominantly approach zero, with only a few exceptions. This behavior can be constructed via a hyper-Laplacian distribution (Krishnan and Fergus, 2009). More extensively, various gradient features of the image x can be signified by:  
log pX(x) ∝− ∑ j∈{h,v} ||vec(∇jx)||α.  

Employing a sparse prior when α ≤ 1, a shrinkage prior when α = 2; typical natural images possess α values from [0.5, 0.8] (Simoncelli, 1999). Collectively, expression (2.5) can thus be interpreted as Lα-penalty terms ||vec(∇hx)||α and ||vec(∇vx)||α relevant to the desired image. Following this, by merging expressions (2.4) and (2.5), we can redefine the optimization issue from equation (2.4) as:  
bx = arg min x [ λ1 n ∑ i=1 ||yi −ki ∗x||2 F + ∑ j∈{h,v} ||vec(∇jx)||α ],  

K-Step: As gradient images suppress low-frequency components while emphasizing high-frequency details such as edges present in natural images, convolution mainly influences high-frequency components within x, exerting negligible effects on low-frequency components. This suggests that estimating kernels based on original images (y, x) may introduce bias due to irrelevant low-frequency information. It is inferred that estimating kernels in the gradient domain will yield better results than in the pixel domain (Cho and Lee, 2009). Therefore, keeping x constant, the estimation of ki’s proceeds via minimizing the least square function formulated for the gradient model (2.2):  
bqi = arg min qi [ ∑ j∈{h,v} ||∇jy −qi ∗∇jbx||2 F + µ||vec(qi)||1 ].  

Hence, the procedure for estimating ki is expressed as:  
bki = min ki ||qi −ki||2 F, with the constraint that ki remains within the probability simplex.  

Within the X-step, the latent image estimation is performed by enforcing a penalty within the gradient image space. However, the outcome quality greatly depends on the noise levels present in the captured images. Reducing noise in the acquired images {yi}n i=1 can significantly sharpen the reconstructed latent image bx. To address the noise reduction, we consider optimizing the problem as outlined in (2.6), disregarding the penalty term temporarily for P j∈{h,v} ||vec(∇jx)||p. Proposition A.1 in Appendix A indicates that, within the frequency domain, the sharp image reconstruction can be expressed as a weighted average of the deconvolved images {exi}n i=1, wherein the deconvolved image exi denotes the deconvolution of the blurred image yi utilizing its estimated blur kernel bki. Consequently, enhancing the noise in exi can refine the quality of the latent image estimate bx. This leads us to improve the {exi}n i=1 collection to enhance bx. Recognizing that RSA images are taken sequentially at regular angles allows for some common scene features to be shared within the deconvolved images {exi}n i=1. Thus, we propose an enhancement method wherein each exi is substituted with a weighted average (denote this by bx∗ i) of nearby deconvolved images, leading to the following refined sharp image estimate:  
bx = F −1 [ n ∑ i=1 F(eki) ⊙F(eyi) / n ∑ i=1 F(eki) ⊙F(eki) ] = F −1 [ n ∑ i=1 F(eki) ⊙F(eki) / n ∑ j=1 F(ekj) ⊙F(ekj) ⊙F(bx∗ i) ].  

Here, eyi denotes a denoised convolved image represented as:  
F(bx∗ i) ⊙ F(eki) = F(eyi), with eki as the padded version of bki as elaborated in Appendix A. In the upcoming subsection, we will introduce a new algorithm in which for each i, we utilize eyi instead of averaging the acquired images directly in the vicinity of yi. This focuses on avoiding potential bias in the denoising process due to kernel discrepancies that arise when RSA images are captured at angles with varying PSFs. Additionally, we can further enhance the algorithm by imposing a penalty on the gradient images when computing exi.  

**2.2 MAP blind manifold deconvolution: IMR-procedure**  
Let’s assume the acquired images represent noisy blind convolutions of PSFs combined with a sharp image embedded in a low-dimensional manifold. Following the ideas previously articulated, we expand the multi-frame blind deconvolution methodology by incorporating manifold fitting, executed in three steps:  
- IX-step: Compute the deconvolved images {exi}n i=1 from the RSA captured images {yi}n i=1, effectively reverting the observed RSA images to the latent source image space.  
- MF-step: Calculate the deconvolved manifold images derived from the findings in the IX-step.  
- RC-step: Reconstruct the latent high-resolution image. The convolution is reintroduced into {exi}n i=1, generating denoised convoluted images {eyi}n i=1 followed by a non-blind deconvolution process.  

**2.2.1 IX-step**  
To derive the deconvolved images {exi}n i=1 from {yi}n i=1, we implement the XK-procedure to compute bki, its padded counterpart eki, and bx. The alternating iterations will continue until a predetermined maximum number of iterations is reached, and recorded estimates for the blur kernels will be utilized for calculating individual bxi later. It is essential to recognize that the objective function in equation (2.6) lacks convexity. Thus, two auxiliary variables γh ∈ RC×a×b and γv ∈ RC×a×b are introduced within the framework of half-quadratic splitting (Zhou et al., 2021)(refer to Appendix B). This approach encompasses an Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS) algorithm along with a two-dimensional discrete Fourier transform as detailed in Appendix A. With bx established, the optimization issue in equation (2.7) can be reformulated into a standard multivariate lasso problem in Lagrangian form (see Appendix C). The optimization equation (2.7) can thus be effectively resolved by Celer, a cutting-edge solver for lasso regression (Massias et al., 2018 and 2020). Projecting the estimated generalized kernels bqi onto the probability simplex allows us to retrieve the estimates bki. Herein, we apply an O(s2 log s) algorithm by Wang and Carreira-Perpinan (2013) for projection. In the IX-step, our aim is to restore the underlying image for each acquired image while delving into its low-dimensional manifold structure. Due to RSA imaging, each restored image captures only a fragment of the latent image. Hence, for each i, we compute the deconvolved image exi using the acquired image yi and the estimated blur kernel eki under a penalization mechanism, which entails solving the optimization issue:  
exi = arg min x { λ1 ||yi −bki ∗x||2 F + ∑ j∈{h,v} ||vec(∇jx)||α }.  

This results in a superlative estimate compared to deriving from the equation F(exi)⊙F(eki) = F(yi). As with the resolution for equation (2.6), we introduce auxiliary variables for equation (2.9) and apply alternating minimization in line with Zhou et al. (2021). The comprehensive algorithm for determining {exi}n i=1 is encapsulated in Algorithm 1. In contrast to (yi)n i=1, (exi)n i=1 aligns more closely with the latent image, provided that (yi)n i=1 arise from the convolution of the latent image along with heterogeneous kernels and additional noise. The convolution effects on observed images can be alleviated through solving the optimization problem in equation (2.9).  

**Algorithm 1: XK-procedure for generating {exi}n i=1 from {yi}n i=1**  
*Input:* Blurred images {yi}n i=1, kernel support s, regularization weights λ1 and µ, number of iterations T, τ    
*Output:* {exi}n i=1  
1: Initialize bki as a Gaussian kernel for i = 1, 2, . . . , n  
2: For iter t = 1 : T do  
3: bx ←bxt: compute bxt by solving equation (2.6) (using half-quadratic splitting).  
4: For i = 1 : n do  
5: Reformulate the problem equation (2.7) as per equation (C.13) and solve to obtain bqi.  
6: bki ←bki t: determine bki t by projecting bqi onto the probability simplex.  
7: End for  
8: If min i Sc[vec(bki t), vec(bki t−1)] ≥τ, where Sc signifies the cosine similarity, then  
9: Break  
10: End if  
11: End for  
12: For i = 1 : n do  
13: Resolve the problem defined in equation (2.9) using half-quadratic splitting.  
14: End for  

In the following step, we implement manifold fitting to reduce noise in exi, bringing each deconvolved image closer to M, an estimated manifold surrounding the latent image.  

**2.2.2 MF-step**  
The manifold fitting algorithm is grounded on the hypothesis that natural images, as high-dimensional data, frequently situate near a low-dimensional manifold within the ambient space, displaying an inherent low-dimensional structure (Fefferman et al., 2016; Osher et al., 2017). Our objective is to estimate this low-dimensional manifold, encompassing the latent image within the high-dimensional space. Subsequently, the estimated manifold enables denoising through sample projection onto it (Gong et al., 2010). Yao et al. (2023) introduced a novel fitting method that circumvents iterative processes. The basic premise is representing a refined sample as a weighted average of the samples within a “rectangular” neighborhood surrounding the unrevised sample. This technique necessitates an initial estimator for the latent manifold M, which should not deviate significantly from M. In contrast to the blurred image yi, the deconvolved image exi achieved in the prior step is markedly closer to the latent high-resolution image, as the convolution impact has been substantially reduced via the MAPx,k technique. Consequently, {exi}n i=1 can serve as an initial estimate of the latent manifold. Noise present in {exi}n i=1 can be further mitigated using the manifold fitting methodology, composed of two stages: 1) contraction direction estimation; 2) local contraction.  

**Estimation of contraction direction.** We express exi in vector form as zi ∈ RD (D = Cab) and define z∗ i := arg min z′∈M ||z′ −zi||2, measuring the contraction direction using z∗ i −zi. A suitable estimate of z∗ i −zi can be determined as F(zi) −zi, where  
F(zi) = ∑ j=1, j̸=i αj(zi)zj.  

The weight αj(zi) is determined by:  
eαj(zi) = {  
−1 − ||zi−zj||2 2 r2 1, ||zi −zj||2 ≤r1,  
0, otherwise,  
  
and  
αj(zi) = eαj(zi) / ∑ t=1, t̸=i eαt(zi).  

Here, k ≥ 2 is a constant integer, and the selection for r1 should ensure a limited number of zj’s near zi.  

**Local contraction.** We denote the contraction matrix of zi as bUi and define  
bUi = [F(zi) −zi][F(zi) −zi]T / ||F(zi) −zi||2 2.  

Based on bUi, zj −zi (where j ̸= i) can be decomposed into uj,i and vj,i, such that  
zj −zi = uj,i + vj,i, where  
uj,i = bUi(zj −zi) and vj,i = zj −zi −uj,i.  

Thus, the estimate for z∗ i is articulated as  
G(zi) = ∑ j=1, j̸=i βj(zi)zj.  

The weight βj(zi) is defined by:  
wu(uj,i) = {  
1, if ||uj,i||2 ≤r2 2;  
{1 − ((2||uj,i||2−r2)/r2)2}k, if ||uj,i||2 ∈ (r2 2, r2);  
0, otherwise,  
  
wv(vj,i) = {  
1 − ||vj,i||2 2 / r2 1, if ||vj,i||2 ≤r1;  
0, otherwise,  
  
and  
βj(zi) = wu(uj,i)wv(vj,i) / ∑ t=1, t̸=i wu(ut,i)wv(vt,i), where r2 >> r1.  

Utilizing this methodology, the estimated manifold comprises G(z1), · · · , G(zn), where G(zi) represents the projection of zi onto the estimated manifold. In other words, G(zi) stands as the denoised rendition of zi.  

**2.2.3 RC-step**  
Our ultimate aim is to retrieve the latent high-resolution image. Though the projections onto the latent manifold, namely {G(zi)}n i=1, are no longer influenced by convolution and noise, they merely represent partial features of the latent sharp image. We can express G(zi) in the format bx∗ i ∈ Rc×a×b. The objective of this stage is to amalgamate these projected samples and reconstruct the latent image. Initially, refined images need to be generated with convolution reintroduced into bx∗ i as follows:  
eyi = bki ∗bx∗ i.  

Based on both {bki}n i=1 and {eyi}n i=1, the sharp image is reconstructed by resolving the optimization problem expressed as:  
bx = arg min x { λ1 n ∑ i=1 ||eyi −bki ∗x||2 F + ∑ j∈{h,v} ||∇jx||α }.  

Similarly, the half-quadratic splitting approach is applied to solve this issue (2.17). The entire integrated algorithm is encapsulated in Algorithm 2.

**3 Numerical Results**  
To evaluate our proposed method's effectiveness, we simulate blurred images using a real image and then reconstruct the latent image based on these blurred samples.  

**3.1 Dataset**  
For our analysis, a color (RGB) image (dimensions: 512 × 512) depicting an astronaut is sourced from skimage.data, and its pixel intensities are normalized from {0, 1, …, 255} to the [0, 1] range (unless specified otherwise, all images maintain pixel intensity representation within this interval). In this phase, 36 sparse kernels of size 25 × 25 are generated for convolution with this RGB image, where each kernel exemplifies a unique orientation's PSF. Subsequently, i.i.d. Gaussian noise characterized by a standard deviation of 0.05 is introduced to these convolved images. The blurring stage adheres to equation (2.1), with an illustration of the resultant blurring presented in Figure 1.  

**Algorithm 2: IMR-procedure: Enhanced Multi-frame Blind Manifold Deconvolution**  
*Input:* Blurred images {yi}n i=1 and tuning parameters: s, λ1, µ, T, τ, r1, and r2  
*Output:* Estimated sharp image bx  
1: Initialize bki as Gaussian kernel for i = 1, 2, ···, n  
2: Employ Algorithm 1 to acquire estimated blur kernels {bki}n i=1 and deconvolved images {exi}n i=1  
3: For i = 1 : n do  
4: Contraction Direction Estimation: Calculate F(zi) as laid out in equation (2.10), with αj(zi) derived from equation (2.11)  
5: Local Contraction: Use the contraction matrix from equation (2.12) to dissect zj −zi, computing βj(zi) and G(zi) via equations (2.15) and (2.14), respectively.  
6: Reintroduce Convolution: Generate enhanced convolved images {eyi}n i=1 using equation (2.16).  
7: End for  
8: Non-blind Deconvolution: Address the optimization problem in equation (2.17) to procure bx.

**3.2 Implementation Details**   
Upon applying Algorithm 1, we commence with estimating the blur kernels. The tuning parameters are established as follows: µ = 0.04, τ = 0.9980, α = 0.80, and T = 10. For resolving the optimization challenges in equations (2.6) and (2.7) iteratively, we set λ1 = 667, while λ1 = 2000 for issue equation (2.9). The aforementioned λ1 and µ values have been pre-validated with a distinct validation set. Figure 2 portrays the estimated kernels alongside their corresponding real (simulated) counterparts. By employing the blurred images {yi}n i=1 and estimated kernels {bki}n i=1 (shown in the second row of Figure 2), the deconvolved images {exi}n i=1 are developed through non-blind deconvolution via equation (2.16). However, due to noise present in yi, a significant portion of exi displays noticeable roughness (see the first row in Figure 3).  

![Figure 2: The first row showcases 12 estimated blur kernels; the second row displays the corresponding real (simulated) blur kernels.](URL)  

The manifold fitting leverages data from {exj : || exj−exi||F ≤r1 and j ̸= i} to bolster the smoothness of exi. Herein, the primary purpose of this step is to denoise exi through projection onto the latent manifold. The manifold fitting parameters are configured with r1 = 108 and r2 = 10 × 108, ensuring each exi possesses a minimum of five neighboring images within its local vicinity. As illustrated in each column of Figure 3, the enhanced deconvolved image bx∗ i appears substantially smoother in the majority of local regions than its associated exi counterpart. Two performance metrics, PSNR (peak signal-to-noise ratio) and SSIM (structural similarity index), are utilized to assess the efficiency of enhancement achieved through the manifold fitting. The PSNRs of the four deconvolved images in Figure 3 experience improvements of 32.96%, 26.95%, 27.22%, and 33.51%, respectively; likewise, the SSIM values show enhancements of 84.27%, 69.31%, 72.59%, and 89.61%.  

![Figure 3: The first row displays 4 deconvolved images; the second row shows the corresponding enhanced deconvolved images. The baseline image is the ground-truth sharp image x. The PSNR (peak signal-to-noise ratio) and SSIM (structural similarity) values of each showcased image are evaluated against the ground-truth image x.](URL)  

 In Figure 4, the box plots indicate that manifold fitting indeed refines the deconvolved images. The effectiveness of manifold fitting can further be validated by contrasting those convolved images. According to equation (2.16), convolution is reinstated onto bx∗ i. Leveraging the simulated blur kernels {ki}n i=1, we can delineate the ground-truth convolved images {Yi}n i=1 as:   
Yi = ki ∗x, where i = 1, · · · , n.   

In Figure 6, it becomes evident that the noise in the enhanced convolved image eyi is substantially minimized while the structure of Yi is adequately reaffirmed. An individual enhanced deconvolved image bx∗ i may not comprehensively capture all local features, such as the astronaut’s teeth (as noted in the second row of Figure 3), resulting in residual convolution and noise influences. Thus, a singular bx∗ i does not satisfy as a wholly satisfactory estimate for the sharp image x, though it adequately approximates the latent image x concerning PSNR and SSIM, as demonstrated in Figure 4. Hence, considering the entire set {bx∗ i }n i=1 is necessary. By reintroducing convolution, enhanced convolved images {eyi}n i=1 are generated with the aid of {bki}n i=1 (as articulated in equation (2.16)). Figure 5 outlines this methodology, contrasting an enhanced convolved image (Figure 5(d)) with its corresponding ground-truth convolved variant (Figure 1(c)). Observations suggest that the eyi (Figure 5 (d)) is considerably smoother than its original version yi (Figure 5(a)), with most noise significantly reduced.  

![Figure 5: The denoising process comprising (a) one blurred image yi; (b) its associated deconvolved representation bxi; (c) the corresponding enhanced deconvolved image bx∗ i; (d) the enhanced convolved outcome eyi.](URL)  

Manifold fitting can also be applied directly to the blurred images {yi}n i=1, resulting in additional enhanced convolved images denoted as ¨y1, · · · , ¨yn, with tuning parameters r1 = 61 and r2 = 10 × 61. The values of r1 and r2 were selected to ensure a comparably adequate number of neighboring images for each sample, consistent with the manifold fitting application to the deconvolved images {bxi}n i=1. Nevertheless, as depicted in Figure 6, the enhancement resulting from applying manifold fitting directly to {yi}n i=1 is not as pronounced compared to the results for {bxi}n i=1. Engaging manifold fitting directly on {bxi}n i=1 presupposes that the latent manifold aligns with the ground-truth image x, while applying it to {yi}n i=1 implies that the latent manifold corresponds to the ground-truth convolved images {Yi}n i=1. As the convolution effects in {yi}n i=1 have been alleviated by resolving equation (2.16), the {bxi}n i=1 contribute informatively to estimate x. The core concept of manifold fitting is to compute the weighted average of neighboring samples surrounding a specified sample, significantly reducing the noise within {bxi}n i=1. However, when n is limited, substantial variability exists in the blur kernel angles associated with each yi, leading to an insufficient number of neighboring blurred images for each yi, often tending to have widely differing blur kernels in angle. This discrepancy curtails the capability of manifold fitting in differentiating convolution effects from noise. Therefore, the application of manifold fitting on {bxi}n i=1 yields superior results relative to its direct application on {yi}n i=1, particularly with limited sample sizes n. As n increases, the blurred images within any given neighborhood tend to become approximately identically distributed owing to similar blur kernels. Consequently, applying manifold fitting to {yi}n i=1 will yield results akin to those achieved through the application on {bxi}n i=1.  

![Figure 6: Comparisons of blurred images {yi}n i=1, enhanced images (achieved by directly applying manifold fitting to the blurred images), {¨yi}n i=1, and enhanced convolved images {eyi}n i=1. The baseline images are {Yi}n i=1, corresponding PSNR (peak signal-to-noise ratio) and SSIM (structural similarity).

**3.3 Simulation Results and Discussion**   
In the final phase, we employ non-blind deconvolution (i.e., by solving equation (2.16)) to reconstruct the sharp image (see Figure 7(d)), achieving a PSNR of 28.89 dB and an SSIM of 0.7869. The tuning parameters are as follows: λ1 = 2000 and α = 0.80. Our proposed methodology significantly bolsters the reconstructed image quality, culminating in a 13.34% rise in PSNR and a 36.19% boost in SSIM over traditional blind deconvolution (refer to Figure 7(a)). The observable noise in Figure 7(a) emanates from the blurred images {yi}n i=1. Yet, by diminishing this noise via manifold fitting, our method produces an improved outcome in Figure 7(d), where the local regions display minimized noise along with enhanced texture smoothness. This demonstrates that our strategy adeptly recovers a high-quality sharp image with pixel intensities more accurately estimated and preserved structural details, relying on the enhanced convolved images {eyi}n i=1.  

In addition, we reconstruct the latent image (Figure 7(b)) based on an alternative set of enhanced deconvolved images {¨yi}n i=1, obtained by directly applying manifold fitting to {yi}n i=1. This alternative approach yields moderate advancements, recording increases of 6.00% in PSNR and 11.65% in SSIM. As illustrated in the magnified locales (the facial region), despite considerable noise reduction in Figure 7(b) in comparison to Figure 7(a), the image exhibits a blurred and nonsmoothed appearance. Conversely, our proposed method enhances the deconvolved images, ensuring manifold fitting is predicated on better approximated identically distributed samples, thus facilitating the generation of more trustworthy enhanced convolved images. Consequently, the reconstructed image (Figure 7(b)) boasts superior quality when juxtaposed with Figure 7(d). The sharp image depicted in Figure 7(c) emerges from minimizing the expression n ∑ i=1 ||eyi −bki ∗x||2 F. A comparison between Figures 7(c) and 7(d) indicates that inclusion of the prior in equation (2.12) can further enhance the PSNR and SSIM results. The prior term, log pX(x), effectively stabilizes the solution, suppresses noise, and maintains critical structural details, which are essential characteristics of both blind and non-blind deconvolution techniques.  

![Figure 7: Reconstructed sharp images. (a) Zhou et al. (2021) (input images: {yi}n i=1); (b) Zhou et al. (2021) (input images: {¨yi}n i=1); (c) standard multi-frame blind deconvolution, F -1 [ n ∑ i=1 F( eki)∗F(eyi) / n ∑ i=1 F(eki)∗F(eki)] ; (d) proposed method. The baseline image is the ground-truth sharp image x, indicating the PSNR (peak signal-to-noise ratio) and SSIM (structural similarity) values for each reconstructed sharp image are computed concerning the ground-truth image x.](URL)  

We also examine the influence of the tuning parameter r1 utilized in manifold fitting on reconstructing the latent image across both methodologies, assessing PSNR and SSIM as evaluation metrics. The PSNR curves reveal significant fluctuations for lower r1 values (ranging from 90 to 105). Compared with the method lacking convolution reintroduction (i.e., reconstruction via equation (2.8)), our proposed approach consistently achieves superior PSNR values, peaking at r1 = 110. Beyond this threshold, PSNR tends to decline for both approaches. For SSIM, our proposed technique similarly outshines the alternative. Initially, SSIM curves for both strategies exhibit fluctuations, subsequently increasing and stabilizing around 0.8. These findings illustrate that the proposed method's optimal r1 value hovers around 110 concerning reconstruction quality. We also evaluate the sensitivity of PSNR and SSIM to variations in the tuning parameter r2, discovering that the proposed method's performance remains stable against changes in r2, given a fixed r1. This indicates that selecting five neighbors, as determined by r1, r2, and exi, suffices for achieving optimal improvement using our method.  

![Figure 8: Comparison of the effects of r1 on latent image reconstruction quality, assessed using two metrics: PSNR (peak signal-to-noise ratio) and SSIM (structural similarity): (a) Without prior (Equation 2.8). (b) With prior (Equation 2.9, proposed).](URL)  

**4 Conclusion**  
In this study, we have posited that images acquired by an RSA imaging system can be characterized as noisy, multi-frame convolutions of a latent sharp image combined with a sequence of PSFs and that this latent image exists embedded within a low-dimensional manifold within a higher-dimensional ambient space. Under this framework, we have formulated a novel approach to enhance images captured by the RSA imaging system and reconstruct a sharper image through blind manifold deconvolution. The proposed procedure involves first deconvolving the RSA captured images utilizing an improved MAP framework, afterward applying a manifold fit to the deconvoluted images for further enhancement by delving into their low-dimensional manifold structures. Subsequently, we reintegrate a convolution operation to produce denoised convolved images that facilitate the reconstruction of a sharp image. The results from our simulations indicate that the proposed methodology outperforms conventional multi-frame blind deconvolution approaches in terms of accurately estimating pixel intensities and maintaining structural details. Additionally, the findings demonstrate that fitting low-dimensional manifolds to deconvolved RSA images yields more favorable outcomes compared to directly fitting manifolds to captured images. Future enhancements to the proposed method might include incorporating contemporary advancements in deep-learning-based deconvolution (Ren et al., 2020; Kotera et al., 2021) and image fusion methodologies (Zhi et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2024). In this regard, our approach lays the groundwork for a flexible image fusion framework centered around refined observed images, potentially integrating deep learning techniques to deblur each captured image and reconstruct the ultimate sharp image.

arXiv:2501.19373v1 [stat.ML] 31 Jan 2025 Beyond Fixed Horizons: A Theoretical Framework for Adaptive Denoising Diffusions Sören Christensen∗ Claudia Strauch† Lukas Trotner‡ Abstract In this paper, we present a novel class of generative diffusion models that, in contrast to traditional denoising diffusion models, establish a time-homogeneous framework for both the noising and denoising stages, enabling the number of steps to be adjusted adaptively according to the noise level. This is achieved by conditioning the forward process through Doob’s h-transform, which allows the process to conclude at a suitable sampling distribution within a random time frame. The model is especially effective in generating data with lower intrinsic dimensions, as the termination criterion reduces to a first-hitting rule. A significant advantage of this model is its flexibility in adapting to the target data, facilitating a range of downstream tasks utilizing a pre-trained unconditional generative model. These tasks encompass natural conditioning via the appropriate initialization of the denoising process as well as classifying noisy data.
Denoising Diffusion Models [20, 36] have received considerable attention in recent years, owing to their capacity to generate high-quality data samples by iteratively refining simple distributions, guided by learned dynamics of a time-reversed forward noising process initiated from the target data distribution [14, 17, 21, 30, 39, 40]. Nonetheless, a significant drawback of these models is their dependency on a fixed time horizon, which imposes an artificial temporal constraint in the drift function of the reverse process. Consequently, the generative denoising procedure adheres to a specified number of steps, irrespective of the actual noise level encountered during the generated trajectory. To address this issue, we propose a new category of diffusion models that adaptively respond to the state of the denoising process. By substituting the fixed deterministic time horizon with a stochastic one and guiding the forward process to conclude at a specified target distribution, our method offers enhanced flexibility and state awareness. The core of our approach is grounded in Doob’s ℎ-transforms with respect to underlying exponential times. Although the theoretical basis for this concept is established, its practical application and thorough investigation—especially in relation to deterministic time horizons—has not been adequately represented in existing literature. A distinctive characteristic of our model is its inherent adaptability: the number of denoising steps adjusts dynamically according to the noise level present in the data, introducing a stochastic component. This randomness not only enriches the generation process but also facilitates denoising to commence from data that is partially noisy, naturally embedding conditioning. Furthermore, the time expended for denoising serves as an intuitive gauge of the divergence between noisy observations and the underlying data distribution, laying the groundwork for applications such as classification and anomaly detection. The architecture of the model also accommodates natural conditioning mechanisms, enabling easy adaptation to various tasks without necessitating specific design alterations. With its flexible, time-homogeneous framework, our model presents a novel perspective on generative tasks that enhances the adaptability and versatility of diffusion models, and establishes a solid foundation for transfer learning. Contributions and structure: To succinctly outline our principal contributions and the organization of the paper, we first review related work in Section 2. We then present theoretical findings concerning the ℎ-transform and time reversal for exponential time horizons in Section 3. Building on this foundation, we introduce a universal and adaptable diffusion model, along with its associated learning theory, in Section 4. Within this framework, we highlight the polarity of the data distribution as a key assumption for effective learning, providing a new viewpoint on the manifold hypothesis. Lastly, we explore the model's adaptability across various application domains via transfer learning in Section 5.
This section examines significant literature related to the enhancement of diffusion models beyond traditional temporal dependencies, including aspects like random horizons, Doob’s ℎ-transform, and conditioning. Ye, Wu, and Liu [41] present the concept of first hitting diffusion models, which utilize first hitting times to reflect the inherent geometry of data manifolds. Their methodology is akin to ours in that it employs a random time horizon (specifically through first hitting times) while also utilizing Doob’s ℎ-transform. However, their technique establishes a backward process designed to ensure that the produced data remains within a designated manifold. On the other hand, our approach reverses this viewpoint by employing a forward process to establish a more adaptable generative framework that isn't limited to predefined manifolds. Rather, the data manifold is learned in a dynamic manner. De Bortoli et al. [12] investigate diffusion generative modeling through the perspective of Schrödinger Bridges (SB) and address transport problems. Unlike conventional techniques that necessitate running forward SDEs over extended periods, SB methods can generate samples in finite time. Nevertheless, their approach is confined to a deterministic time horizon, where established connections exist between Schrödinger Bridges and ℎ-transforms. Additional advancements in this area are also discussed by Peluchetti [32] and Shi et al. [35]. Conversely, our framework supports random time horizons, permitting both finite and extended durations. The work by Zhao et al. [42] offers an extensive review of conditional sampling techniques within generative diffusion models. It analyzes strategies that depend on joint distributions or pre-trained marginal distributions with explicit likelihoods to produce samples conditioned on specific information, tackling challenges prevalent in fields like Bayesian inverse problems. In these methods, the original unconditional processes undergo various modifications to incorporate conditionality. Likewise, Didi et al. [15] merge conditional training and sampling into a unified framework based on the ℎ-transform. However, the dependence on a fixed time horizon results in significant differences from the framework proposed in our study.
Doob’s h-transform is a powerful mathematical tool used to modify the behavior of a stochastic process. It rigorously defines how to condition the process based on particular events that occur at random times. This section presents the fundamental outcomes pertinent to our methodology. For a deeper exploration, including supporting literature and proofs, it is suggested that readers refer to the Appendix. 

3.1. Doob’s h-transform for random time horizons 

In this study, we utilize h-transforms of a base non-degenerate and symmetric d-dimensional diffusion process dZt = b(Zt) dt + σ(Zt) dWt to analyze both the forward and backward stochastic processes. Normally, Z refers to either a Brownian motion or a symmetric Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process within the domain I = ℝd; however, other self-dual processes are also viable. The process Z without killing has the r-Green kernel Gr(x, y) defined as ∫∞0 e^(-rt)pt(x, y) dt, where pt(x, y) represents the symmetric transition densities of Z concerning a reference measure m. The measure m can align with the ordinary Lebesgue measure but it is not a necessity. Gr describes the probability density function (pdf) of Z evaluated at an independent exponential time when properly scaled. For instance, in the case of Brownian motion, Gr can be explicitly calculated; see Remark A.1 for further details. 

To clarify the implementation of conditioning at a random moment, we introduce two significant adjustments for Z: 1. The drift is altered to draw the process toward the desired states. 2. A random stopping time ζ, known as the lifetime, is introduced to conclude the process at the juncture where the preferred distribution is achieved. Both modifications can be effectively carried out through the h-transform. The h-transform is formulated with the aid of an r-excessive function h, which can be established through a probability measure β on the state space I and a reference state x0 ∈ I. To condition the process Z to follow the distribution given by β at its killing time ζ initiated from x0, we define h(x) as ∫ Gr(x, y) Gr(x0, y) β(dy) = ∫ Gr(x, y) κ(dy), where κ(dy) = κx0,β(dy) = 1/(Gr(x0, y) β(dy)); κ is referred to as the representing measure of h. Consequently, the h-transformed process Zh becomes a Markov process defined by the transition kernel ℙx(Zh t ∈ dy) = E_x[ e^(-rt) h(Zt) / h(x) 1{Zt ∈ dy}]. 

The critical properties of Zh are as follows: 

Proposition 3.1. 1. Zh is terminated at a random stopping time ζ, the lifetime, which is almost surely a finite random variable. 2. Outside the support of β, Zh is an Itô diffusion characterized by the dynamics dZh t = bh(Zh t) dt + σ(Zh t) dWt, where bh(y) = b(y) + σ(y) σ(y)⊤ ∇log h(y). 3. The distribution of Zh at its lifetime is concentrated within the support of β, given by ℙx(Zh ζ− ∈ dy) = Gr(x, y) h(x) κ(dy). In particular, ℙx0(Zh ζ− ∈ dy) = β(dy). 

3.2. Optimality properties of the h-transform 

The h-transform exhibits inherent optimality characteristics, underscoring its significance as a standardized method. We now illustrate that it arises as a solution to a stochastic stopping and control challenge. Within this framework, the running cost aspect can be interpreted as an effort to minimize the expected lifetime of the process while discouraging significant drifts. By contextualizing the h-transform within this stochastic control framework, we draw a connection to the KL divergence. 

Proposition 3.2. Let k(u) = r + 1/2‖u‖² and g(y) = −log h(y), examining the controlled process dZu t = (b(Zu t) + σ(Zu t)ut) dt + σ(Zu t) dWt for an admissible control u. The stochastic stopping and control problem aimed at minimizing J(u, x) = E_x[∫₀^τ k(ut) dt + g(Zu τ−)] (3.1) in both u and τ is resolved by the h-transformed process Zh with the first entrance time into the support of β serving as the stopping time. Additionally, the variation in problem (3.1) can be interpreted as the KL divergence between Zu and the h-transformed process until the lifetime. Further insights can be found in Appendix B. It is noteworthy that, in the cases we explore later, the first entrance time into the support aligns with the lifetime ζ. 

3.3. Connection to time-inversion 

In contrast to the deterministic scenario, the time reversal originating from a random moment is considerably less explored within literature. Nevertheless, in relation to the h-transform, the findings are unequivocal: for the h-transformed process Zh with a finite lifetime ζ, we examine the time-reversed process Żh s = Zh ζ−s, where 0 < s < ζ, which is killed at s = ζ. Let α denote a fixed initial distribution of Zh, and define Żh(x) = ∫ Gr(x, y) h(y) α(dy). (3.2) 

Proposition 3.3. 1. Żh shares the same distribution as Żh, specifically, dŻh s = ḃh(Żh s) dt + σ(Żh s) dŻs, where ḃh(y) = b(y) + σ(y) σ(y)⊤ ∇log Żh(y), Ż being a Brownian motion outside the support of α. 2. Żh is terminated on the support of α. 3. Starting at x, the distribution of Żh at its lifetime ζ is expressed as ℙx(Żh ζ− ∈ dy) = Gr(x, y) Żh(x) h(y) α(dy). The interpretation of time reversal in the context of the h-transform has intriguing implications. Let’s revisit the notion of a polar set: for Zh, A ⊆ I is labeled as polar if ℙx(Zh t ∈ A for some t > 0) = 0 for all x ∈ I. Common instances of polar sets for diffusions are those situated on lower-dimensional submanifolds. For example, if Zh represents a d-dimensional Brownian motion, any set with a Hausdorff dimension less than d − 2 is polar, as outlined by Mörters and Peres [28]; similarly, a related finding for general diffusions is noted in Ramasubramanian [34]. 

Proposition 3.4. Assuming the support of the initial distribution α is polar for Zh, then Żh is killed upon its first entry into the support of α. Consequently, the distribution of Żh is entirely dictated by the drift ḃh and the support of α.

1. In the scenario where β(dy) = rGr(x0, y) m(dy) (the distribution of Z evaluated at the exponential time when initiated from x0), we identify h(x) = ∫ Gr(x, y) Gr(x0, y) β(dy) = ∫ rGr(x, y) m(dy) = 1. Thus, Zh’s dynamics are congruent with that of Z, while ζ acts as an independent Exp(r)-time. The time-reversed process can be represented as Żh(x) = ∫ Gr(x, y) α(dy). 

2. In the case where β(dy) = δx1 for a certain x1 ∈ I, we derive h(x) = Gr(x, x1)/cx1, cx1 = Gr(x0, x1). Therefore, Zh amounts to an exponential bridge killed at x1, regardless of the initial position, with drift ḃh(x) = b(x) + σ(x) σ(x)⊤ ∇log Gr(x, x1). In this instance, Żh(x) equals ∫ Gr(x, y) Gr(x1, y) α(dy). 

3. When Z = W is a Brownian motion, we explore radially symmetric functions h(x) = f(|x|) of the form h(x) = ∫∂BR Gr(x, y) σR(dy), where σR signifies the surface measure on a sphere with radius R. For larger dimensions d and moderate values of |x|, it holds that ḃh(x) ≈ 2r/d (see 10.41 in [29]), indicating that the forward process Zh can be approximated using the (non-stationary) Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process dynamics dZ̃t = 2r/d ̃Z(t) dt + dWt. 

4. Proposed model 

Standard diffusion generative frameworks utilize a deterministic time horizon, resulting in time-dependent backward processes and inefficiencies in the forward process due to excessive noise application. Two viable enhancements for these models are identifiable: (1) substituting the deterministic time horizon with a stochastic one to achieve time-homogeneous backward dynamics, and (2) incorporating conditioning into the forward process to minimize the necessity for excessive noise. We simultaneously implement both adaptations within a unified framework via the aforementioned h-transform. To this end, we select an appropriative choice of the process Zh as our forward process and Żh as the backward process, as elaborated subsequently. 

4.1. Three potential implementations for unconditional sampling 

The examples from Section 3.4 directly indicate feasible realizations of our framework. Specifically, we utilize Zh as a forward process initiated within the data distribution α to derive the drift of the backward process Żh (further details will follow in ensuing sections). To acquire unconditional samples from α, suitable initial distributions for Żh are required, which can be (approximately) represented in the following examples: 

1. Long exponential time horizons: If we select an ergodic diffusion Z (e.g., an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process) and set h = 1, we can opt for a small r and allow ζ to adhere to an Exp(r) distribution. With this configuration, ℙα(Zh ζ− ∈ dy) closely aligns with the stationary distribution of Z. Thus, initializing the backward process Żh within the stationary distribution of Z (if it exists) becomes feasible. 

2. Exponential bridge: In the second scenario, the forward process Zh acts as an exponential bridge targeting a specific state x1. Here, we can draw samples from the data distribution by initiating the backward process Żh at Zh ζ− = x1. 

3. Hitting a large sphere: In this third case, if the radius R is chosen sufficiently large, ℙα(Zh ζ− ∈ dy) approximately represents a uniform distribution across the sphere, which can then serve as the initial distribution for Żh. If beneficial, the forward process may be approximated using (3.3), facilitating more direct sampling. In the idealized configuration where α is known analytically, the generation via the backward process for unconditional sampling—that is, sampling from α—follows the description found in Algorithm 1. This algorithm is derived from the findings elaborated in Section 3.3. The simulation of the backward process until the lifetime ζ can be executed using established numerical techniques, such as the Euler–Maruyama scheme. In the most generalized setting, the backward process concludes at a randomized Markovian stopping time delineated as ζ = inf{t: Aℎ t ≥ E},

4.2. The polarity hypothesis 

The target distribution α often remains unknown in practical applications. Consequently, we lack direct access to ḣ as defined in (3.2), which is essential for the utilization of the backward generative process Y = Żh. Therefore, ḣ must be inferred from the data. As mentioned in Section 3, both the drift of the backward process and the mechanism governing killing must be learned. While the killing mechanism can be expressed via a measure on the state space I (the killing measure), this adds substantial complexity to the learning process. A natural method is to conclude the backward process as soon as a meaningful element of the data distribution is encountered. Proposition 3.4 establishes a criterion for when this is viable: specifically, when the data distribution is concentrated within a polar set for the forward process, such as a lower-dimensional manifold. This aligns seamlessly with the manifold hypothesis: a well-explored concept within the literature positing that high-dimensional data typically exists on or near a low-dimensional manifold (or their union) [25], and it has been empirically substantiated for image datasets [7, 33]. Within our framework, we adopt a slightly broader assumption, termed the polarity hypothesis, asserting that the data lies within a polar set. This generalization allows us to disentangle the learning of the drift and the killing mechanism, as will be delineated in the forthcoming sections. 

4.3. Learning the drift 

We will focus on the condition that the polarity hypothesis holds, as reflected in Proposition 3.4 where the lifetime of Żh is given by the first hitting time of Ω ≔ supp α, which we initially assume to be known. Based on Proposition 3.3, we seek to fit the data to a category of time-homogeneous diffusion processes dYθ s = ḃθ(Yθ s) ds + σ(Yθ s) dWs, Yθ 0 ∼ ℙα(Zh ζ− ∈ ⋅), ḃθ(y) = b(y) + σ(y) σ(y)⊤ sθ(y), instigated by a relevant class of candidate functions ℳ = {sθ:θ∈Θ}, and for an optimization target and corresponding optimizer θ* to be determined below, we run the backward process Yθ* until a fitting stopping time. Ideally, we would like to conclude at the first hitting time of Ω by Yθ*, that is, at ζθ* = τΩ(Yθ*), indicating τA(X) = inf{t: Xt ∈ A} for a process X and a set A ⊆ ℝd. However, typically where Ω is a lower-dimensional manifold with no straightforward structure, designing a candidate class ℳ that guarantees ℙ(ζθ* < ∞) = 1 presents a challenging and highly specific endeavor (e.g., a C² submanifold Ω is polar for non-degenerate diffusions if its Hausdorff dimension does not exceed d − 2 [18, Chapter 11], [34]). Instead, for some small ε > 0, we define the closed ε-environment Ωε = {x ∈ ℝd: d(x, Ω) ≤ ε} and run Yθ* until ζθ* ε = τΩε(Yθ*). Therefore, we do not target α directly, but rather the distribution of Żh ζε for ζε = τΩε(Żh). This approach is validated for small ε > 0, since continuity of sample paths indicates that τΩε(Żh) almost surely converges to ζ as ε ↓ 0 if Ω is closed, thereby resulting in a.s. convergence limε ↓ 0 Żh ζε = Żh ζ− ∼ α. This is akin to the early termination of the generating process in standard diffusion models with deterministic time horizons, suggesting that the generative model is aimed at the original dataset blurred by a degree of small Gaussian noise. On a forward time scale, the first entrance time in Ωε of the backward process Żh aligns with the last exit time ζε of Ωε by the forward process Zh, represented as ζε = sup{t < ζ: Zh t ∈ Ωε} = ζ−ζε. As a natural optimization goal, we thus target the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the law Ż ℙε of the theoretical generating process Żh killed at ζε and the law ℙθ,ε of the parametric generating process Yθ killed at the first entrance into Ωε, specifically at ζθ ε = τΩε(Yθ). Consequently, we establish θ* ∈ arg min θ∈ℳ ℒex(θ), ℒex(θ) = E[ ∫ ζε 0 ‖sθ(Żh t) − ∇log Żh t‖² dt] = E[ ∫ ζ ζε ‖sθ(Zh t) − ∇log Żh t‖² dt], which serves as the natural analogue to the explicit score matching target in conventional diffusion models. Next, provided sufficient integrability conditions, Girsanov’s theorem implies that KL(Ż ℙε ∥ ℙθ,ε) = 1/2 E[ ∫ ζε 0 ‖σ^(-1)(Żh t)(ḃh(Żh t) − ḃθ(Żh t))‖² dt] ≤ Cσ² ℒex(θ), with Cσ = sup x ∈ ℝd ‖σ(x)‖². However, the inherent unavailability of Żh, and thus of ℒex, necessitates finding a manageable training objective comparable to ℒex. This will be established in our subsequent finding, which for our framework can be perceived as an analog to the denoising score matching loss [38] typically used in standard diffusion models.

4.4. Learning the manifold 

Now, we will address the most generalized scenario in which the polar data support Ω = supp α remains unknown. Given that the generative mechanism outlined in Algorithm 2 entails Ωε as an input, a logical strategy is to devise an estimator Ω̂ε based on the provided dataset during a preprocessing phase, followed by employing a plug-in approach to sample according to Algorithm 2. This framework is structured formally in Algorithm 3. To establish Ω̂ε based on a data sample {Yᵢ}^n_{i=1} iid ∼ α, we might enlist one of two practical methodologies: Firstly, we could target Ωε directly by initially blurring the data through Yεi = Yi + ηεi, where (ηεi)^n_{i=1} symbolizes iid noise independent from the data sample and absolutely continuous with support over B(0, ε)—for example, ηεi ∼ U(B(0, ε)). Consequently, Yεi would retain absolute continuity with support across Ωε and density πε(x) = ∫Ω πηε(x − y) α(dy). Extracting the compact support Ωε from a data sample is recognized as a thoroughly investigated statistical challenge. The most prevalent strategies include plug-in estimators [10] that implement Ω̂ε = { π̂ε > δn} for a non-parametric estimator π̂ε of πε and a tuning parameter δn → 0, or the straightforward yet intuitive Devroye–Wise estimator [13] identified by Ω̂ε = n ⋃_{i=1} B(Yεi, δn). The minimax optimality of these estimators concerning metrics such as the Hausdorff metric or the symmetric difference volume has been established under various assumptions towards the data density πε and the geometry of Ωε [5, 10, 11, 23, 27]. However, these rates generally significantly decrease exponentially relative to the ambient data dimension d, which underpins the motivation for the second method that permits exploitation of the lower-dimensional structure inherent to Ω. For this alternative approach, rather than directly estimating Ωε, we may first create an estimator Ω̂ of the actual data support Ω from the unaltered data sample (Yᵢ)^n_{i=1} and subsequently set Ω̂ε = (Ω̂)ε. This process may be more favorable for high-dimensional datasets, given that substantial advancements have been made in recent years regarding statistical theory and algorithmic implementation for estimating support of distributions concentrated on lower-dimensional manifolds. Important contributions that furnish estimators Ω̂ with confident convergence rates solely based on smoothness s and the dimensionality d′ < d of the data manifold include [1–3, 19, 22, 26]. Although computationally more complex than the straightforward estimators based on noise-infused data discussed previously, estimators from [1–3] are both constructive and implementable.

General Transfer Learning The concept of transfer learning discussed in the previous section can be applied more broadly. We have presented a pioneering category of diffusion models based on Doob’s ℎ-transform. This theoretical framework offers a comprehensive and flexible base for time-homogeneous diffusion models, removing the need to incorporate artificial time dependencies, thus improving interpretability. A significant advancement in our model is the formulation of the polarity hypothesis, which closely resembles the manifold hypothesis prevalent in machine learning. This attribute facilitates an intuitive and effective method for deciding when to end the denoising process, thereby tackling a vital issue in the realization of our generative model. Additionally, our framework introduces a methodological simplification for learning the dynamics of the denoising process. In contrast to standard diffusion models that require the estimation of temporally inhomogeneous dynamics, our approach divides the tasks of estimating the data manifold and acquiring a time-independent backward drift via denoising score matching. This creates an intriguing connection between recent developments in manifold learning and denoising diffusion generative modeling, potentially reducing both computational and modeling complexities. The time-homogeneous characteristic of the model presents numerous opportunities for practical implementations. While its effectiveness will rely on the specific demands of each application, the theoretical groundwork laid out here serves as a solid basis for experimental investigations, particularly regarding transfer learning.
