**Greedy Stein Variational Gradient Descent: An Algorithmic Approach for Wave Prospection Problems**

*Jos´e L. Varona-Santana1, Marcos A. Capistr´an*  
aCentro de Investigaci´on en Matem´aticas A.C, De Jalisco s/n, Valenciana, 36023 MX, Guanajuato, M´exico  
bCentro de Investigaci´on en Matem´aticas A.C, Parque Cient´ıfico y Tecnol´ogico de Yucat´an Km 5.5 Carretera Sierra Papaca, 97302 MX, Yucat´an, M´exico

**Abstract**  
In this work, we introduce a Variational Inference algorithm aimed at approximating posterior distributions. Building on previous techniques, we present the Gradient-Steered Stein Variational Gradient Descent (G-SVGD) method. This approach features a new loss function that merges a weighted gradient with the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) to improve both convergence speed and accuracy. The learning rate is derived via suboptimal minimization of this loss function within a gradient descent structure. We compare the G-SVGD method to the traditional Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD) technique, utilizing the ADAM optimizer for adapting the learning rate, and also juxtapose it with the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method. We evaluate performance across two wave prospection models representing low-contrast and high-contrast subsurface conditions. To ensure sturdy numerical solutions in the forward model solver, we employ a five-point operator, while an adjoint method enhances the precision of gradient calculations regarding the log posterior. Our results indicate that G-SVGD accelerates convergence and enhances performance in scenarios where gradient assessment is computationally intensive. The abstract emphasizes the algorithm’s relevance in wave prospection models and its potential for wider applications in Bayesian inference. We also address the advantages and limitations of G-SVGD, underscoring its role in boosting computational efficiency in uncertainty quantification.  
**Keywords:** gradient descent, learning rate, Bayesian model, surrogate model, full wave inversion, SVGD, G-SVGD

**1. Introduction**  
Our study delves into geophysical applications of wave prospecting models in one-dimensional contexts, concentrating on deducing the velocity field in both low-contrast and high-contrast stratified materials. We propose a Bayesian model that encapsulates the density of the parameter space, offering insights into the velocity profile. Sampling from the posterior distribution is pivotal in Bayesian inference but presents notable computational hurdles, particularly within high-dimensional parameter domains. While standard approaches like Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) can be computationally taxing, Variational Inference (VI) provides an alternative by approximating the posterior through optimization, thereby minimizing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between a candidate distribution and the posterior. VI methods have gained traction in machine learning and artificial intelligence due to their scalability and efficiency. These approaches often leverage gradient descent to optimize the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO). *Ruder (2016)* offers a detailed survey of gradient descent techniques, emphasizing their relevance for optimizing complex models. The introduction of Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD) by *Liu and Wang (2016)* presented a particle-based VI method that iteratively updates particles to approximate a target posterior distribution. Utilizing functional gradient descent, SVGD aims to minimize KL divergence through Stein's identity and kernelized Stein discrepancy, combining smooth particle transformations with Stein's operator-derived gradients for efficient posterior approximation and guaranteed convergence. The boosting variational inference (BVI) approach described by *Guo et al. (2016)* seeks to enhance posterior approximation by adding components incrementally, employing gradient boosting and Taylor expansion to derive functional gradients, and using stochastic Newton's method for learning rate estimation. Certain methodologies grounded in minimizing KL divergence through ELBO optimization—like *Blei et al. (2017)*—show their acceleration and scalability compared to MCMC, particularly for intricate models and extensive datasets. Key techniques include mean-field VI, which simplifies assumptions of independence among latent variables, and extensions like Coordinate Ascent Variational Inference (CAVI) and Stochastic Variational Inference (SVI), which enhance computational efficiency by scaling well with massive data. More sophisticated methods, like SVGD and boosting techniques, bolster flexibility and efficacy in high-dimensional parameter spaces. Recent works, such as *Locatello et al. (2018)*, present enhancements to the Frank-Wolfe algorithm to approximate posterior distributions by optimizing within the convex hull of a tested density family. Meanwhile, *Egorov et al. (2019)* proposed the MaxEntropy Pursuit Variational Inference approach, which addresses the constraints defined by a test distribution family through the incorporation of Maximum Entropy regularization for improved optimization flexibility. 

This backdrop sets the stage for our development of a VI algorithm that possesses theoretical convergence guarantees. Our work builds upon the foundational hypotheses of *Liu and Wang (2016)* while leveraging insights regarding ELBO from *Blei et al. (2017)*. We significantly focus on three crucial areas identified in previous literature: the initial particle set, learning rate selection, and conditions for convergence termination. By employing Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) as the test distribution, we aim to enhance the convergence behavior towards a Gaussian distribution centered around local posterior modes. To achieve this, we devise a loss function incorporating both the ELBO and the gradient of the log-posterior, further improving robustness in gradient evaluation by utilizing an adjoint method that confines error to the numerical precision of the PDE solver. To minimize numerical inaccuracies, we leverage the five-point operator to refine derivative approximations. Our method identifies a near-optimal learning rate through the minimization of our proposed loss function, ensuring efficient convergence while balancing accuracy with computational effectiveness. The structure of this document includes a theoretical framework alongside numerical results: In Section 2, we delve into the theory underpinning our algorithm, addressing the wave equation and the relevant solution methods, including a description of the five-point operator derived from Taylor’s polynomial. Additionally, we discuss the distinctions between the surrogate and continuous models in our forward investigations, followed by considerations on the weighted gradient and Bayesian inference via Variational Gradient Descent. The section culminates with a detailed exposition of our loss function, the Greedy Stein Variational Algorithm, and our adjoint method's contextual application. Section 3 provides insights into our numerical findings. Initially, we compare derivative approximations across traditional finite difference and the five-point operator. Subsequently, we deliver numerical results pertaining to our methodology as applied across two wave prospecting models.

**2. Theoretical Framework**  
In this segment, we delineate the theoretical underpinnings of our project. We begin by examining the wave equation in both homogeneous and non-homogeneous media, addressing the principles underlying wave superposition. The five-point operator plays a crucial role in the numerical approximation of first and second derivatives, facilitating accurate solutions. Following this, we elucidate the forward models developed for our case studies, transitioning to discussions around Stein Variational Gradient Descent, the gradient descent methodology, and the significance of ELBO in our strategy. The section concludes with a thorough examination of the loss function, a comprehensive outline of the G-SVGD algorithm, and an introduction to the adjoint method as it applies to our wave prospection models. 

**2.1. Stratified Medium**  
Throughout this document, we define the following concepts: *Stratified medium*: A non-homogeneous medium comprised of diverse material types, exhibiting variability in physical properties across spatial points. *High-contrast stratified medium*: A material setup where properties undergo drastic shifts across even small spatial regions. *Low-contrast stratified medium*: A scenario characterized by gradual alterations in material properties. We aim to investigate these transitions, particularly focusing on velocity fields, which for a high-contrast stratified layer may be denoted by a piecewise function that lacks smooth transitions due to material discontinuities. High-contrast scenarios can be conceptualized as compositions of low-contrast layers, where local regions assumed to be homogeneous fail to exhibit smooth transitions in wave propagation. In contrast, low-contrast stratified layers facilitate smooth variations in transverse wave velocity, with wave characteristics transitioning smoothly across space.

**2.2. Wave Equation**  
To model the velocity field of waves across these layers, we utilize the wave equation. With it as the governing framework, we develop wave prospection models that depict static materials subjected to external perturbative forces represented as waves entering the structure at defined boundaries. When we state "uninterrupted," we imply the absence of any additional disturbances impinging on the system. For high-contrast contexts, we model each homogeneous subregion disturbed by waves propagating in opposing directions while treating the entire structure as a continuous amalgamation of these subregions to analyze wave reflection, transmission, and propagation characteristics. Low-contrast scenarios are modeled differently, concentrating on a uniform region influenced by a wave arriving from one boundary and exiting unobstructed through another. This creates an opportunity to investigate the wave dynamics within a non-homogeneous setting while ensuring that the discrete approximation of the differential model aligns with theoretical expectations. Our modeling adheres to the Displacement formulation of the one-dimensional wave equation, simplifying computations by excluding damping terms.

**2.2.1. One-Dimensional Wave Equation in a Homogeneous Layer**  
In the high-contrast stratified model, we conceptualize a static layer where external forces induce disturbances that propagate without interruption, exiting through boundaries. To mathematically represent this scenario, the corresponding displacement-based formulations are:

∂2_t u_r − c²∂2_x u_r = 0, x ∈ (0, L), t ∈ (0, T]  
u_r(x, 0) = 0, x ∈ [0, L]  
∂_t u_r(x, 0) = 0, x ∈ [0, L]  
u_r(0, t) = F_l(t), t > 0  
∂_t u_r(L, t) = -c∂_x u_r(L, t), t > 0 

Similarly, for another homogeneous layer:

∂2_t u_l − c²∂2_x u_l = 0, x ∈ (0, L), t ∈ (0, T]  
u_l(x, 0) = 0, x ∈ [0, L]  
∂_t u_l(x, 0) = 0, x ∈ [0, L]  
∂_t u_l(0, t) = c∂_x u_l(0, t), t > 0  
u_l(L, t) = F_r(t), t > 0 

Systems (2) and (3) encompass the same static structure responding to external forces F_l and F_r. They model wave interactions across homogeneous layers through absorbing boundaries. The first-order open boundary conditions are derived from equations found in *Buckman et al. (2012)*, facilitating modeling based on the principle of superposition, which holds that when two or more waves traverse the same medium, their displacements result in an additive interference pattern. If ul and ur represent waveforms in this model, the resultant wave can be expressed as:

u(x, t) = u_r(x, t) + u_l(x, t)  

**2.2.2. One-Dimensional Wave Equation in Non-Homogeneous Layer**  
In our subsequent modeling, we consider a non-homogeneous layer. In this case, the transverse wave velocity is not constant but rather spatially dependent, necessitating adaptations of the wave equation system. The formulation for waves perturbing a non-homogeneous static medium—acting through one open boundary while the other serves as a source—is characterized as follows:

∂²_t u − ∇ · (c²(x) ∇ u) = 0, x ∈ (0, L), t ∈ (0, T]  
u(x, 0) = 0, x ∈ [0, L]  
∂_t u(x, 0) = 0, x ∈ [0, L]  
∂_t u(0, t) = F_l(t), t > 0  
u(L, t) = -c(L)∂_x u(L, t), t > 0  

This equation represents a hyperbolic partial differential structure sensitive to discontinuities in the velocity field, necessitating meticulous considerations for numerical solutions.

**2.3. The Five Points Finite Differences Operator**  
The finite difference method serves as a fundamental numerical strategy for approximating the solutions to differential equations via the estimation of function derivatives. The method's precision in wave and transport equation applications has been firmly validated by various authors, including *Quarteroni et al. (2006)*, *Quarteroni and Valli (2008)*, *Langtangen and Linge (2016)*, and *Igel (2017)*. This numerical approach is particularly prevalent in computational seismology, notably using a five-point operator for spatial derivative approximations. When applying this strategy to the wave equation, two considerations are pivotal: the Courant number—and the spatial resolution required to attain the desired approximation accuracy. Conventional finite difference techniques, such as centered difference and backward difference methods, achieve third-order derivative approximations based on Taylor polynomial expansions. To characterize these derivatives and coefficients, let α_i denote coefficients in a column vector, and T_i represent a corresponding column vector capturing Taylor polynomial evaluations. The n-th derivative and coefficients for the five-point operator are subsequently derived from Taylor polynomial representations. 

**2.4. Forward Model**  
This section articulates the forward models devised for each scenario. 

**2.4.1. Forward Model for the High-Contrast Stratified Medium**  
In Section 2.2.1, we delineate the wave equation in a homogeneous layer using the wave superposition principle. In the high-contrast stratified medium, we conceptualize our medium as a composite of layers, each layer being homogeneous. Thus, we define the solution as a sum of solutions for each partition.

Let S represent a continuous one-dimensional spatial domain, and {s_i} be a partition of S, where intersections of each continuous partition only occur at shared boundaries. Therefore, S = ∪_i∈{i}s_i and s_i ∩ s_(i+1) = ∂s^+_i ≡ ∂s^-_(i+1). Henceforth, the solution within the stratified medium can be articulated as the aggregate of solutions across these partitions. To preserve elastic properties, specific conditions governing wave behavior must be observed at the common boundaries. In *Stein and Wysession (2009)*, the authors elucidated interaction dynamics at each partition border, largely in terms of material density properties ρ and wave velocity c. These insights can be reframed to solely consider wave velocity alterations, thus gaining the following expressions. Considering partitions s_i and s_(i+1), we define parameters for the wave amplitudes as follows. With the incoming wave’s amplitude from s_i to s_(i+1) denoted as A, B represents the reflected wave, and C signifies the transmission amplitude. The reflection coefficients R_(i,i+1), R_(i+1,i) and transmission coefficients T_(i,i+1), T_(i+1,i) are determined by:

R_(i,i+1) = (c_(i+1) - c_i)/(c_i + c_(i+1))  
T_(i,i+1) = 2 * c_(i+1)/(c_i + c_(i+1))  
R_(i+1,i) = -R_(i,i+1)  
T_(i+1,i) = 2 - T_(i,i+1) 

These relations enable calculations of coefficients essential for characterizing wave behaviors at boundaries.   

**2.5. Stein Variational Gradient Descent**  
The algorithm outlined by *Liu and Wang (2016)* presents a methodology to transition a random sample from an initial distribution to a target distribution, utilizing Stein’s operator for approximating KL divergence. However, incorporating this framework into parameter identification linked with a differential equation necessitates heightened attentiveness to parameter space constraints. This section delineates our strategy for leveraging Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD) for parameter identification challenges. We commence by detailing methods for learning rate selection before addressing constraints inherent to support handling.

**2.5.1. Learning rate or stepsize**  
Choosing the learning rate is pivotal within gradient descent methods, as it greatly influences both convergence speed and accuracy. *Liu and Wang (2016)* elucidate the role of step size in approximating a target distribution via linear transformations of test distributions. Specifically, T(x) = x + αϕ(x) denotes the perturbation direction (ϕ) alongside the perturbation magnitude (α). To maintain the map’s invertibility, it’s critical to keep |α| sufficiently low. 

Methods to select the step size can encompass numerous strategies. A review by *Ruder (2016)* details various optimizing techniques applicable in different machine learning contexts. One prominent method is the ADAM approach suggested by *Kingma and Ba (2014)*, which combines the strengths of AdaGrad and RMSProp. ADAM yields adaptive learning rates for parameters by tracking moving averages of gradients and their squares, ensuring rapid convergence while remaining robust against noise and sparse data. This method forms our basis for step size in Stein Variational Gradient Descent, yielding Algorithm 1. To derive the learning rate, we pursue suboptimal solutions via optimization.

**2.6. The Evidence Lower Bound**  
The Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) quantifies the test distribution’s proximity to a target distribution, structured as follows:

ELBO(q) = E[log p(z)] + E[log p(x | z)] − E[log q(z)], 

which can be reformulated as: 

ELBO(q) = E[log p(x | z)] - KL(q(z) || p(z)). 

Here, the expectations relate to the test distribution q. The symbols denote the parameter vector (z), observation vector (x), and KL divergence.

To estimate the expectation for E[log p(x | z)], we can use MCMC integration. 

Thus, we characterize ELBO as:

ELBO(q) ≈ (1/N) Σ^N_i=1 log p(x | z_i) - ... 

**2.7. Loss Function**  
The purpose of optimization is to minimize the total loss throughout the dataset, ensuring that predictions better align with actual values. Through iterative adjustment of model parameters, the gradient of the loss function governs the direction of descent. By steering parameters in the opposite direction, gradient descent effectively reduces the loss value. In the context of variational inference, loss functions commonly take the form of negative ELBO. Hence, maximizing the ELBO ensures close approximation of the true posterior by balancing likelihood with a regularization term enforcing prior constraints. Our loss function synthesizes the qualities of gradient descent, the weighted gradient from *Liu and Wang (2016)*, and ELBO, expressed as:

L(Θ, q) = (1 - ω) ||∇_x log (Θ, y)||_∞ - ω ELBO(q).  

Here, Θ encompasses particle sets, y denotes observations, and q is the test distribution. The ω parameter mediates between gradient-driven optimization and posterior alignment.

**3. Results**  
This section unpacks the numerical results accrued from applying the outlined methodologies to wave prospecting models exhibiting similar properties. An initial step involved identifying the spatial resolution for precise discrete approximations that mirror the continuous physical model. Following that, we outlined numerical experiments, capturing the efficacy of our G-SVGD approach relative to benchmark methods such as t-walk and A-SVGD.

**4. Discussion**  
Our research centered on wave propagation behaviors in both high- and low-contrast stratified media with critical implications in geophysical contexts. Accurate modeling of velocity fields can significantly enhance subsurface interpretation, facilitating advancements in seismic exploration and resource assessment.

summary: E-processes enable hypothesis testing with ongoing data collection while maintaining Type I error control. However, when testing multiple hypotheses simultaneously, current $e$-value based multiple testing methods such as e-BH are not invariant to the order in which data are gathered for the different $e$-processes. This can lead to undesirable situations, e.g., where a hypothesis rejected at time $t$ is no longer rejected at time $t+1$ after choosing to gather more data for one or more $e$-processes unrelated to that hypothesis. We argue that multiple testing methods should always work with suprema of $e$-processes. We provide an example to illustrate that e-BH does not control this FDR at level $\alpha$ when applied to suprema of $e$-processes. We show that adjusters can be used to ensure FDR-sup control with e-BH under arbitrary dependence.

contents:
**Carefree Multiple Testing with E-Processes**  
Yury Tavyrikov1, Jelle J. Goeman2, and Rianne de Heide∗3  
1Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam 2Leiden University Medical Centre 3University of Twente  
February 3, 2025  

**Abstract**  
E-processes facilitate hypothesis testing while data collection is in progress, ensuring control over Type I error. However, when conducting multiple hypothesis tests concurrently, prevailing e-value based methods for multiple testing like e-BH demonstrate sensitivity to the sequence of data collection across various e-processes. This order dependency can result in unanticipated outcomes, such as a hypothesis that is rejected at time t being accepted at time t + 1 simply due to the decision to gather additional data for one or more e-processes that do not pertain to that hypothesis. We propose that multiple testing procedures should consistently operate using the suprema of e-processes. An illustrative example highlights that the application of e-BH does not guarantee control of the False Discovery Rate (FDR) at level α when employed on the suprema of e-processes. We demonstrate that adjusters can be implemented to ensure control of FDR-sup with e-BH, regardless of dependence structure.

**1 Introduction**  
E-processes constitute a novel conceptual framework for hypothesis assessment. Specifically, an e-process is defined as a nonnegative stochastic process (Et)t≥0, initialized at E0 = 1, and is continuously updated in response to newly acquired information. If the null hypothesis H0 holds true, the process does not increase in expectation: EP (Eτ) ≤ 1 for every stopping time τ, and for all P ∈ H0. As a result, we can reject H0 at any time point t whenever Et ≥ 1/α, effectively maintaining Type I error control. Under the assumption that H0 is valid, Ville’s inequality (as referenced in Ramdas and Wang [2024], Fact 6.4) ensures that the e-processes satisfy the condition P  sup t∈N Et ≥ 1/α  ≤ α. (1) Unlike p-values, e-processes allow repeated evaluations until a rejection is achieved at some time t, enabling researchers to amass data for as long as necessary. Significantly, while the definition of e-processes incorporates a stopping time, the Type I error control property (1) hinges upon the process's supremum. Consequently, data collection becomes a non-regretful endeavor: researchers can conduct further data gathering without concerns about previous decisions. For instance, if a researcher opts to collect Et+1 prior to evaluating Et, they can still reject H0 based on the inequality (1) if they discover Et ≥ 1/α but later find Et+1 < 1/α, effectively nullifying the effect of gathering Et+1, provided α was predetermined (or even in scenarios where it wasn’t, as suggested in Koning [2024], Grünwald [2024]). When multiple hypotheses are at stake, however, multiple testing principles become relevant. The existing literature on e-based multiple testing is extensive, with the e-BH procedure [Wang and Ramdas, 2022] being particularly noteworthy for generalizing the Benjamini-Hochberg approach to regulate the False Discovery Rate (FDR). Nevertheless, most research has primarily concentrated on e-value based multiple testing, which involves singular instances of e-processes, meaning random variables E where E(E) ≤ 1 if H0 is upheld. When assessing parallel e-processes E1 t , . . . , EK t, as we will demonstrate, e-BH ensures that sup t∈N FDR �E1 t , . . . , EK t  ≤ α. (2) Regrettably, data gathering associated with this guarantee (2) is not entirely without concern. Take, for instance, the case of K = 2 e-values: e-BH rejects hypotheses for which the e-value surpasses 2/α, and both hypotheses if both exceed 1/α. If, at time t, it is true that 1/α ≤ E1 t < 2/α and E2 t < 1/α, yet when further data is collected for both e-processes, the scenario might shift to E1 t+1 < 1/α and 1/α ≤ E2 t+1 < 2/α. At this point, the researcher might regret their decision to gather additional data for E1 since (2) no longer allows for any rejection, whereas it would have supported the rejection of both null hypotheses had the researcher opted to halt at E1, retaining E1 t+1 = E1 t. The absence of the carefree nature significantly complicates experimental design. To maintain a carefree data collection process, researchers should always have the option to revert any e-process to its prior time point. The optimal reversion should be to the highest value reached up to that point. Thus, a carefree procedure should ensure that sup s∈N FDR(max t≤s E1 t , . . . , max t≤s EK t ) = FDR(sup t∈N E1 t , . . . , sup t∈N EK t ) ≤ α. (3) We contend that (3), the FDR-sup, represents the correct criterion for FDR in the context of e-processes. In this work, we explore the development of procedures that can control (3).

**2 FDR Control with E-Processes**  

**2.1 The E-BH Procedure**  
Let H1, . . . , HK represent K hypotheses, and denote their indices with K = {1, . . . , K}. Let P ∗ represent the actual data-generating probability measure. For each k ∈ K, Hk is regarded as true if P ∗ ∈ Hk. Denote N as the set of indices corresponding to true null hypotheses and let K0 represent its size. Each hypothesis Hk is linked to an e-value Ek. When only a single observation is available for each hypothesis’ e-value, it has been established [Wang and Ramdas, 2022] that the classical Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure can be adapted to accommodate e-values. A pivotal advantage of this e-BH procedure is its ability to maintain FDR control across any dependency configuration among the e-values, contrasting with the traditional BH procedure, which relies on the positive regression dependence assumption for a subset (PRDS). Both the conventional BH and the Benjamini-Yekutieli (BY) procedures can be seen as special instances of the e-BH procedure.

**2.2 E-BH with E-Processes**  
Formally, a non-negative process E is categorized as an e-process when E[Eτ] ≤ 1 for any stopping time τ, with the expectation calculated under any distribution where null hypotheses apply. Each hypothesis Hk for k ∈ K is linked with an e-process (Ek t )t≥0, and let τ1, τ2, . . . , τK denote arbitrary stopping instances. Define Sk = Ek τk as the halted e-processes.  

*Procedure 1 (Naive E-BH with E-Processes).* Let S[k] denote the k-th ordered statistic of S1, . . . , SK, organized by size such that S[1] is the largest halted e-process. The halted e-BH procedure G(α): [0, ∞]K → 2K thus rejects hypotheses with the largest k∗ se halted e-processes, where k∗ se = max (k ∈ K : S[k] ≥ 1/(α K k)).  

**Fact 1.** The halted e-BH procedure, when applied to e-processes with arbitrary dependencies, maintains an FDR of at most K0α/K. Given that a halted e-process has an expectation under the null bound by one, i.e., ESk = EEk τk ≤ 1, the set of halted e-processes {Sk}k∈K constitutes a set of e-variables. Therefore, this procedure effectively aligns with the standard e-BH procedure for the halted e-processes {Sk}k∈K, and the FDR guarantee [Wang and Ramdas, 2022] remains intact.

**2.3 Related Work**  
Research on online multiple testing has been approached classically using p-values [Fischer et al., 2024] as well as e-values [Fischer and Ramdas, 2024a,b; Xu and Ramdas, 2023]. Here, the term "online" refers to the dimension of the hypothesis space: time points represent the introduction of new hypotheses. To our knowledge, the only work examining multiple testing with e-values in a sequential data context is [Xu and Ramdas, 2023], introducing a doubly sequential framework. In the realm of p-values, interim analyses and group-sequential multiple testing have been addressed, such as in [Sarkar et al., 2019] regarding FDR; however, to the best of our knowledge, there is no existing research on methods that maintain validity across different points in time.

**3 FDR with the Running Maximum of an E-Process**  
We maintain that multiple testing methods for e-processes should display a carefree characteristic, meaning that sequential data collection should not result in regrets concerning earlier rejections. This requires procedures to incorporate the running maximum of the e-process: M k t = max1≤s≤t Ek s. It is clear that with such a procedure, the set of rejected hypotheses forms a monotonically non-decreasing set. Consequently, if a hypothesis is rejected at a given time point, it will remain rejected in all future evaluations. This inherently fulfills the accept-to-reject property described in [Fischer and Ramdas, 2024b]: a multiple testing method that can convert previous non-rejections into a rejection later, without the reverse occurring. While prior discussions focused on adding hypotheses rather than data points, we assert that this accept-to-reject principle should be regarded as a favorable trait within any multiple testing methodology.

*Procedure 2 (Running Maximum E-BH Procedure).* Define M [k] t for k ∈ K as the k-th ordered statistic of M1 t , . . . , MK t, organized in descending order such that M [1] t is the largest maximum from an e-process. The halted e-BH procedure G(α): [0, ∞]K → 2K subsequently rejects hypotheses that correspond to the largest k∗ m maxima of e-processes, with k∗ m = max (k ∈ K : M [k] t ≥ 1/(α K k)).  

Although the running maximum of an e-process is not inherently an e-process itself (for further details, see Choe and Ramdas [2024]), the assurance of FDR control for this procedure under independent e-processes is straightforward. This is fundamentally due to the fact that the inverse of the running maximum of the e-processes, represented as 1/Mk, constitutes a valid p-process [Choe and Ramdas, 2024]. Thus, employing this procedure on the running maximum is tantamount to utilizing the classical BH approach. However, introducing arbitrary dependencies among e-processes will result in the loss of FDR control accessible via the e-BH procedure, as evidenced by the subsequent proposition.  

**Proposition 1.** The running maximum e-BH procedure, when applied to e-processes with arbitrary dependence, does not maintain FDR control at level α.

**3.1 Proof of Proposition 1**  
We present a counterexample demonstrating that the e-BH procedure, applied to the running maxima of e-processes, fails to control FDR at the designated level α. We will evaluate FDR numerically. Consider two true null hypotheses associated with corresponding e-processes E1 t and E2 t, defined as: E1 t = X1 0 tY s=1 e1 s, E2 t = X2 0 tY s=1 e2 s, where initial values (X1 0, X2 0) are distributed as: (X1 0, X2 0) ∼ ( (0, 0), with probability 1 − 2α, (1, 2α, 1(2α)), with probability 2α, and the increments (e1 s, e2 s) distributed as: { (-1/2, 1/2), with probability 1/3, (-2, 1/2), with probability 1/3, (-1/2, 2), with probability 1/3. The variables X1 0, X2 0, along with all e1 s, e2 s are independent. It is easily verified that the expected values of E1 t and E2 t equal 1 at all instances, i.e., E[E1 t] = E[E2 t] = 1, confirming both E1 t and E2 t qualify as valid e-processes. However, the processes E1 t and E2 t exhibit dependence since the random variables e1 s and e2 s, as well as X1 0 and X2 0, are correlated. Given that the null hypotheses are valid, the FDR-sup equals the likelihood of rejecting at least one hypothesis. This corresponds to the events: M 1 t ≥ 2α, M 2 t ≥ 2α, or both M 1 t , M 2 t ≥ 1α, where M k t = max1≤s≤t Ek s as previously defined. To validate this example, simulations of the specified e-processes were performed (check the code in Appendix B). The simulation outcomes reveal that in this scenario, the FDR of the e-BH procedure applied to the running maxima approaches 1.08α. In our simulations, we utilized M = 10^6 Monte Carlo iterations. Thus, employing the standard error formula √[p(1 − p)/M], we found the estimated standard deviation of the error to be approximately 0.001. This indicates that when utilizing running maxima, additional adjustments or calibrations are essential to guarantee adequate FDR control.

**4 Adjusting Running Maxima**  
As Proposition 1 indicates that e-BH does not securely manage the FDR-sup, one approach is to employ adjusters that can modify the running maximum process into an e-process. Adjusters were foreseen in the realm of option pricing [Dawid et al., 2011a] and game-theoretic probability [Dawid et al., 2011b; Shafer et al., 2011], safeguarding against capital or evidence loss, and were discussed in [Choe and Ramdas, 2024] as means to amalgamate evidence across various filtrations. An acceptable adjuster, as posited by Choe and Ramdas [2024], is an increasing function A: [1, ∞] → [0, ∞] if it fulfills the criteria of right-continuity, A(∞) = limE→∞ A(E) = ∞, and  ∫ ∞ 1 A(E)/E² dE = 1. Several examples already exist in the aforementioned literature, and they may go by names like lookback adjuster, capital calibrator, martingale calibrator, or simply adjusters. If M k t = sups≤t Es represents the running maximum of an e-process pertaining to a set of null hypotheses H0, then (A(M k t ))t≥0 also qualifies as an e-process for H0. The adjusted process remains non-decreasing, ensuring that researchers will never regret additional evidence collection.

**4.1 FDR-sup Control with the Adjusted Running Maximum**  
**Theorem 1.** The e-BH procedure, when applied to the adjusted running maxima of e-processes, maintains control of FDR-sup at level K0α/K. One method to validate this is to follow the classical proof structure established by Wang and Ramdas [2022], which is elaborated in Appendix A.

**4.2 Example: E-BH with the Adjusted Running Maximum**  
Two examples of admissible adjusters are: A1(E) = E - 1 - log E/log² E, and A2(E) = √(E - 1). (4) Figure 1 depicts an instance of running e-BH using the running maximum of an e-process, adjusted by the functions stated in (4). Complete code for generating these visualizations can be found in Appendix B. We performed simulations to assess the efficacy of three procedures: standard e-BH, running maximum e-BH, and adjusted running maximum e-BH. This simulation involved 200 hypotheses, wherein the null hypothesis (H0) posits a normal distribution with mean µ = 0, while the alternative hypothesis (H1) presumes µ = 0.1. Data for each hypothesis are sequentially generated, resulting in a time series of observations. Dependencies among the hypotheses were incorporated via a predetermined correlation matrix for the multivariate normal distributions for X1 t , X2 t , . . . , XK t. Each simulation generated T = 2000 observations for every hypothesis, and performance metrics (including FDR, power, and number of rejections) were averaged across M = 10000 repetitions. This methodological setup enables an assessment of the efficiency and FDR management of the three approaches amidst a dependent data framework. Results show that standard e-BH applied to the running maximum does not meet the α level. Known for its conservative nature [Wang and Ramdas, 2022; Lee and Ren, 2024; Xu and Ramdas, 2024], e-BH tends to maintain FDR control, which explains the observed performance despite Proposition 1's claims regarding its limitations in general scenarios. It is also evident that the adjusted maximum processes consistently remain below the α threshold, albeit at the expense of power. Strategies such as conditional calibration [Lee and Ren, 2024] or stochastic rounding [Xu and Ramdas, 2024] could potentially mitigate power loss; nonetheless, this remains a significant limitation in the context of establishing FDR-sup control.

**5 Conclusion**  
We have put forth the notion that multiple testing frameworks predicated on e-processes should operate with a carefree perspective, implying that researchers ought not to forgo any rejections due to the decision to accumulate additional data across multiple e-processes. Absent this carefree aspect, experimental design becomes considerably intricate, with crucial decisions on data gathering for specific e-processes bearing substantial implications. For multiple testing processes to remain carefree, they must function based on the running maxima of e-processes. Although these maxima are not e-processes by nature, they can be converted into e-processes through the application of adjusters. However, this adjustment incurs a cost, particularly regarding power.

name of paper: What is causal about causal models and representations?
author: gpt-4o
summary: Causal Bayesian networks are 'causal' models since they make predictions about interventional distributions. To connect such causal model predictions to real-world outcomes, we must determine which actions in the world correspond to which interventions in the model. For example, to interpret an action as an intervention on a treatment variable, the action will presumably have to a) change the distribution of treatment in a way that corresponds to the intervention, and b) not change other aspects, such as how the outcome depends on the treatment; while the marginal distributions of some variables may change as an effect. We introduce a formal framework to make such requirements for different interpretations of actions as interventions precise. We prove that the seemingly natural interpretation of actions as interventions is circular: Under this interpretation, every causal Bayesian network that correctly models the observational distribution is trivially also interventionally valid, and no action yields empirical data that could possibly falsify such a model. We prove an impossibility result: No interpretation exists that is non-circular and simultaneously satisfies a set of natural desiderata. Instead, we examine non-circular interpretations that may violate some desiderata and show how this may in turn enable the falsification of causal models. By rigorously examining how a causal Bayesian network could be a 'causal' model of the world instead of merely a mathematical object, our formal framework contributes to the conceptual foundations of causal representation learning, causal discovery, and causal abstraction, while also highlighting some limitations of existing approaches.

contents: What attributes make causal models and representations ‘causal’? Frederik Hytting Jørgensen, Luigi Gresele, and Sebastian Weichwald Copenhagen Causality Lab, Department of Mathematical Sciences, and Pioneer Centre for AI, University of Copenhagen, Denmark Abstract Causal Bayesian networks are termed ‘causal’ models because they offer predictions regarding interventional distributions. To bridge the gap between these causal model predictions and actual outcomes in the real world, it is essential to identify which actions correspond to which interventions in the model. For instance, to consider an action as an intervention on a treatment variable, that action must likely a) alter the treatment distribution in a manner that aligns with the intervention and b) leave other aspects unchanged, such as the dependence of the outcome on the treatment; even though the marginal distributions of certain variables may change as a result. We propose a formal framework to specify these requirements for various interpretations of actions as interventions. Our findings reveal that the apparent interpretation of actions as interventions is circular: under this interpretation, every causal Bayesian network that accurately depicts the observational distribution is consequently interventionally valid, and no action produces empirical evidence that could potentially refute such a model. We establish an impossibility result, indicating that no interpretation is both non-circular and satisfies a set of natural desiderata simultaneously. Instead, we explore non-circular interpretations that may compromise some desiderata and demonstrate how this could facilitate the refutation of causal models. By systematically investigating how a causal Bayesian network can serve as a ‘causal’ model of the real world, rather than merely a mathematical construct, our formal framework enhances the foundational concepts of causal representation learning, causal discovery, and causal abstraction, while also underscoring certain limitations present in existing methods. 1 Introduction Causal Bayesian networks serve as mathematical frameworks that generate multiple distributions over a collection of random variables [Spirtes et al., 2001, Pearl, 2009, Peters et al., 2017]. A causal Bayesian network outlines one primary distribution, known as the observational distribution, along with a method for obtaining interventional distributions. Thus, a causal Bayesian network acts as a succinct mathematical representation of several distributions categorized by interventions. Engaging in causal reasoning through causal models seems intuitive once we assign names to the variables in the model that correspond to real-world entities they seek to capture. The notion of ‘intervention’ is suggestive, allowing us to utilize interventions on model variables to infer actions that alter the relevant real-world entities. However, without explicitly delineating the correspondence between model interventions and actions, we risk blurring the distinction between a mathematical model and its real-world affirmation. This ambiguity leads us to question what predictions the model generates about the consequences of actions in the real world and how interventional predictions can be applied to challenge a causal model. 1.1 Dialogue – What constitutes an intervention? The following dialogue illustrates the conflict encountered when applying a causal Bayesian network, a mathematical model, to reason about actions and observations related to certain real-world variables while using the term ‘intervention’ in a vague manner. Omar: I have two variables modeled as random variables A and B. After measuring them, the data appears to fit perfectly with the joint normal distribution LO(A, B) = N(0, 0, 1, 1, 2). I’m certain there’s no unobserved confounding, but I’m uncertain whether A causes B or B causes A. Can you help determine whether A → B or A ← B is accurate? Sofia: I’m convinced that A causes B. Omar: How can you be certain? Sofia: Attempt to intervene on B. If A truly causes B, we should expect that intervening on B alters its conditional distribution given A but does not change the marginal distribution of A. For instance, if you intervene to fix B at 5, you’ll find that (A, B) adheres to the joint distribution Ldo(B=5)(A, B) = N(0, 1) ⊗ δ5, where δ5 is the Dirac distribution supported on {5}. Omar: Alright, I tried. I did something and now A and B appear to follow the joint normal distribution N(2, 0, 4, 3, 7). Sofia: Now B follows the distribution N(0, 7). I suggested you intervene and set B to have a point mass at 5. Could you try again? Omar: Oh, I apologize. I mistakenly thought I had followed your suggestion, but it’s clear now that I did not. I will take different action so that B centers around 5: Now, A and B follow the distribution δ1 ⊗ δ5. So B has the distribution δ5, yet I did not observe the interventional distribution you said I would see. Does that imply A does not cause B? Sofia: Haha, you also intervened on A and set it to 1! When you intervene on B, you should only alter B. Ensure that you solely adjust the conditional distribution of B given A, without affecting A’s marginal distribution. 1 This assumption simplifies this example presentation but is not essential for the issue this example exemplifies. 2 Omar: Got it, now I believe I acted correctly, and indeed, just as you predicted, I obtained N(0, 1) ⊗ δ5. Sofia: See, as I predicted, A causes B and not the other way around. 1.2 Analyzing the issue What if we accept Sofia’s assertion that A→B is correct? According to her valid model (and the observational distribution), she predicts: (P) If you intervene do(B = 5), then we would observe the distribution N(0, 1) ⊗ δ5 over (A, B). Proposition (P) is ambiguous: while it is clear what distribution Sofia’s model implies following the intervention do(B = 5), the conditions under which the antecedent is satisfied in reality remain unclear. Pearl, Glymour, and Jewell provide insight: The difference between intervening on a variable and conditioning on that variable should, ideally, be evident. When we intervene on a variable in a model, we fix its value. We alter the system, leading to changes in other variables as a consequence [Pearl et al., 2016, page 54]. One way to comprehend this concerning (P) is proposed as follows: (P1) If you perform an action that adjusts the system so that B = 5 with certainty, then you will observe the distribution N(0, 1) ⊗ δ5 over (A, B). Even if Sofia is convinced that A causes B, she seems to believe that (P1) is incorrect. When Omar alters circumstances so that (A, B) aligns with the distribution δ1 ⊗ δ5 and satisfies the antecedent of (P1), she argues that he has intervened on both variables. She renames this as (P2) as another analysis of (P): (P2) If you perform an action that alters the system so that you observe B = 5 with certainty while maintaining A’s marginal distribution, then you’ll see the distribution N(0, 1) ⊗ δ5 over (A, B). Interpreting (P) as (P2) cannot be validated: If A←B, then (P) is false whereas (P2) is true. (P2) is a mathematical certainty, independent of whether A→B or A←B. In Corollary 3.3, we illustrate that interpreting (P) as (P2) means that every causal Bayesian network accurately depicting the observational distribution is interventionally valid (consult Definition 2.7). 1.3 Contribution We introduce a mathematical framework that explicitly links causal models with the real-world data-generating processes they represent. This provides a clear and formal basis for demonstrating that the seemingly obvious interpretation of actions as interventions is indeed circular, suggesting that interventional predictions (layer 2 [Ibeling and Icard, 2020, Bareinboim et al., 2022]) are not inherently free from the philosophical complexities associated with falsifiability, previously discussed in connection with counterfactual predictions (layer 3) [Dawid, 2000, Shpitser and Pearl, 2007, Raghavan and Bareinboim, 2024]. Our findings challenge the prevailing belief that interventional predictions can lead to the falsification of causal models.2 Our formalism also permits us to devise interpretations that facilitate the falsification of causal models through interventional predictions, allowing for detailed discourse regarding their advantages and disadvantages (refer to Section 5). This is vital for understanding causal discovery and causal representation learning, where it is assumed that not all causal Bayesian networks yielding the correct observational distribution are also interventionally valid. Additionally, our contributions accentuate that intuition and common understanding may not be the most reliable guides for determining if and how causal models generate falsifiable predictions about the effects of certain actions. We provide numerous examples throughout this article to illustrate our theoretical findings and their formal implications. Some instances may appear contrived and abstract, but this is intentional: they serve to clarify the principles and subtle technical nuances involved in establishing a formal connection between causal models and real-world data-generating processes. 1.4 Article outline Section 2 – Framework: We lay out the framework employed in this article. Rather than presupposing that the underlying data-generating mechanism is a causal model, we consider a generic set of distributions indexed by actions. A crucial distinction is drawn between 1) a model mimicking the distributions of a representation and 2) a model that serves as an interventionally valid representation. Section 3 – A circular interpretation: We formalize the seemingly obvious interpretation of actions as interventions and demonstrate that it is circular, which results in every CBN accurately modeling the observational distribution being interventionally valid. Section 4 – An impossibility result for interpretations: We explore various intuitive characteristics of interpretations of actions as interventions and show that an interpretation fulfilling four intuitive desiderata must be circular. Section 5 – Non-circular interpretation: We define and explore five non-circular interpretations of actions as interventions, allowing for the potential falsification of a causal model. Section 6 – Implications for related research: We discuss the implications of our findings for causal representation learning, causal discovery, and causal abstraction. The discussion extends to connections with the philosophical discourse on the logic of conditionals. Section 7 – Conclusion 2 For instance, Loftus [2024, Position 4] contends that "Causal models can be falsified in more ways than predictive models. This is generally favorable."; Peters et al. [2017, Section 6.8] assert that "if an interventional model accurately predicts the observational distribution but fails to predict outcomes in a randomized experiment, it is still regarded as falsified"; and Raghavan and Bareinboim [2024] state that "It is widely believed that, in real-world settings, samples can only be collected from observational and interventional distributions [... while sampling from] counterfactual distributions is thought to be nearly inaccessible by definition." 4 2 Framework We formalize causal models as causal Bayesian networks [Spirtes et al., 2001, Pearl, 2009, Peters et al., 2017] instead of structural causal models (SCMs). This choice simplifies the mathematical presentation in this manuscript, while we maintain that the considerations discussed here are equally applicable to SCMs. Definition 2.1. Causal Bayesian network. A causal Bayesian network (CBN) C, also referred to as a causal graphical model, comprising real-valued random variables Z = (Z1, . . . Zn) is characterized by a directed acyclic graph (DAG) G over nodes [n] = {1, . . . n} and a collection of Markov kernels {pai 7→ pC i (· | pai) · νi | i ∈ [n]}. These Markov kernels induce a joint distribution known as the observational distribution, denoted by LC(Z) with density pC Z(z1, . . . , zn) = ∏n i=1 pC i (zi | pai). Given some non-empty subset J ⊆ [n], interventional distributions are achieved by replacing, for each j ∈ J, the kernel of j with a novel kernel paj 7→ qj(· | paj) · µj. We denote this intervention by do(j ← qj, j ∈ J). The interventional distribution under the intervention do(j ← qj, j ∈ J) is represented by LC; do(j←qj,j∈J)(Z), with its density defined as pC; do(j←qj,j∈J) Z (z) = ∏n i=1 pC; do(j←qj,j∈J) i (zi | pai) = ∏ i /∈ J pC i (zi | pai) ∏ i∈ J qi(zi | pai). Here, pC; do(j←qj,j∈J) i denotes the i’th kernel derived from C and the intervention d = do(j ← qj, j ∈ J), meaning pC; do(j←qj,j∈J) i = pC i for i /∈ J, and for i ∈ J, pC; do(j←qj,j∈J) i = qi. In this work, interventions that alter the DAG G are not considered. We assume that interventions yield distributions distinct from the observational distribution, i.e., they satisfy LC; do(j←qj,j∈J)(Z) ≠ LC(Z). This notably eliminates the possibility of intervening solely on source nodes,7 without affecting at least some of their marginal distributions. 3 Throughout, we assume acyclicity to guarantee that the collection of Markov kernels induces a well-defined distribution under any intervention. 4 While the nodes of a graph G are formally represented by the natural numbers [n], for the sake of clarity, we will also regard the coordinates of Z = (Z1, ..., Zn) as the corresponding nodes of G. 5 Here, PAi denotes the variables of Z corresponding to the parents of i in G, and pai ∈ R|PAi| represents some value of these variables. The conditional distribution LC(Zi | PAi = pai) possesses a density pC i (· | pai) with respect to a σ-finite measure νi on R. The measure νi remains consistent for all pai. 6 An intervention do(j ← qj, j ∈ J) can modify both the densities pj(· | ·) and the measures νj, despite the change of measure being concealed in the notation. Sometimes, we may state do(Zj = z) to denote that the kernel of j is replaced with paj 7→ δz, where δz is the Dirac distribution supported on {z}. In other cases, we may express it as do(Zj ← N(0, 1)), signifying that the kernel of j is supplanted with paj 7→ N(0, 1), effectively making Zj adhere to a standard normal distribution independent of its parents. 7 A source node is defined as a node having no parents. 5 We consider a DAG G as complete if, for every pair of distinct nodes Zj and Zi, either Zj → Zi or Zj ← Zi is true; we classify a CBN as complete if its DAG is complete. ◦ Definition 2.2. Types of interventions. We denote an intervention do(j ← qj, j ∈ J) a single-node intervention if |J| = 1, and a multi-node intervention if |J| > 1. Furthermore, we classify an intervention as minimal if for every nonempty proper subset J∗ ⊊ J and kernels {q∗ j}j∈J∗, the equation LC; do(j←qj,j∈J)(Z) ≠ LC; do(j←q∗ j ,j∈J∗)(Z) holds, ensuring no intervention on a proper node subset results in the same interventional distribution. We describe an intervention as decomposable if do(j ← qj, j ∈ J∗) constitutes an intervention for every nonempty subset J∗ ⊆ J, implying that LC; do(j←qj,j∈J∗)(Z) ≠ LC(Z) for every nonempty subset J∗ ⊆ J. We call a kernel pai 7→ pC i (· | pai) · νi perfect if the measure pC i (· | pai) · νi is the same across all pai. An intervention do(j ← qj, j ∈ J) is deemed perfect if qj is perfect for all j ∈ J. ◦  A notable aspect of this work is our decision not to presuppose that the data-generating mechanism is structured as a causal Bayesian network or a structural causal model. Instead, we remain neutral regarding how the data is formed and investigate whether a representation of the data-generating process can be effectively modeled using a causal Bayesian network. Definition 2.3. Data-generating process. A data-generating process is represented as a tuple D = (A, {La(X∗)}a∈A) where • A refers to a set of actions, • one action O ∈ A denotes the observational regime, and • X* ∈ Rm is a multivariate random variable, termed low-level features, with distributions specified by La(X*) for each action a ∈ A. ◦ In general, we presume that observed data consists of low-level features, such as image pixels, which might not be directly amenable to causal modeling (see, for instance, Schölkopf et al. [2021]). Instead, we may aim to model causally a high-level representation defined by functions of these pixels, rather than the individual pixels themselves. Unlike many studies focused on causal representation learning, we do not concentrate on the challenges associated with learning or identifying such representations. Instead, we scrutinize the implications of positing that a representation is accurately modeled by a causal model. Definition 2.4. Representation. A representation of a data-generating process D = (A, {La(X∗)}a∈A) is expressed as a multivariate random variable Z∗ = (Z∗ 1, . . . , Z∗ n) = h(X∗) = (h1(X∗), . . . , hn(X∗)) for measurable functions h1, . . . , hn. ◦ Refer to Definition 6.3 for a specification of ‘causal representation’. We will examine the correlation between variables Z = (Z1, ..., Zn) in a causal Bayesian network and a representation Z∗= (Z∗ 1, ..., Z∗ n) of a data-generating process.8 The observational distribution of the representation Z∗ is determined by the push-forward measure LO(Z∗) = h(LO(X∗)). We say that a CBN C over nodes Z is compatible with the representation Z∗ if LC(Z) = LO(Z∗), thereby implying that Z and Z∗ share an identical dimension. Alongside the observational distribution, for each action a ∈ A, we derive a distribution La(Z∗) = h(La(X∗)). Likewise, the causal Bayesian network C generates various interventional distributions LC; do(j←qj,j∈J)(Z) for diverse interventions do(j ← qj, j ∈ J). In Definition 2.7, we articulate what it indicates for the CBN C to be an interventionally valid representation of a data set. Consult Figure 1 for a visual representation summarizing the context explored in this work. Throughout this piece, we assume that the distribution of Z∗ under action a ∈ A, denoted by La(Z∗), possesses a density with respect to some product of σ-finite measures. We express La(Z∗ j | Y ∗) ∼p to denote that the kernel y∗ 7→ p(· | y∗) · ν is a regular conditional probability distribution of Z∗ j given Y ∗ ⊆ Z∗ under distribution La(Z∗). An overview of our notation is provided in Appendix A. 2.1 Emulation and interventional validity Given that CBNs are practical tools for representing multiple distributions, we often utilize a CBN to specify the distributions of a representation. Definition 2.5. Representation emulated by a CBN. Given a data-generating process D = (A, {La(X∗)}a∈A) and a CBN A over nodes Z = (Z1, . . . , Zn), we assert that 8 We denote variables whose distributions derive from the data-generating process with a superscript ∗ and their corresponding variables in a CBN without the superscript. 7 a representation Z∗= (Z∗ 1, . . . , Z∗ n) of D is emulated by A and interventions I∗ if I∗ constitutes a set of interventions in A, and a surjective function g : A \ {O} → I* exists such that 1. LO(Z∗) = LA(Z), and 2. La(Z∗) = LA;g(a)(Z) for each a ∈ A \ {O}. We refer to g as the link. ◦ Notably, asserting that a representation is emulated by a CBN A and interventions I∗ does not imply any additional claims about the data-generating process than the distributions it induces for that set of actions. Moreover, for every data-generating process D = (A, {La(X∗)}a∈A) and representation Z∗, there exists a CBN A and a set of interventions I∗ such that Z∗ is emulated by A and I∗. This is evident by selecting a complete CBN A where LA(Z) = LO(Z∗), and designating a corresponding intervention da for each a ∈ A \ {O} to ensure La(Z∗ i | PA∗ i ) ∼pA;da i for all i ∈ [n] (this is feasible since La(Z∗) features density with respect to a product of σ-finite measures). Consequently, La(Z∗) = LA;da(Z) for each a ∈ A \ {O} given A is complete, affirming that Z∗ is emulated by A and I∗ = {da | a ∈ A \ {O}}. Instead, it accentuates that causal models can be impactful even when conceptualized through varied mathematical frames.
