The Case for Time in Causal DAGs  
Alexander G. Reisach1  
CNRS, MAP5 Université Paris Cité  
F-75006 Paris, France  
Alberto Suárez  
Departamento de Ingeniería Informática, Escuela Politécnica Superior, Universidad Autónoma de Madrid, Spain  
Sebastian Weichwald  
Department of Mathematical Sciences and Pioneer Centre for Artificial Intelligence, University of Copenhagen, Denmark  
Antoine Chambaz  
CNRS, MAP5 Université Paris Cité  
F-75006 Paris, France  

**Abstract**  
We propose the integration of time explicitly in the definition of variables within causal directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Causality inherently requires a temporal order where causes precede effects, indicating that causal relationships among variables may differ across various time orders. Thus, any causal framework necessitates a temporal perspective. We formally introduce a concept of time for causal variables, asserting that this approach clarifies ambiguities present in causal DAGs and is vital for evaluating the validity of the acyclicity assumption. When variables exist in temporal separation, their causal links must be acyclic. Conversely, without such separation, acyclicity hinges on the nonexistence of causal cycles allowed by the temporal arrangement. We delineate a formal distinction between both conditions and explore their consequences. Furthermore, we discuss the correlations of our work with diverse aspects of the wider causality literature and examine the implications of incorporating time for both the interpretation and the application of DAGs as causal frameworks.  

**Prologue**  
*Democritus:* I would prefer to reveal a single cause than to inherit the kingdom of Persia.  
*Socrates:* Suppose you find that the quest for knowledge induces later happiness.  
*Democritus:* Very well.  
*Socrates:* Is it conceivable that later happiness could be the cause of earlier knowledge seeking?  
*Democritus:* Impossible!  
*Socrates:* Yet, might intermittent happiness incite a consistent pursuit of knowledge?  
*Democritus:* Quite likely.  
*Socrates:* So between the pursuit of knowledge and happiness, which stands as the cause once more?  
*Democritus:* ... I must consult a merchant of kingdoms.  

1Correspondence to alexander.reisach@math.cnrs.fr  

**1 Introduction**  
Causal directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), made notable by Pearls' work (2000), have largely been developed as non-temporal models for causation. In the second edition of his seminal work, Pearl (2009), specifically in Chapter 7.5.1, remarks on the application of time in causative analyses: “The reliance on temporal details comes with its costs, as it inherently excludes cases where temporal order lacks precision.” Nevertheless, time is a tangible entity, inescapable in its effects, regardless of the possible costs associated with either utilizing or ignoring temporal data. Thus, we advocate for a clear emphasis on time, aiming to uncover both its limitations and the possibilities it offers.

**Time and Causation.** A crucial concept underpinning this discourse is the principle that causes must precede effects—this is fundamental to our understanding of causality. When Wright (1934) introduced the method of path coefficients, a precursor to causal graphical models, he emphasized that “only such paths are attempted which align appropriately in temporal direction,” ensuring that constructed paths form a DAG. The Bradford Hill criteria for causation (Hill 1965), widely accepted in epidemiology, recognizes this principle under the term ‘temporality’ as one of nine criteria to establish causal evidence. Analogously, Granger (1969), Suppes (1970), and Shoham (1990) also depend on the temporal sequence between cause and effect in their causal theories. In their foundational research on causal discovery, Spirtes et al. (1993) (refer also to Spirtes et al. 2001 for the second edition) highlight that causal models must respect a defined temporal order, ensuring the uniqueness of the DAG. Despite their focus on causal reasoning devoid of a time structure, canonical literature on causal graphical models, such as Pearl (2009) and Peters et al. (2017), agree that causality must conform to time.

**The Absence of Time in Causal DAGs.** In spite of its pivotal role in causation, time is notably absent from formal discussions surrounding causal DAGs within the existing scholarship. Unlike other causal analysis approaches, particularly those rooted in the potential outcomes framework (e.g., Imbens and Rubin 2015), causal DAGs have been explicitly designed for ‘non-temporal statistical data’ (Pearl 2009). This term encompasses two distinctive attributes: first, all DAGs are stationary, meaning any distribution compatible with them remains independent of time. Second, more controversially, there are no explicit temporal conditions among components of an individual sample beyond those implied by the causal order defined by the DAG's acyclicity. The first property can be viewed as ‘between-sample’, while the second pertains to ‘within-sample’ considerations (see forthcoming Figure 1 for illustration). Rather than depending on a temporal sequence to establish a causal order, much of the literature aligns with Pearl's (2009) assertion that causal variables maintain Markovian relationships relative to a DAG. This offers a robust unified theory, irrespective of whether the causal ordering derives from a temporal sequence or the absence of cyclic causal structures (Pearl 2009, Section 7.5.1). However, this generalized approach masks the necessity for temporal precedence in causation and obscures the justification for the potential validity or invalidity of the acyclicity assumption. This has resulted in widespread applications of causal DAGs, even in contexts—such as neuroimaging (Ramsey et al. 2017) or gene regulatory networks (Lee et al. 2019)—where the legitimacy of a causal DAG is questionable. Oftentimes, this pursuit for non-temporal causal relationships has led to variables which resist straightforward interventions, exemplified by the Altitude →Temperature case (see, for instance, Peters et al. 2017, Section 2.1). The lack of an explicit temporal context has also resulted in reliance on time proxy variables like ‘age’ or ‘hour of day’ (Mooij et al. 2016), as well as modeling time itself as a causal factor (Huang et al. 2015).

**The Case for Time in Causal DAGs.** We argue for a formal and clear integration of time in the definition of variables within causal DAGs for two primary reasons. First, time is indispensable for understanding causal relationships because causes must chronologically precede effects. For instance, the claim “X does not cause Y” gains significance when X precedes Y, while it becomes an ambiguity if the temporal order is reversed. However, without incorporating a temporal component, these two scenarios appear identical in a causal DAG (notably, DAGs are unable to articulate the absence of causal knowledge as delineated by Dawid 2010, Sections 9 and 10). Second, a time-sensitive perspective is critical to validate the acyclicity assumption upon which the model class is founded. If either causal variable X or Y occurs prior to the other, there must exist a (potentially empty) DAG between them; however, absent such a temporal order raises the prospect of reciprocal influence, hence the possibility of a causal cycle. An explicit consideration of time aids in resolving ambiguities surrounding the causal relationships that DAGs aim to represent and is vital for analyzing the validity of the acyclicity assumption.

**Contribution.** We start by acknowledging that causal relationships are inherently time-relative and propose a formalism that integrates time into the definition of causal variables. On this basis, we identify two distinct yet individually sufficient conditions for establishing acyclicity: acyclicity via a temporal order that restricts cycles, and acyclicity derived from the absence of causal cycles when no temporal order is present. We elucidate their implications, particularly as they pertain to evaluating the validity of the acyclicity claim, revealing how they can unveil instances of faithfulness violations. We relate our contributions to critical discourses concerning causal DAGs, cyclic causal graphs, discrete and continuous-time causal models, and the potential outcomes framework. Lastly, we address the consequences of incorporating time into DAGs concerning their interpretation and utility as causal frameworks.  

**2 Time in Causal DAGs**  
We present a justification for and formalize a conceptualization of time alongside the temporal sequencing for variables in causal DAGs.

**Causal DAGs.** DAGs serve as the fundamental mechanism for depicting causal relationships through graphical models (Pearl 2009). A DAG G = (V, E) includes sets of vertices V, and directed edges E ⊆V × V, where an edge (X, Y ) ∈E indicates a directed connection from X to Y. We define a ‘directed path’ as an ordered series of directed edges where the endpoint of the k-th edge aligns with the starting point of the (k + 1)-th edge. By definition, DAGs are acyclic, implying no directed paths initiate and conclude at the same node. A causal DAG reflects an external causal system (Dawid 2010, Section 5). Each vertex represents a random variable, whose joint distribution is presumed to uphold Markov compatibility relative to the DAG (e.g., Pearl 2009, Definition 1.2.2; Peters et al. 2017, Definition 6.21). A directed edge (X, Y ) ∈E, also expressed as X →Y , signifies that X serves as a direct cause of Y within the graph’s variables. In literature on causal graphical models, ‘causal structure’ and ‘causal model’ are understood as a DAG and a DAG supplemented by a set of additional parameters, respectively (Pearl 2009, Definitions 2.2.1 and 2.2.2). The broader category known as ‘structural causal models’ (Pearl 2009, Definition 7.1.1) does not inherently necessitate acyclic structures, although it is most frequently employed alongside DAGs (refer to Pearl 2009, Chapter 1.2; Peters et al. 2017, Chapter 6.2), which continue to be the focal object of interest and study within causal graphical models due to their favorable characteristics.

**2.1 Causal Relationships are Relative with Respect to Time**  
Given that causes must precede effects, causal relationships are inextricably linked to the temporal relationships among variables. Causal relationships cannot exist absent temporal qualifications.  

**A time-relative causal relationship.** Consider the DAG Aspirin →Headache, a frequently cited example in the literature (e.g., Shpitser and Pearl 2008; Imbens and Rubin 2015; Pearl and Mackenzie 2018). Aspirin clearly cannot alleviate a prior headache, hence the effect is contingent on time. Moreover, could headaches induce subsequent consumption of aspirin? The absence of an edge connecting headaches to aspirin raises the question of whether this is relevant to the temporal order or if it represents a broader phenomenon. The existing causal edge suggests a temporal precedence where aspirin occurs prior to headaches, or alternatively, if each variable encompasses multiple time points, that some temporal aspect of aspirin precedes aspects of headaches—it does not, however, precisely delineate the temporal connection. A causal DAG with entirely separate variables would not provide insight into temporal orders at all, rendering the interpretation of absent edges overwhelmingly ambiguous. By contextualizing aspirin and headache as time-specific variables—such as ‘morning aspirin’ and ‘afternoon headache’—one can introduce a directed edge from the former to the latter. However, it is likely there exists a counter edge connecting ‘morning headache’ to ‘afternoon aspirin’, thus if both temporal instances were consolidated back into aspirin and headache broadly, no valid DAG would remain since the two edges would generate a cycle. This example illustrates that a DAG cannot effectively relate general concepts of aspirin and headache; rather, it necessitates the consideration of specific time instantiations. Such instantiations are prevalent in potential outcomes research (see Imbens and Rubin 2015, Chapter 1). Recognizing the relativity of causal relationships with respect to time clarifies the types of variables that can be interrelated through causal DAGs. 

**Time at the level of individual samples.** The prevailing literature on causal graphical models adopts Laplace's (1814) viewpoint by treating natural processes as outputs of deterministic transformations acted upon random inputs (see Pearl 2009, Section 1.4). These transformations embody the causal mechanisms. Given the independence of certain random inputs, their correspondingly produced outputs are also independent. This differs from time-series causality (see Assaad 2021), where the output of a causal mechanism at a particular time influences the input at the subsequent time step, generating dependence. Nonetheless, even amid mutually independent inputs, the steps of a causal mechanism unfold over time within single applications. Consequently, output elements must correspond to one or several time points. Peters et al. (2017, Remark 6.7) express this air of independence stating that “in the [structural causal model], variables do not explicitly denote measurements taken at fixed time intervals.” Our analysis concerns the relative time differences between elements of the output, which must exist for causes to precede effects temporally. Outputs can be perceived as individual samples extracted from the distribution following the application of a causal mechanism on random inputs. The time differences between elements of a singular output are within-sample, whereas the time distinctions between distinct outputs are between-sample. For convenience and to maintain independence from the initial time, we set the earliest time point for each sample to 0 by deducting the earliest time point from each sample. Figure 1 illustrates the concept of within-sample and between-sample time.

**2.2 A Formal Notion of Time for Causal Variables**  
Since causal relationships are shaped by their temporal context, no single DAG can depict these relationships in a time-invariant manner (except, trivially, in the case of an empty DAG indicating no causal effects across time). To articulate a unique, non-empty DAG between variables, it is essential to equip the variables with a suitable conception of time. For this purpose, we present a formal treatment of within-sample time for causal variables. For clarity, we will utilize the notation: for any k ∈N∗, for any set S of cardinality greater than or equal to k, Pk(S) designates the collection of subsets of S comprising k elements. Let Tx ⊂R+ denote a countable set of time points, and let kx ∈N∗ represent a deterministic integer less than or equal to |Tx|. We define a real-valued stochastic process X = (Xt)t∈Tx over these time points, with Tx ⊆Tx being a random subset containing kx time points. The support Sx of the distribution of Tx forms a subset of Pkx(Tx). We measure the variables Xt for every t ∈Tx. Let fx : Rkx →R signify a real-valued deterministic aggregation function, such that X = fx((Xt)t∈Tx) corresponds to an aggregated variable derived from measurements (Xt)t∈Tx, serving as its temporal components. We further stipulate that if x, x′ ∈Rkx exist such that a t ∈{1, . . . , kx} satisfies xs = x′ s for every s different from t but xt ̸= x′ t, then fx(x) ̸= fx(x′). This ensures that intervening on one temporal component leads to adjustments in the respective aggregate variable. For instance, fx cannot serve as a mere component selector; it cannot multiply variables with zero values. To underline that aggregate variables Z inherit their temporal structure from the underlying stochastic process, we introduce the notation XTx := fx ((Xt)t∈Tx), which encapsulates that a causal variable can be viewed as the aggregation of one or multiple temporal components. Given the centrality of time in causation, we opt to keep the time index explicit, even after aggregating into a single real-valued random variable. For a minimal instance, we could select Tx = {t}, making the stochastic process X consist of an isolated variable, and setting kx = 1 using fx as the identity function, leading to XTx = Xt (forthcoming examples will leverage processes with multiple variables to showcase the attributes of our formalism). In summary, we define a causal variable XTx in terms of the components outlined in Table 1.

| **XTx** | Causal variable featuring an explicit notion of time. |  
| --- | --- |  
| **X** or **(Xt)t∈Tx** | Stochastic process of measurements. |  
| **Tx** | Set of potential measurement time points. |  
| **Tx** | Random subset of kx time points, selected from Tx, used for XTx. |  
| **kx** | Count of measurements for each individual sample of XTx. |  
| **fx** | Aggregation function for (Xt)t∈Tx. |  

*Table 1: Components utilized to define a causal variable XTx endowed with an explicit concept of time.*  

Going forward, all causal variables will conform to the form specified in Equation (1), and we assume an underlying ‘atomic’ causal DAG exists among all time-point-specific components of the stochastic processes tied to the phenomena of interest. From this atomic causal DAG, we can derive a directed graph connecting these aggregate variables, which may or may not maintain acyclicity. For an in-depth consideration of inference rules concerning macro-variables, refer to Anand et al. (2023). By default, we consider the time points Tx of a variable XTx as the intervals in which X is measured, but alternative specifications are feasible (e.g., using proxy measurements from past incidents or measures reflective of multiple time points). The scope for interventions applicable to a causal variable XTx extends to any subset of (Xt)t∈Tx. Designating the support of the joint distribution for two sets of time points (Tx, Ty) as Sxy ⊆Sx × Sy ⊆Pkx(Tx) × Pky(Ty), we assert that XTx induces another causal variable YTy if there exist (tx, ty) ∈Sxy such that Xtx influences Yty within the atomic DAG (we do not account for self-loops at the aggregate variables level—for example, if Xtx1 affects Xtx2 for some tx1, tx2 ∈Sx).  

**Example 1 (Separation in Time).** Consider a general medical treatment-health context that follows the formalization previously discussed. Let XTx represent an aggregate of kx = 2 treatment measurements across (Xt)t∈Tx, where Tx = {0, 0.4}. Let YTy reflect an aggregate variable of ky = 2 health measurements within (Yt)t∈Ty, where Ty = {0.6, 1}. Consequently, Tx = Tx and Ty = Ty. The only feasible combination of time points is Sxy = P2(Tx) × P2(Ty) = {({0, 0.4}, {0.6, 1})}. Assuming the aggregation functions fx and fy both sum their inputs, we have XTx = ∑t∈Tx Xt and YTy = ∑t∈Ty Yt. This scenario may correspond to patients receiving treatment repeatedly at both possible time points, followed consistently by a health assessment either at of the two subsequent time points.  

| **Time** | | |  
| --- | --- | --- |  
| 0 | 0.4 | |  
| XTx | | |  
| 0.6 | 1 |  
| YTy | | |  

*Figure 2: Two aggregate causal variables that are separated in time.*  

Figure 2 offers visual representation regarding the example, including the timeline, the stochastic process time points (Xt)t∈Tx (denoted blue ×) and (Yt)t∈Ty (denoted red ×), and the aggregation into the respective aggregate variables XTx (blue bracket) and YTy (red bracket). The aggregate variables XTx and YTy can be interpreted as time-dependent representations of the abstract ideas ‘treatment’ and ‘health’. Any causal link connecting them is customarily associated with this instantiation.  

| **Time** | **Atomic Causal DAG** | **Causal DAG Between Aggregate Variables** |  
| --- | --- | --- |  
| 0 | 0.4 | |  
| XTx | | |  
| 0.6 | 1 |  
| YTy | | |  

*Figure 3: An atomic causal DAG and corresponding aggregate causal DAG compatible with Example 1.*  

Figure 3 illustrates an atomic causal DAG (Figure 3a) aligned with the example, alongside its corresponding causal DAG among aggregate variables (Figure 3b). The temporal components of each aggregate variable are represented along distinct (gray) time arrows linked to the same within-sample timeline, as indicated by vertical connections. Solid black arrows exhibit causal connections.  

Employing our formalization, we can rigorously define the concept that causes must precede effects. Let a wavy arrow ⇝ denote a causal path, be it direct or indirect, linking two variables within a causal directed graph, either cyclical or not. Definition 1 (Causes Precede Effects). We assert that causes precede effects if and only if, within the atomic causal DAG corresponding to the temporal components of any two stochastic processes (Xt)t∈Tx and (Yt)t∈Ty, for all tx ∈Tx, and ty ∈Ty,  
**Xtx ⇝Yty ⟹ tx < ty.**  
This rigorously confirms the foundational requirement that causes must precede effects concerning variables of the format provided in Equation (1). For instance, a path XTx ⇝YTy in Example 1 would comply with Definition 1; however, the inverse YTy ⇝XTx would not. In the entirety of our discourse, we shall presume that all causal relationships honor the principle that causes precede effects as delineated by Definition 1.

**3 A Tale of Two Acyclicities**  
We segregate the acyclicity assumption into two distinct yet individually sufficient conditions, each possessing unique characteristics: acyclicity through a temporal order that disallows cycles, and acyclicity arising from the absence of causal cycles in instances where time does not impose restrictions. The acyclicity across the causal relationships between two variables XTx and YTy can be elaborately articulated through the atomic relationships governing the temporal components of these variables.  

**Definition 2 (Acyclicity).**  
Acyclicity is asserted between two causal variables XTx and YTy if and only if, within the atomic causal DAG, there exists at least one (tx, ty) ∈Tx × Ty such that  
**Xtx ⇝Yty ⟹ ∀(t′x, t′y) ∈Tx × Ty, ¬ [Yty ⇝Xtx].**  
Additionally, we define a graph G as acyclic if acyclicity holds for every variable pair within G.  

**3.1 Acyclicity I: By Time Order**  
A sufficient criterion for establishing an acyclic causal relationship between two variables XTx and YTy is met if all time points of one variable consistently precede those of the other. We denote the temporal precedence of XTx with respect to YTy with the shorthand Tx ≺Ty := ∀(sx, sy) ∈Sxy, max(sx) < min(sy). The order relation ≺ is inherently transitive, and thus we define ‘time-acyclicity’ as follows.  

**Definition 3 (Time-acyclicity).**  
Time-acyclicity holds between two causal variables XTx and YTy if and only if  
**(Tx ≺Ty) ∨(Ty ≺Tx).**  
Moreover, we classify a graph G as time-acyclic if this condition is upheld for every variable pair located within G. The constraint imposed on Sxy by Definition 3 trivially ensures acyclicity in accordance with Definition 2 since we adhere to the principle that causes precede effects as outlined in Definition 1. This is particularly evident in scenarios involving two variables conforming to the format specified in Equation (1), each possessing a singular measurement time point, thus sharing the same causal DAG as the atomic causal DAG.  

**Example 1 (Separation in Time) revisited.**  
Example 1 displays time-acyclicity as delineated by Definition 3, a fact which can be observed through the horizontal separation of blue and red brackets along the time axis. The aggregate treatment variable XTx could potentially influence the aggregate health variable YTy, but not vice versa due to the established time order XTx ≺YTy. A path XTx ⇝YTy affirms that at least one of the treatments being measured impacts at least one of the health outcomes, as illustrated in the atomic causal DAG presented in Figure 3.  

**Example 2 (Non-obvious Time-Acyclicity).**  
Consider a variation of the standard treatment-health framework from Example 1. Let ZTz comprise an aggregate of kz = 1 diagnostic measurement in (Zt)t∈Tz, where Tz = {0}. Let XTx consist of an aggregate with kx = 1 treatment measurement in (Xt)t∈Tx, where Tx = {0.25, 0.7}. Let YTy aggregate ky = 1 health measurements in (Yt)t∈Ty, where Ty = {0.6, 1}. Consequently, Sxy = {({0.25}, {0.6}), ({0.25}, {1}), ({0.7}, {1})}. Note that ({0.7}, {0.6}) /∈Sxy, thus establishing that XTx ≺YTy notwithstanding the fact that max(Tx) > min(Ty). This scenario might represent patients receiving a diagnostic assessment followed by treatment at one of two time points, leading to a health evaluation conducted at one of two subsequent time points, always occurring post-treatment.  

| **Time** | | |  
| --- | --- | --- |  
| 0 | | ZTz |  
| 0.25 | 0.7 | XTx |  
| 0.6 | 1 | YTy |  

*Figure 4: An illustration of Example 2, where the time order inhibits causal cycles.*  

The acyclicity assumption can indeed be confirmed via time-acyclicity (Definition 3), although this validation necessitates a deep understanding of the joint distribution of measurement timings. The example depicted in Figure 4 illustrates that while it may seem as though there is no time order connecting XTx (in blue) and YTy (in red) due to the bracket overlaps on the timeline, the joint distribution of Tx and Ty actually ensures that XTx ≺YTy, thereby affirming time-acyclicity. The variable ZTz provides a reference point in time, suggesting that within the same sample, tx and ty are confined such that tx cannot exceed ty.  

**3.2 Acyclicity II: By Absence of Causal Cycles**  
Discussions surrounding the acyclicity presumption in the causality literature conventionally concentrate on the presence or absence of causal cycles, such as feedback loops (see Brouillard et al. 2024). However, given that causes precede effects, causal cycles can only manifest if there exists a lack of time-acyclicity (Definition 3). This leads us to label acyclicity in the absence of causal cycles where conditions permit ‘effect-acyclicity’ and define it accordingly.  

**Definition 4 (Effect-acyclicity).**  
Effect-acyclicity persists between two causal variables XTx and YTy if and only if:  
**¬ ((Tx ≺Ty) ∨(Ty ≺Tx))**, yet acyclicity is preserved according to Definition 2. Additionally, we characterize a graph G as effect-acyclic if this condition holds true for every variable pair found within.  

**Example 3 (Effect-Acyclicity).**  
Consider yet another variation of our medical treatment and health example. Let XTx represent an aggregate of two treatment measurements within (Xt)t∈Tx, where Tx = {0, 0.6}. Let YTy consist of two health measurements within (Yt)t∈Ty, where Ty = {0.4, 1}. Here, Tx = Tx and Ty = Ty, and Sxy = P2(Tx) × P2(Ty) = {({0, 0.6}, {0.4, 1})}. The aggregation functions fx and fy here simply sum their respective inputs. In this case, no instance of time-acyclicity exists, implying that a causal cycle between the aggregate causal variables XTx and YTy is plausible. This loop may occur within an adaptive treatment protocol, whereby a patient receives treatment at time t = 0, positively influencing their health at t = 0.4, which subsequently influences treatment at t = 0.6, which in turn affects health at t = 1.  

| **Time** | | |  
| --- | --- | --- |  
| 0 | 0.6 | |  
| XTx | | |  
| 0.4 | 1 | YTy |  

*Figure 5: An illustration of Example 3, where the temporal order accommodates causal cycles.*  

In this scenario, the acyclicity supposition can be upheld solely by virtue of effect-acyclicity (Definition 4). The accompanying figure illustrates the example shown in Figure 5; the overlap of red and blue brackets renders clear that there is a lack of established time order concerning Equation (3) between both variables XTx and YTy. The assumption of acyclicity must therefore lean on effect-acyclicity (Definition 4) since these variables cannot be represented properly within a causal DAG. Provided that no causal cycles are present, the temporal structure permits any causal interaction between XTx and YTy. For a causal DAG to contain a path XTx ⇝YTy, it must confirm that Y0.4 lacks influence over X0.6. Similarly, a causal DAG including YTy ⇝XTx would necessitate that X0 not influence either Y0.4 or Y1, and that X0.6 does not impact Y1. The example elucidates that effect-acyclicity is dependent on specific causal interactions residing within the atomic causal DAG among the temporal components of differing variables. 

**Effect-Acyclicity regardless of Time.**  
There exists a special case of effect-acyclicity between two causal variables when there is a categorical absence of one variable influencing another, regardless of their temporal interconnection. We designate this condition as ‘total effect-acyclicity’ and define it formally.   

**Definition 5 (Total Effect-Acyclicity).**  
Total effect-acyclicity between two real-valued stochastic processes (Xt)t∈Tx and (Yt)t∈Ty is said to hold if, and only if, in the atomic causal DAG  
**¬ [∃(tx, ty) ∈Tx × Ty, such that Xtx ⇝Yty] ∨ ¬ [∃(tx, ty) ∈Tx × Ty, such that Yty ⇝Xtx].**  
In this instance, we argue that total effect-acyclicity prevails for all corresponding XTx and YTy. Moreover, we define a graph G as totally effect-acyclic if this condition is satisfied throughout each variable pair within G.  

**Example 4 (Total Effect-Acyclicity).**  
Consider a hypothetical causal model linking solar flares with power outages. Here, solar flares may induce power outages, yet outages cannot inflict solar flares. Let XTx1 represent an aggregate of kx1 = 2 measurements of solar flare incidents from (Xt)t∈Tx, where Tx = {0, 0.24, 0.76, 1}. Let XTx2 reflect another solar flare aggregate with kx2 = 2, where Sx2 = {({0.76, 1})}. Let YTy comprise an aggregate of ky = 2 measurements relative to power outages in (Yt)t∈Ty, with Ty = {0.38, 0.62}, which means that Ty = Ty. This leads to Sx1y = {({0, 0.24}, {0.38, 0.62})} and Syx2 = {({0.38, 0.62}, {0.76, 1})}. The aggregation functions fx1, fx2, and fy each perform addition across their respective inputs.  

| **Time** | | |  
| --- | --- | --- |  
| 0 | 0.24 | 0.38 | 0.62 | 0.76 | 1 |  
| XTx1 | | YTy |  
| XTx2 | | |  

*Figure 6: An illustration of Example 4, depicting the temporal relationships between two disparate measurements of solar flare activities, XTx1 and XTx2 (both in blue), and the power outages represented as YTy (in red).*

The causal relationship forming between XTx1 and YTy, alongside the link between XTx2 and YTy, is categorized as total effect-acyclicity per Definition 5. The explanation lies in the fact that power outages hold no influence over solar flares, regardless of the temporal sequencing. Figure 6 further elucidates the example. For one measurement instance of solar flares to precede a measurement of power outages suggests there may exist a directed path XTx1 ⇝YTy; however, no analogous path exists in the opposite direction involving YTy and XTx2 due to the temporal ordering. More generally, no temporal aspect of power outages elicits repercussions upon any of the solar flare occurrences, which confirms total effect-acyclicity holds by Definition 5. Only under conditions of total effect-acyclicity can the existence of a directional path rule out the existence of paths in the opposite direction across all temporal components. It contrasts with the standard approach utilized in non-temporal DAGs, wherein one path X ⇝Y categorically negates any path Y ⇝X.

**4 Assessing Acyclicity and Faithfulness**  
We outline how time-acyclicity (Definition 3) and effect-acyclicity (Definition 4) provide two distinct methodologies for assessing the validity of the acyclicity assumption, demonstrating they afford a natural framework for untangling cyclic causal relationships through the lens of time.

author: gpt-4o
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model representations into a sparse set of linear latent vectors. Recent works have improved SAEs using language model gradients, but these techniques require many expensive backward passes during training and still cause a significant increase in cross entropy loss when SAE reconstructions are inserted into the model. In this work, we improve on these limitations by taking a fundamentally different approach: we use low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to finetune the language model itself around a previously trained SAE. We analyze our method across SAE sparsity, SAE width, language model size, LoRA rank, and model layer on the Gemma Scope family of SAEs. In these settings, our method reduces the cross entropy loss gap by 30% to 55% when SAEs are inserted during the forward pass. We also find that compared to end-to-end (e2e) SAEs, our approach achieves the same downstream cross entropy loss 3$\times$ to 20$\times$ faster on Gemma-2-2B and 2$\times$ to 10$\times$ faster on Llama-3.2-1B. We further show that our technique improves downstream metrics and can adapt multiple SAEs at once. Our results demonstrate that improving model interpretability is not limited to post-hoc SAE training; Pareto improvements can also be achieved by directly optimizing the model itself.

contents:
**Low-Rank Adapting Models for Sparse Autoencoders**

*Matthew Chen* 1  
*Joshua Engels* 1  
*Max Tegmark* 1

**Abstract**  
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) break down language model representations into a sparse collection of linear latent vectors. Recent studies have advanced SAEs by utilizing language model gradients; however, such approaches necessitate numerous costly backward passes during training and significantly elevate cross-entropy loss when SAE reconstructions are incorporated into the model. This paper addresses these challenges by adopting a fundamentally different strategy: we employ low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to fine-tune the language model itself based on a pre-trained SAE. We evaluate our method against various parameters, including SAE sparsity, SAE width, language model size, LoRA rank, and model layer using the Gemma Scope family of SAEs. In these contexts, our technique diminishes the cross-entropy loss gap by 30% to 55% when SAEs are added during the forward pass. Additionally, our approach, compared to end-to-end (e2e) SAEs, achieves similar downstream cross-entropy loss 3× to 20× quicker on Gemma-2-2B and 2× to 10× quicker on Llama-3.2-1B. We further demonstrate that our method enhances downstream metrics and simultaneously adapts multiple SAEs. These findings reveal that advancing model interpretability is not confined to post-hoc SAE training; direct optimization of the model itself can yield Pareto improvements.

1. **Introduction**  
Language models exhibit remarkable proficiency across various tasks, including in-context learning, mathematical reasoning, and coding (Brown et al., 2020; OpenAI, 2024; Team et al., 2023; Bubeck et al., 2023; Anthropic, 2024), yet the underlying mechanisms driving these capabilities remain largely enigmatic. Mechanistic interpretability (MI) (Bereska & Gavves, 2024) aims to unravel these mechanisms by re-engineering them into algorithms comprehensible to humans. This study prioritizes a more profound comprehension of features—the "variables" through which model computations unfold (Olah et al., 2020; Mueller et al., 2024; Marks et al., 2024). A prevalent hypothesis in MI, the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH) (Elhage et al., 2022a; Park et al., 2023), suggests that features represent one-dimensional vectors within activation space. Despite recent investigations casting doubt on certain aspects of this hypothesis (Engels et al., 2024a; Csordás et al., 2024; Engels et al., 2024b), the LRH has been supported through empirical validation for numerous language model features observed "in the wild" (Nanda et al., 2023; Heinzerling & Inui, 2024). Following from these insights, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) (Makhzani & Frey, 2013) have recently been employed to decompose hidden states within language models into various linear features (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023). The latents derived from SAEs are found to be significantly more interpretable and singular in meaning than their original neuron bases (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023). While SAEs facilitate the discovery of interpretable latents, they do so at a price: re-inserting SAE reconstructions back into the model and executing the forward pass markedly increases the ensuing cross-entropy loss (LSAE), compared to the loss of the original model (LBASE). For instance, inserting reconstructions from a TopK SAE into GPT-4 results in an LSAE that parallels the LBASE of a model trained with a mere 10% of GPT-4's pretraining compute (Gao et al., 2024). Consequently, previous research has focused intensively on refining SAE architectures to obtain Pareto improvements regarding the trade-off between SAE sparsity and LSAE. Such efforts encompass TopK SAEs (Gao et al., 2024), Gated SAEs (Rajamanoharan et al., 2024a), JumpReLU SAEs (Rajamanoharan et al., 2024b), ProLU SAEs (Taggart, 2024), Switch SAEs (Mudide et al., 2024), and e2e SAEs (Braun et al., 2024). Nevertheless, it remains an open question whether the models themselves can be further optimized following SAE training to achieve additional Pareto enhancements in the context of sparsity versus LSAE. In this study, we affirmatively address this question: utilizing Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2021), we aim to minimize the KL divergence between the logits produced by the original model and those generated with an SAE incorporated. The resulting model-SAE amalgamation improves both LSAE performance and various downstream SAE metrics. Compared to existing methods focused on training more interpretable models with SAEs (Lai & Heimersheim, 2024; Lai & Huang, 2024), we estimate our LoRA approach to be 107 times faster overall. To summarize, we find that implementing low-rank adapting models constitutes a straightforward and efficient means to enhance the interpretability versus performance balance. Our contributions are as follows: 1. To our knowledge, we are the first to concentrate on improving the model in conjunction with an existing SAE. 2. In Section 4.1, we delve into LoRA SAE training using the Gemma Scope (Lieberum et al., 2024) family of SAEs. Across dimensions such as SAE width, SAE sparsity, language model size, LoRA rank, and model layers, our findings indicate an improvement in LSAE of 30% to 55%, yielding final values ranging from 0.01 to 0.17 nats, particularly demonstrating significant enhancements under low sparsity constraints and for larger models. 3. In Section 4.2, we juxtapose our method against e2e SAEs concerning training time versus LSAE on Gemma-2-2B (Team et al., 2024) and Llama-3.2-1B (AI@Meta, 2024). Our results show that our method reaches equivalent LSAE to e2e SAEs with 2× to 20× reduction in computational cost, alongside 130× fewer language model backward passes. 4. In Section 4.3, we initiate LoRA SAE training with multiple SAEs integrated into Llama-3.1-8B (AI@Meta, 2024), achieving substantial reductions in LSAE, showcasing the versatility of our method for circuit analysis. 5. In Section 5, we present quantitative enhancements across a variety of downstream tasks. 6. In Section 6, we determine that much of the advantage of full-parameter LoRA can be obtained by solely training an adapter on the layer following the SAE, which tends to concentrate most improvements on tokens exhibiting low LSAE. 2. **Related Work**  
**Improvements to SAE Architecture.** Initial SAEs tailored for language models employed a straightforward linear encoder, ReLU activation with an L1 penalty (effectively approximating L0), and a linear decoder (Bricken et al., 2023; Cunningham et al., 2023). The subsequent generation introduced TopK and BatchTopK SAEs, which maintain sparsity by retaining the largest k activations (Gao et al., 2024; Bussmann et al., 2024). Gated SAEs and JumpReLU SAEs utilize gating functions and straight-through estimators to approximate direct L0 optimization (Rajamanoharan et al., 2024a;b). These advancements enhance the LSAE versus sparsity trade-off; however, no single approach has been universally identified as superior across downstream tasks (Karvonen et al., 2024). Beyond imposing sparsity penalties, Braun et al. (2024) enhance SAEs to minimize KL divergence in relation to the model's logits, directly decreasing LSAE. Meanwhile, Olmo et al. (2024) integrate model gradients into TopK activations to yield more causal representations. However, gradient-based techniques introduce computational burdens and face significant limitations, as SAEs are usually trained on cached activations without accessible gradients (Lieberum et al., 2024).  

**Fine-tuning SAEs.** While this paper emphasizes fine-tuning a model around an SAE, another research avenue involves fine-tuning SAEs themselves. Some scholars have adapted SAEs to specific domains via context oversampling (Bricken et al., 2024) or training on domain-specific activations (Drori, 2024). Kissane et al. (2024) observed that training SAEs on chat data encapsulates the refusal latent, in contrast to training on the Pile dataset (Gao et al., 2020). Kutsyk et al. (2024) further explore the conditions under which base model SAEs can generalize to a chat-tuned model, indicating its dependence on the employed language model.  

**Training interpretable models.** Two prior inquiries evaluate the training of interpretable models utilizing SAEs: both (Lai & Heimersheim, 2024) and (Lai & Huang, 2024) engage in concurrent training of SAEs and models, achieving improvements in LSAE. Nonetheless, this concurrency necessitates training models from inception, limiting its applicability to existing models and demonstrating effectiveness only in constrained scenarios; in contrast, our method is notably efficient and operates effectively on models with up to 27 billion parameters. Numerous former studies target this domain without utilizing SAEs. Elhage et al. (2022b) unveil the softmax linear unit (SoLU) activation function, increasing the count of interpretable neurons without hindering downstream performance; Liu et al. (2023) advocate for a novel loss term that penalizes spatially distant connections in the network, yielding visually interpretable networks; Liu et al. (2024) introduce Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks as an alternative to conventional MLPs, comprising trainable activation functions potentially substitutable with symbolic formulas; and Heimersheim (2024) optimizes LayerNorm components in GPT-2 while minimally affecting downstream loss.  

2. **Low-Rank Adapting Models for SAEs**  
(Visual representation included in the original document)  

**Parameter Efficient Fine Tuning.** Parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) diminishes the full supervised fine-tuning costs by adjusting fewer effective parameters. Among the most straightforward and effective PEFT methodologies is low-rank adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2021). LoRA functions by maintaining a frozen pretrained weight matrix \(W_0 \in R^{d \times k}\), alongside low-rank matrices \(A \in R^{d \times r}\) and \(B \in R^{r \times k}\) with \(r \ll \min(d, k)\), such that the original forward pass \(h(x) = W_0x\) is modified to become \(\hat{h}(x) = W_0x + ABx\). Here, \(A\) and \(B\) are trainable while the rest of the model remains fixed, yielding a low-rank update to the base model.  

3. **Optimizing Models for Sparse Autoencoders**  
In this section, we rigorously outline existing methods for training SAEs alongside our approach for adapting models to SAEs. For a decoder-only transformer characterized by \(L\) layers, a hidden dimension \(d\), an input \(x_0\), and an output \(y\), we denote the activation post the \(i^{th}\) layer as \(x_i\). The \(i^{th}\) transformer block can be described as a function \(h_i\), such that the network can be denoted as \(x_i = h_i(x_{i−1})\) for \(1 \leq i \leq L\) and \(y = softmax(x_L)\).  

3.1. **TopK Sparse Autoencoders**  
SAEs learn an encoder \(W_{enc} \in R^{m \times d}\) with \(m \gg d\), alongside a decoder \(W_{dec} \in R^{d \times m}\) containing unit norm columns, and biases \(b_{enc} \in R^m\), \(b_{dec} \in R^d\). The m columns of \(W_{dec}\) constitute the latents. For an activation \(x_l\), the TopK SAE (Gao et al., 2024) reconstructs the activation as follows:  
\(z = TopK(W_{enc}(x_l − b_{dec}) + b_{enc})\)  
\(\hat{x}_l = W_{dec}z + b_{dec} = \sum_{i} w_i f_i\)  
During training, the SAE minimizes the reconstruction error \(L = \|x_l − \hat{x}_l\|^2\). We train TopK SAEs with \(k = 64\) for Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.2-1B using 2B and 4B tokens, respectively, from the RedPajama dataset (Weber et al., 2024).  

3.2. **End-to-End Sparse Autoencoders**  
In an e2e SAE (Braun et al., 2024), the SAE aims to minimize KL divergence relative to the base model instead of reconstruction error. Formally, if we define \(\hat{x}_l = SAE(x_l)\), \(\hat{x}_i = h_i(\hat{x}_{i−1})\) for \(l < i \leq L\), and \(\hat{y} = softmax(\hat{x}_L\), then the e2e SAE minimizes \(L = KL(\hat{y}, y)\). For both e2e and TopK SAEs, we utilize a TopK activation function with consistent sparsity to maintain fair comparison.  

3.3. **JumpReLU Sparse Autoencoders**  
We additionally evaluate our method using the Gemma Scope JumpReLU SAEs. Rather than the TopK function, JumpReLU SAEs (Rajamanoharan et al., 2024b) implement the JumpReLU activation function, \(JumpReLU_{\theta}(z) := zH(z − \theta)\), where \(H\) denotes the Heaviside step function and \(\theta > 0\) signifies the threshold for JumpReLU. The SAE is trained to minimize \(L = \|\hat{x} − x\|^2 + \lambda \|z\|_0\), where \(z\) is defined in Equation (4).  

3.4. **Method for Low-Rank Adapting Models to SAEs Formulation**  
We thoroughly describe our methodology for optimizing models with respect to SAEs, utilizing notation from Equations (2) through (4). We position a frozen SAE directly after layer \(\ell\), with the resulting reconstructed activation \(\hat{x}_\ell = SAE(x_\ell)\) propagating through the remaining layers to yield \(\hat{x}_i = h_i(\hat{x}_{i−1})\) for \(\ell + 1 \leq i \leq L\) and \(y = softmax(x_L)\). For JumpReLU SAEs, only subsequent layers can be adapted to prevent average sparsity disruption, whereas TopK SAEs permit adapter training across all layers by upholding the TopK constraint during training. We integrate low-rank adapters of rank \(r\) within each MLP and attention sublayer of every affected layer. Specifically, for each frozen weight matrix \(W_i \in R^{d_1 \times d_2}\), we append \(A_i \in R^{d_1 \times r}\) and \(B_i \in R^{r \times d_2}\), subsequently modifying the forward pass in accordance with Equation (1). The training process focuses solely on the low-rank adapters \(\Theta = \{A_i\} \cup \{B_i\}\). In all experiments, the training objective aims to minimize the KL divergence between the next token probability distribution with and without the SAE inserted:  
\(\text{arg min} \Theta \, KL(\hat{y}, y)\).  
The freezing of both the SAE and original model permits a parameter-efficient method that aligns the SAE-supported model accordingly to the behavior of the original model with minimal added cost.  

3. **Low-Rank Adapting Models for SAEs**  
(Visual representation included in the original document)  

0.05 0.10 0.15 CE Improvement (Figure Visualization)  

3. **Results**  
This section investigates how our methodology enhances the cross-entropy loss gap (LSAE − LBASE) before and after implementing LoRA across a broad spectrum of SAEs and language models. Unless specified otherwise, we employ a layer 12 residual stream SAE.  

4.1. **Scaling Laws for Downstream Loss**  
We initially scrutinize the scaling behavior of low-rank adapting models in relation to SAEs across SAE sparsity, width, language model size, LoRA rank, and model layer. Specifically, we utilize Gemma Scope’s JumpReLU SAEs (Rajamanoharan et al., 2024b). To avoid affecting the overall sparsity of these JumpReLU SAEs, we exclusively fine-tune the layers subsequent to the SAE. Across a range of sparsities, widths, and layers, we monitor both absolute and percentage improvements in LSAE − LBASE following low-rank fine-tuning. Training is conducted on 15 million random tokens from The Pile (an uncopyrighted dataset) (Gao et al., 2020), with evaluation involving a held-out validation set of 1 million random tokens. Results are depicted in Figure 4 for model size and in Figure 3 across additional scaling axes. We confirm that in all scaling regimes analyzed, we consistently reduce the LSAE − LBASE gap by at least 30%, and up to 55% in certain instances. The utilization of larger rank LoRA adapters reliably contributes to decreased final LSAE; additionally, considering we adapted using only 15 million tokens without fully converging the adapters implies greater success potential with more computational resources. Interestingly, we recognize the most significant improvements occur in middle layers, although this finding is not exceptionally robust (considering factors such as referenced studies (Lad et al., 2024), attributing this to middle layers showcasing richer, more expressive representations compared to what local SAEs can reconstruct). The effectiveness of our technique appears heightened for lower sparsity, width, and larger models; this trend may arise as these SAEs commence with an initially higher cross-entropy loss gap. Notably, it is promising to observe that our method's effectiveness correlates positively with larger models.  

4.2. **Downstream Loss vs. Computational Cost**  
Next, we explore the interplay between LSAE and training duration for TopK SAEs, e2e SAEs, and low-rank adapted TopK SAEs. To pursue this analysis, we must train our own TopK and e2e SAEs to establish their training curves. We employ checkpoints from the TopK training run to gauge the training curve for the amalgamated TopK SAEs + LoRA; after each 10% training checkpoint of the TopK SAEs, we low-rank adapt the model checkpoint with rank 64 LoRA over all layers. Training is conducted on layer 12 of Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-2-2B, where TopK and e2e SAEs engage in training for 4 billion tokens on Llama-3.2-1B and for 2 billion tokens on Gemma-2-2B (in alignment with the token counts utilized for Gemma Scope SAEs).  

4. **Low-Rank Adapting Models for SAEs**  
(Similar figures and comparative data included in the original text)

5. **Adapting Multiple SAEs**  
Integrating multiple SAEs into a language model results in swift inflation of LSAE (as evidenced in Figure 6, where incorporating five SAEs leads to a cross-entropy error nearing 10 nats, below even that of a unigram model (Gao et al., 2024)). Nevertheless, introducing multiple SAEs simultaneously is advantageous for circuit analysis, allowing for the determination of dependencies among SAE latents (notably, prior SAE circuits work (Marks et al., 2024) utilized error terms to evade this limitation, leading to less interpretable circuits). Consequently, we adapt our methodology to facilitate simultaneous integration of multiple SAEs; we incorporate all SAEs during training while adhering to the framework established in Section 3.4. Our technique's efficacy is assessed with Table 1.  

6. **Downstream Improvements**  
A common critique levelled at preceding SAE optimization endeavors is the insufficiency of grounded metrics for evaluating an SAE's performance. Earlier efforts have primarily depended on unsupervised metrics as described in Section 4. Recent studies have, however, instituted evaluative metrics geared towards assessing model and SAE efficacy against downstream tasks (Karvonen et al., 2024; Pres et al., 2024). In light of these developments, we will assess our methodology against an array of downstream benchmarks: 1. In Section 5.1, we demonstrate that the implementation of LoRA across all layers enhances downstream task performance on SAEBench. 2. In Section 5.2, we propose a novel steering metric, showcasing enhancements achieved through our method. This introduction of a new metric arises from the observation that SAEBench metrics do not adequately assess the effects of SAEs upon next-token generation. 3. In Section 5.3, we affirm that our approach fosters improvements in overall model performance with the SAE incorporated 
on MMLU, HellaSwag, and TruthfulQA.  

**5.1. SAEBench**  
In addressing the pivotal challenge of quantifying how effectively a model and SAE collaborate, Karvonen et al. (2024) introduced SAEBench, a benchmarking suite of SAE metrics aimed at being representative of potential real-world applications. For the Gemma-2-2B TopK SAE (with \(L_0 = 64\)) trained in Section 4.2, both the model with the SAE and the model incorporating the SAE + LoRA are evaluated on SAEBench. In particular, analyses are conducted on measures including spurious correlation removal (SCR), targeted probe perturbation (TPP), SPARSE PROBING, automated interpretability (AUTOINTERP), and feature absorption (ABSORPTION). SCR gauges how well latents for different concepts are distinguished, with superior scores denoting enhanced ability to debias a classifier. TPP assesses the effects of ablating specific latents on probe accuracy, where higher scores suggest effective isolation of latents corresponding to classes within a dataset. SPARSE PROBING measures the efficacy of a k-sparse probe trained on SAE latents, with higher scores indicating more proficient feature learning. AUTOINTERP measures the interpretability of SAE latents, as judged by a language model (GPT-4o-mini (OpenAI, 2024)). ABSORPTION quantifies the extent to which latents coalesce together to improve sparsity. All employed metrics range from 0 to 1, with higher scores being preferable except for ABSORPTION.  

(Results further illustrated including tables/figures in original document)  

7. **Analyzing Why Our Method Works**  
**6.1. Per Token Improvement Breakdown**  
In an experiment assessing the influence of LoRA on LSAE improvements, we evaluate the distribution of \(\Delta LSAE\) between both the original and LoRA-infused models across 15 million validation tokens. Results reveal considerable variability in per-token loss alteration, with losses on 37% of tokens registering as worsened (the histogram of degradation detailed in the figure). The majority of total improvement stems from minor per-token reductions in loss (approximately \(10^{-2}\) to 1 nats), suggesting that LoRA enhances loss uniformly across numerous tokens rather than yielding a bimodal distribution.

**6.2. Activation Distances**  
A concern raised by Braun et al. (2024) pertains to potential shifts in distribution of activations when optimizing towards KL divergence, potentially leading them to deviate from the original model's computational path. We find this is not the case with our approach: as depicted in Figure 11, across a validation set comprising 500k tokens, our method exhibits a slight decrease in distance between activations following the SAE and activations from the original model, while cosine similarities exhibit a mild increase.  

8. **Conclusion**  
Low-rank adapting models for SAEs provide a swift, cost-effective, and efficient methodology for constructing interpretable model and SAE systems. Moreover, models trained via low-rank adaptation demonstrate superiority in utilizing their SAEs for downstream tasks. Importantly, our work challenges the prevailing notion that enhancing interpretability must rely exclusively on post-hoc model decomposition. We posit that our technique's rapidity surpasses e2e training due to the broader scope it avails for optimization, suggesting that concentrating on a wider spectrum of potential modifications to language models may emerge as a fruitful avenue. We aspire for the findings in this paper to pave the way for subsequent techniques in this domain. 

(Acknowledgments and References retained as outlined in original text).

**Abstract**

## 1 Introduction  
“To enable a new era of medicine through research, technology, and policies that empower patients, researchers, and providers to work together toward the development of individualized care.” – Mission Statement, Precision Medicine Initiative, 2015 [1]  

Precision Medicine (PM) is an innovative healthcare methodology that customises and personalises medical care according to each individual’s characteristics [10, 48, 62, 127]. By employing detailed health information, PM aims to enhance prevention, diagnosis, and treatment methods, thus revolutionising the “one-drug-fits-all” model. The Polygenic Risk Score (PRS), a pivotal element of the PM paradigm, estimates an individual’s genetic risk for a variety of diseases prior to their manifestation [32, 76, 77]. Researchers identify common genetic variants correlated with specific ailments and assign weights based on their impact on disease risk [29]. These weighted effects are tallied to yield a comprehensive risk score, reflecting the likelihood of developing certain diseases according to one's genetic composition [28, 29]. Technically, PM applications, such as PRS, depend heavily on the capacity to efficiently process, interpret, and communicate insights derived from intricate, multi-faceted healthcare datasets [62, 112]—predominantly biological data with genetics in a central position [34, 132]. This task presents considerable computational hurdles through machine learning, high-performance computing, and various specialised AI techniques [16, 41].   

Conversely, questions remain about how these advanced PM technologies can be effectively integrated into real-world healthcare practices, ensuring information is communicated in ways that are understandable, usable, and responsibly empowering for patients and healthcare professionals alike [65, 69, 132, 133]—this is where HCI can play a critical role [107]. PRS exemplifies an opportunity to investigate the confluence of HCI and PM. As a highly advanced and well-established system within the PM landscape, PRS stands as a thorough and thought-provoking case for exploring both the possibilities and the challenges of introducing genetic data into PM. Despite having the potential to transform PM by facilitating early disease risk detection and personalised prevention strategies, PRS faces numerous challenges and barriers to broad adoption [63, 85, 101] and responsible utilisation [2]. These obstacles include worries regarding the accuracy of PRS for individuals from varying genetic backgrounds due to the predominance of European-centric genotype data [63, 85] and possible adverse emotional consequences of receiving risk information [101]. The application of PRS in diverse contexts, such as embryo selection [121], regulation by insurance policies [134], or educational settings (pertaining to academic achievements [109] and bullying [108]), prompts vital conversations regarding privacy, fairness, and the ethical dimensions of such technologies. In the UK, the care.data programme scandal has severely undermined public confidence in healthcare data sharing [115]. As a result, the public has adopted a more cautious and frequently sceptical outlook on such initiatives [64, 79]. However, trust remains a foundational requisite for the acceptance and efficacy of data-driven healthcare technologies [46, 47, 58]. Additionally, consumer-oriented PRS services, especially those from Direct-To-Consumer Genetic Testing (DTC-GT) companies like 23andMe and Ancestry [99, 116], add complexity concerning privacy and the perceived reliability of outcomes [80]. Our inquiry was driven by these apprehensions, aimed at grasping what potential users and beneficiaries see as perceived barriers, benefits, and challenges related to adopting and utilising PRS-based services in their daily lives. Additionally, we sought to investigate how participants’ personal experiences, particularly in terms of sharing personal data and their interaction with health services, might shape their decisions regarding the prospective adoption of PRS.  

We conducted a mixed-methods study comprising a survey of 254 individuals and 11 one-hour interviews, supported by interactive storyboards developed using the ContraVision technique [83]. The survey's goal was to gauge public perceptions of PRS and identify potential barriers to its implementation, yielding both quantitative and qualitative data. The interviews offered nuanced qualitative insights into how people's experiences and narratives impact their informed choices surrounding PRS. Our survey findings pinpointed ten significant obstacles to PRS adoption and revealed a multifaceted landscape of opinions concerning the use of PRS in sensitive social contexts. Although participants generally held a neutral stance on PRS, specific issues, such as embryo selection and sperm/egg donation, drew considerable attention, compared to prevalent negative sentiments regarding its application in education, insurance, and dating, due to societal and ethical dilemmas. Furthermore, interview findings revealed key challenges, such as the difficulty of interpreting PRS results, demographic bias in genetic data repositories, and concerns regarding psychological readiness. Respondents called for clearer information and support, especially regarding the emotional and ethical dimensions of PRS, while voicing varying levels of scepticism regarding trust in the healthcare system and data privacy. 

Our study enhances the HCI field by presenting these empirical findings and formulating design recommendations and implications for PRS and PM at large. We also consider how a responsible PRS framework could tackle systemic complexities by prioritising data diversity, building trust, and ensuring ethical governance. These insights underscore a critical yet underexplored necessity—adapting and extending HCI viewpoints to grapple with the unique complexities of PM, characterised by its reliance on highly personalised data and the ever-evolving nature of patient care. From this, we propose potential future avenues, suggesting Human-Precision Medicine Interaction (HPMI) as a novel area for exploration within HCI that stresses public participation in the co-development and implementation of PM technologies.  

## 2 Related Work  

### 2.1 Precision Medicine (PM) and Human-Computer Interaction (HCI)  
Precision Medicine (PM) 1 tailors treatments based on an individual’s health-related data (including genetic, environmental, and lifestyle influences), utilising data analysis to enhance diagnosis and treatment efficacy [10, 48, 62, 127]. The essence of PM concerns the collection, interpretation, and analysis of data. Diverging from a "one-drug-fits-all" strategy, PM harnesses genetic and other health information alongside biomarkers to deliver “the right drug at the right dose to the right patient” [30]. For instance, in oncology, the genetic examination of tumours enables more targeted therapies [82]. Another PM application involves leveraging the vulnerabilities in breast cancer cells’ DNA repair processes to enhance treatment effectiveness [104]. With technological advancements and data proliferation, PM positions itself for an upward trajectory, offering improved personalisation and precision in healthcare, leading to better management and treatment pathways for patients.  

Although PM as a discipline was formalised around 1998 with its inaugural application in breast cancer care [33], it has garnered significant momentum following the U.S. Precision Medicine Initiative initiated in 2015 [30]. PM is inherently cross-disciplinary, spanning over a hundred fields [132] including genomics, data science, machine learning, and clinical trials [110]. In recent years, the CHI community has exhibited a growing interest in PM. While a few papers overtly reference “precision medicine” or its alternatives 2 to define their research, the field has implicitly addressed relevant themes through various HCI investigations. For example, Calisto et al. concentrated on customising communication between intelligent systems and clinicians during breast cancer diagnoses, effectively reducing medical errors and augmenting decision-making improvements [23]. Similarly, Mitchell et al. meld machine learning with expert systems to deliver tailored nutritional suggestions for individuals with type 2 diabetes, showcasing the potential of HCI research to render complex data-driven insights actionable for patients [43]. However, these studies provoke vital considerations surrounding the balance between automation and human oversight in medical practices. They must carefully navigate the ethical and practical challenges of embedding these systems in everyday clinical workflows, ensuring that technology amplifies rather than overshadows human elements of care. For instance, in oncology, Verma et al. discussed how physicians’ trust in AI is anchored in their contested experiences with AI during actual practice rather than general acceptance [125].  

Beyond explicit PM research, many contributions within this domain target adjacent critical issues pertinent to PM. A primary consideration revolves around data privacy and security, which involves designing interfaces that enhance privacy protections while allowing fine-tuned control over data consent, thus empowering users to manage their sensitive health data effectively [11, 73, 81]. Additionally, researchers have assessed privacy risks and embedded regulatory frameworks such as GDPR into the design of tracking technologies, ensuring the safeguarding of user data and fostering trust in digital health applications [87, 118]. Another pivotal area encompasses patient engagement and empowerment, where personalised interfaces have been established to assist patients in better comprehending and managing their health data, resulting in a more proactive role in medical decision-making [53, 56, 135]. Moreover, studies in this area have facilitated effective communication between patients and healthcare teams, fostering active patient involvement in custom-tailored treatment strategies and cooperative decision-making [15, 78, 88].  

2 The alternatives to PM include, but are not limited to, terms like “personalised medicine,” “customised medicine,” or “individualised medicine.” These terms may be used differently based on context but generally share similar meanings with PM. 

### 2.2 Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)  
Polygenic Risk Score (PRS) 3, a genetics-centered health prediction technology, epitomises PM. PRS calculates an individual's genetic risk for diseases even before they manifest [32, 76, 77].  

**Figure 2** depicts the generation of a PRS. The process commences with constructing a PRS model for a specific disease. Researchers first conduct Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) to identify genetic variants linked to particular diseases [28, 70]. Each identified variant is evaluated and given a weight based on its impact on disease risk [29]. PRS is computed by aggregating an individual's weighted genetic variants, reflecting the likelihood of developing certain diseases [28, 29]. Subsequently, an individual’s genotype profile is essential for PRS generation, typically initiated through services like Direct-To-Consumer Genetic Testing (DTC-GT) such as 23andMe 4 or Ancestry 5, who provide genetic testing via saliva samples for a fee [97]. Following receipt of their genotype data from these services, individuals may opt to share their genetic information with third-party providers for PRS analysis [42]. The analysis varies by provider and usually involves steps like data upload, genetic imputation, risk computation, and report generation, often with options for privacy settings and consultation. Some DTC-GT services also incorporate PRS analysis into their health reports [92]. Moreover, individuals proficient in biostatistics and genetics may use specialised PRS analysis software via academic or research channels [29, 39]. PRS is generally represented using percentiles, conforming to a normal distribution [37, 131]. Most individuals find themselves in the middle range of the distribution, indicating an average risk compared to the overall dataset [71]. A few might fall at the extremes, representing either diminished (decreased) or heightened (increased) risk, depending on their specific position [71]. However, this distribution may fluctuate depending on the specific population and traits chosen for analysis [27].  

PRS holds the potential to revolutionise PM by facilitating early detection of disease risks and enabling custom-tailored prevention strategies. Currently, various PRS models exist for conditions such as coronary artery disease, type 1 and 2 diabetes, obesity, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and Alzheimer's disease, with ongoing clinical evaluation [27, 57, 71, 100]. By shedding light on genetic risks, PRS can motivate lifestyle modifications, encourage regular monitoring, and promote preventive measures to mitigate disease risk [66, 119]. Additionally, PRS allows for the creation of personalised health management plans finely tuned to an individual’s genetic profile, making healthcare delivery more efficient and targeted [27, 119]. Awareness of one's genetic risks equips individuals to make better-informed choices regarding diet, exercise, medication, and health screenings [74]. Importantly, PRS engenders heightened health awareness that promotes proactive health behaviours and enhances overall well-being [27]. Furthermore, it offers critical insights for family health planning, enabling relatives to collaboratively devise strategies, particularly for managing hereditary conditions [66, 74].  

While DTC-GT services typically furnish consumers with relatively straightforward genetic analyses—such as ancestry assessments or single-gene trait evaluations—PRS pushes the envelope further into the territory of predictive analytics. However, this transition from descriptive to predictive data precipitates considerable complexities, raising vital concerns that hinder both the adoption and responsible use of PRS [2, 63, 85, 101]. The speculative nature of PRS engenders inherent uncertainty and variability. This is particularly problematic since PRS relies on existing genotype databases that predominantly represent European populations, decreasing its accuracy for individuals from diverse genetic backgrounds and aggravating health disparities [63, 85]. Moreover, the mental strain associated with receiving risk predictions can induce anxiety and significantly influence decision-making processes [101]. The ethical implications become even more elaborate when considering PRS applications in sensitive spheres such as embryo selection [121], insurance practices [134], and educational environments [108, 109]. Within these contexts, PRS not only gives rise to concerns about privacy and fairness but also about the potential for misuse and discrimination. In recent years, public trust in healthcare data sharing in the UK has been severely compromised, significantly influenced by events like the care.data programme scandal [115]. Users have approached such initiatives with a heightened degree of caution and skepticism [64, 79]. Nevertheless, trust is a fundamental condition for the acceptance and functionality of data-dependent healthcare technologies [46, 47, 58]. Furthermore, consumer-accessible PRS services, including those from DTC-GT companies, add an additional layer of intricacy concerning privacy and the perceived reliability of genetic analyses [80].  

Motivated by these concerns, this research aimed to ascertain the perceived barriers, benefits, and challenges relating to the adoption and use of PRS-based services within everyday contexts. Moreover, we sought to investigate how individual experiences, particularly concerning the sharing of personal data and utilisation of health services, might influence their decision-making processes surrounding potential PRS adoption. A mixed-methods study was conducted integrating a survey with 254 participants and 11 one-hour interviews scaffolded with interactive storyboards designed using the ContraVision technique [83]. The survey aimed to scrutinise public perceptions of PRS while identifying possible barriers to its use, thus yielding both quantitative and qualitative data. Interviews provided nuanced qualitative insights into how individuals’ personal experiences and narratives shape their informed decisions regarding PRS. Survey results highlighted ten pivotal barriers to PRS adoption and unveiled a complex spectrum of opinions concerning its implications in socially sensitive contexts. While participants showed a generally neutral stance towards PRS, specific subjects like embryo selection and sperm/egg donation garnered significant interest compared to stronger negative views regarding its applications in education, insurance, and dating due to ethical concerns. Additionally, findings from interviews indicated principal challenges such as the intricacy of PRS result interpretation, demographic biases in genetic databases, and worries about psychological preparedness. Participants expressed a strong desire for clear information and support—particularly in relation to the psychological and ethical ramifications—while expressing diverse levels of skepticism towards trust in healthcare institutions and data privacy.  

This contribution enriches the HCI domain by presenting empirically based findings, together with formulating design recommendations and implications for PRS and PM at large. We also deliberate on how a responsible PRS framework could help to address systemic complexities by prioritising data diversity, establishing trust, and ensuring ethical governance. These insights illuminate a crucial yet underexplored requirement—adapting and expanding HCI viewpoints to face the particular complexities of PM, which centres on highly individualised data and the fluid dynamics of patient care. Consequently, our proposal of the Human-Precision Medicine Interaction (HPMI) concept aims to open a new avenue of research and practice within HCI, promoting diligence and responsible engagement in co-developing PM technologies.

name of paper: Redefining Machine Unlearning: A Conformal Prediction-Motivated Approach
author: gpt-4o
summary: Machine unlearning seeks to systematically remove specified data from a trained model, effectively achieving a state as though the data had never been encountered during training. While metrics such as Unlearning Accuracy (UA) and Membership Inference Attack (MIA) provide a baseline for assessing unlearning performance, they fall short of evaluating the completeness and reliability of forgetting. This is because the ground truth labels remain potential candidates within the scope of uncertainty quantification, leaving gaps in the evaluation of true forgetting. In this paper, we identify critical limitations in existing unlearning metrics and propose enhanced evaluation metrics inspired by conformal prediction. Our metrics can effectively capture the extent to which ground truth labels are excluded from the prediction set. Furthermore, we observe that many existing machine unlearning methods do not achieve satisfactory forgetting performance when evaluated with our new metrics. To address this, we propose an unlearning framework that integrates conformal prediction insights into Carlini & Wagner adversarial attack loss. Extensive experiments on the image classification task demonstrate that our enhanced metrics offer deeper insights into unlearning effectiveness, and that our unlearning framework significantly improves the forgetting quality of unlearning methods.
