**Redefining Machine Unlearning: A Conformal Prediction-Motivated Approach**  
**Yingdan Shi 1, Ren Wang 1**  

**Abstract**  
Machine unlearning aims to systematically eliminate specified data from a trained model, effectively reverting the model to a state as if the data had never been part of the training process. While evaluative indicators, like Unlearning Accuracy (UA) and Membership Inference Attack (MIA), offer a foundational perspective on unlearning efficacy, they inadequately assess the thoroughness and dependability of forgetting. This inadequacy arises from the retention of ground truth labels as potential entities within the uncertainty quantification framework, thus creating assessment voids relative to genuine forgetting. In this paper, we recognize significant shortcomings in existing unlearning metrics and introduce improved evaluative metrics that draw inspiration from conformal prediction. Our proposed metrics adeptly gauge the degree to which true labels are omitted from the prediction set. Moreover, our analysis reveals that several current machine unlearning techniques are inadequate in forgetting performance when appraised using our new metrics. To counter this, we suggest an unlearning paradigm that amalgamates conformal prediction principles with adversarial attack loss as defined by Carlini and Wagner. Comprehensive experiments on image classification tasks provide evidence that our refined metrics yield more informative insights into unlearning effectiveness, and that our proposed framework markedly enhances the quality of forgetting in unlearning methods.

**1. Introduction**  
The significance of machine unlearning has grown immensely, particularly in relation to data privacy, largely influenced by regulatory frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) (Bourtoule et al., 2021). These regulations underscore individuals' rights to have their data expunged or forgotten, necessitating the development of machine unlearning techniques that enable machine learning models to function as if specific data points had never been utilized during training. Existing post hoc machine unlearning strategies can be segmented into training-based (Graves et al., 2021; Warnecke et al., 2021; Thudi et al., 2022; Tarun et al., 2023) and training-free (Guo et al., 2019; Sekhari et al., 2021; Nguyen et al., 2020; Golatkar et al., 2020b; 2021; Foster et al., 2024) frameworks, depending on whether they necessitate traditional training steps during the unlearning process (Foster et al., 2024). A variety of metrics have been proposed to assess the effectiveness of unlearning by measuring the quality of forgetting and the model's predictive capabilities post-unlearning (Kashef, 2021; Shokri et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021; Brophy & Lowd, 2021; Cao & Yang, 2015). Nonetheless, current metrics, including UA and MIA, fail to provide a comprehensive evaluation of forgetting quality and dependability. These metrics predominantly assess whether models accurately predict forgotten data, overlooking how effectively the model has forgotten it. Merely classifying forgotten data incorrectly does not inherently imply that the model has entirely forgotten that data.

**Conformal Prediction-Motivated Machine Unlearning**  
In pursuit of this understanding, we implement conformal prediction (Papadopoulos et al., 2002; Lei & Wasserman, 2014) within our evaluation of unlearning models. Empirical results identify that even when a model misclassifies certain forgotten data, a notable fraction of these instances continues to be part of the conformal prediction set. This phenomenon is visually represented in Table 1 using Grad-CAM (Selvaraju et al., 2017), which illustrates significant areas of focus in model predictions via Grad-CAM maps. The Finetune unlearning method, despite misclassifying forgotten data, still highlights critical features, as the true label persists in the prediction set. Conversely, our unlearning approach effectively eliminates the true label from the set, resulting in a stark shift of activation regions away from essential object features. This underscores that improved forgetting quality is achieved when true labels can be excluded from the prediction set.

(Graves et al., 2021; Warnecke et al., 2021; Thudi et al., 2022; Tarun et al., 2023) delineates the methodologies into those reliant on training versus those that do not, observing key distinctions that illuminate the effectiveness of forgetting strategies.

To gauge the efficacy of machine unlearning, several traditional metrics, including UA (Brophy & Lowd, 2021; Foster et al., 2024), retain accuracy (RA), test accuracy (TA), and MIA (Shokri et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021), have been applied across three prototype machine unlearning methods: Retrain (RT), Finetune (FT) (Warnecke et al., 2021), and Random Label (RL) (Graves et al., 2021). Our experiments focus on a ResNet-18 model and the CIFAR-10 dataset, particularly under random data forgetting conditions. As demonstrated in Table 2, UA measurements reveal certain forgotten data are still represented in the model post-unlearning, substantiated by MIA outcomes.

While traditional metrics may provide valuable insights into the extent of forgetting, they lack the capability to confirm that forgotten data points have been wholly purged from any aspect of the model’s outputs. We utilize conformal prediction to validate our premise, asserting that true labels of forgotten data frequently appear in the prediction set.

**To this end, Table 3 quantifies misclassified data points and their retention in the prediction set, providing compelling evidence of the inadequacy of metrics like UA and MIA in ascertaining complete forgetting.** 

By introducing new metrics rooted in the concepts of Conformal Prediction, we further aim to address shortcomings in prior methodologies. This leads to the derivation of two central metrics: Conformal Ratio (CR) and Membership Inference Attack Conformal Ratio (MIACR), both of which enable a more nuanced evaluation of unlearning performance. 

**Finally, this work contributes substantial advancements within the domain of machine unlearning, closely aligning metrics with the principles of conformal prediction to foster rigorous performance assessments.**

**Detection Is All You Need: An Optimal Prior-Free Black-Box Method for Piecewise Stationary Bandits**  
Argyrios Gerogiannis

**Abstract**  
We examine the challenge of piecewise stationary bandits that lack prior insights about the underlying non-stationarity. We introduce a groundbreaking black-box algorithm suitable for a wide variety of common parametric bandit frameworks. Our method, named Detection Augmented Bandit (DAB), is modular in design, allowing for any stationary bandit algorithm to be fed into it, enhancing it with a change detection mechanism. Under mild assumptions, DAB achieves optimal regret in the piecewise stationary context. Specifically, we demonstrate that DAB secures the order-optimal regret bound of ˜O(√NT T), where NT represents the number of changes throughout the horizon T, assuming its stationary bandit input has similar optimal regret assurances. When applying DAB across various parametric bandit scenarios, we recover several recent leading results. In particular, for self-concordant bandits, DAB realizes optimal dynamic regret, whereas previous studies yield suboptimal results reliant on knowledge of non-stationarity. In simulations evaluating piecewise stationary contexts, DAB consistently outshines current methodologies, irrespective of the number of changes encountered. Notably, although DAB is engineered for piecewise stationary scenarios, it also proves beneficial in drifting environments, surpassing methods specifically tailored for this type of non-stationarity.

**1 Introduction**  
Bandit models have numerous applications in engineering sectors, including recommendation systems (Li et al., 2010; Lefortier et al., 2014), online advertising (Chapelle and Li, 2011; Sertan et al., 2012; Schwartz et al., 2017), dynamic pricing (Tajik et al., 2024), and real-time bidding (Flajolet and Jaillet, 2017). Originating from the multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem posed by Robbins (1952), many variants have been analyzed. The parametric bandit (PB) context articulated in Auer (2002), Filippi et al. (2010), and Faury et al. (2020) forms a significant subset where an agent interacts with an environment over T different rounds. In each round t, the agent selects a single action At from a chosen set A ⊆Rd and receives a stochastic reward denoted as Xt = ft(At) + εt = µ(⟨θt, At⟩) + εt, where θt represents an unknown governing parameter and µ: R →R is an injective function. The noise εt incorporates zero-mean sub-Gaussian distribution. The agent aims to devise a control policy {πt}T t=1, mapping the action history and stochastic rewards up to time t −1 to an action At for time t, in order to minimize the (dynamic) regret, RT := EAt∼πt " TΣt=1 max a∈A ft(a) − ft(At) #.  

Typically, bandit environments are assumed to be stationary, implying that the reward distribution remains constant across actions (with θt’s unchanged over time). Yet, this assumption often fails in real-world applications; user preferences, product ranges, and market dynamics usually shift over time. Non-stationarity is broadly divided into gradual drifts and abrupt changes. Gradual changes signify slow, continuous alterations, while abrupt shifts represent sudden, decisive changes at defined points, emerging from factors such as evolving user behaviors, new market trends, or competitive actions. This paper delves into piecewise stationary parametric bandits (PS-PBs) characterized by reward distribution shifts occurring abruptly at specific times noted as 1 := ν0 < ν1 < ... < νNT < νNT +1 := T + 1. The governing parameters θt remain constant between these change points, i.e., θt = θt′ for rounds νk ≤ t, t′ < νk+1, changing only at the change points, θνk−1 ̸= θνk. Here, NT indicates the frequency of changes throughout T rounds. Our model extends to PS variations of linear bandits (LBs) where g functions as the identity, generalized linear bandits (GLBs), and self-concordant bandits (SCBs), with εt showcasing a variance influenced by g (⟨θt, At⟩), which possesses a specific self-concordant attribute. The minimax-optimal (information-theoretic) lower bound for PS-MABs is estimably ˜O(√NT T), disregarding problem-dependent constants (Garivier and Moulines, 2011). This finding can be adapted to the PS-PB context, reaffirming the same lower limit. We propose an algorithm that meets this lower bound, established under reasonable conditions regarding minimal gaps between change points. These conditions are lenient, given that permitting rapid succession of change points violates the essence of piecewise stationarity, which necessitates adequate stationary intervals for algorithms to effectively respond to changes.

Non-stationary (NS) bandit algorithms can either be adaptive or restarting. Adaptive techniques continuously adapt control strategies in response to alterations in reward distributions, while restarting methods reset and initiate the learning process periodically. We categorize algorithms based on their adherence to non-stationarity knowledge: those reliant on such knowledge are termed prior-based, while others are acknowledged as prior-free. Prior-based adaptive methodologies comprise discounted and sliding-window algorithms that weigh recent findings more heavily, e.g., Kocsis and Szepesvári (2006); Garivier and Moulines (2011) for NS-MABs, Russac et al. (2019); Cheung et al. (2019); Wang et al. (2023) for NS-LBs, and Russac et al. (2020); Faury et al. (2021); Wang et al. (2023) for NS-GLBs, as well as Russac et al. (2021); Wang et al. (2023) for NS-SCBs. Budget-restarting strategies, seen in Besbes et al. (2014) for NS-MABs, Zhao et al. (2020) for NS-LBs, and Zhao et al. (2020) for NS-GLBs, echo prior-based restarting algorithms. Additionally, detection-centric restarting algorithms can adopt both prior-based and prior-free structures. Liu et al. (2018); Cao et al. (2019) illustrate prior-based methods for NS-MABs, while Auer et al. (2019); Besson et al. (2022); Huang et al. (2025) represent prior-free instances. In the NS-LB realm, one may refer to Hong et al. (2023). This study proposes and examines a prior-free detection-based restarting mechanism for PS-PBs, motivated by the often-lacking prior knowledge of non-stationarity in practical applications and noting that restarting methods can exhibit comparable or lesser complexity than their adaptive counterparts in worst-case evaluations, as shown by Peng and Papadimitriou (2024).

Prior-free algorithms, especially black-box ones, enhance any stationary bandit method to accommodate non-stationarity, avoiding the need for custom solutions for non-stationary contexts. The MASTER algorithm by Wei and Luo (2021) is the sole known order-optimal black-box method applicable across an extensive range of reinforcement learning scenarios. However, the study by Gerogiannis et al. (2024) indicates that the theoretically optimal MASTER algorithm may not function practically as its non-stationarity detection component fails to activate for manageable horizon values (a minimum of 1.24 billion), resulting in performance challenges. This paper aims at establishing a practical detection-restarting black-box algorithm specifically designed for PS-PBs, marking a pioneering effort in this domain. We undertake a modular analysis of its regret upper limit, which aligns with its minimax optimal lower bound up to logarithmic factors. To evaluate the behavior of our approach in diverse types of non-stationarity, we conduct experiments in both piecewise stationary and drifting environments, showing that our method significantly surpasses MASTER and leading approaches in the piecewise stationary context, and even excels in drifting scenarios, despite its lack of specific design for such settings.

**1.1 Our Contributions**  
- We devise a practical prior-free detection-based restarting black-box algorithm that meets order-optimal regret for PS-PBs, resolving an outstanding issue.  
- We utilize change detection by sampling from forced exploration and integrate it with a stationary bandit algorithm to address PS contexts. Our design is modular, straightforward to implement and analyze. For PS-LBs and PS-GLBs, our regret bounds are competitive with state-of-the-art, while we provide significant improvements for PS-SCBs over Wang et al. (2023).  
- Our assessments in abruptly changing environments illustrate that our approach markedly outperforms current prior-free and prior-based strategies.  
- Unexpectedly, our method also shows superior performance against state-of-the-art techniques in gradually changing environments—a condition for which it was not originally optimized. We discuss the reasons for this observation and substantiate our hypothesis with additional experiments.

**2 The Change Detection Mechanism**  
Our restarting strategy is rooted in an efficient mechanism for identifying shifts in reward distributions—an element that is crucial for practical efficacy (as noted by Gerogiannis et al. (2024)). The challenge lies in creating a detection mechanism that resets learning soon after a change-point ν, while also minimizing false alarms. Numerous detection tests are already established within the literature regarding non-stationary bandits (Liu et al., 2018; Cao et al., 2019; Auer et al., 2019; Besson et al., 2022; Hong et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025). We engaged a change detection mechanism consistent with Besson et al. (2022); Huang et al. (2025) while also being closely connected to the comprehensive body of work focused on the quickest change detection (see Poor and Hadjiliadis, 2009; Tartakovsky et al., 2014; Veeravalli and Banerjee, 2013; Xie et al., 2021 for surveys). To outline our change detection methodology, consider a simplified bandit scenario featuring a single change-point (NT = 1) and only one action (A = {a}). Here, ν stands for the change point, and we define r0 and r1 as ft(a) before and after ν, respectively, under the constraint that |r0 − r1| ≥ ∆c > 0. It is presumed that the change will only occur after a pre-change window of m length, meaning ν > m. A change detector D establishes a causal stopping rule τ when a change is identified. Let Pν and Eν denote the probability measure and expectation for the occurrence of the change-point ν, respectively. Vice versa, define P∞ and E∞ when no change happens. The associated latency ℓ for a stopping rule τ reflects the time following a change within which a declaration is made with a probability of at least 1 − δD, i.e., ℓ := inf{t ∈[T] : Pν(τ ≥ ν + t) ≤ δD, ∀ν ∈[m + 1, T − t]}. Here, [a, b] = {a, a + 1, ... , b} and [b] = [1, b] for non-negative integers a < b. An effective change detector D aims to minimize ℓ while ensuring a low probability of false alarms over a finite horizon T, ensuring P∞(τ ≤ T) ≤ δF, where δF ∈(0, 1). Our proof for the regret bound, outlined in Appendix A, reveals that D must satisfy the following condition to ensure an optimal rate of regret growth:

**Property 1**: D should meet the requirement that ℓ, m ≲ log T + log(1/δF) + log(1/δD).

We consider the generalized likelihood ratio (GLR) test described by Huang et al. (2025); Huang and Veeravalli (2025), utilizing the change detection stopping rule τ := inf {n ∈N : Gn ≥ β(n, δF)}, where Gn := sup s∈[n] log sup η0∈R sΣi=1 pη0(Xi) + log sup η1∈R nΣi=s+1 pη1(Xi) − log sup η∈R nΣi=1 pη(Xi), with β(n, δF) defined as:

6 log(1 + log(n)) + 5/2 log(4n3/2/δF) + 11.

Herein, pη signifies the density of a Gaussian random variable with mean η and variance σ². According to Huang et al. (2025), this GLR test fulfills Property 1 for rewards characterized by σ²-sub-Gaussian noise, even if the test statistic relies on the Gaussian density. The statistic Gn can be articulated in closed-form as follows:

Gn := sup s∈[n] s(ˆµ1:s − ˆµ1:n)²/(2σ²) + (n − s)(ˆµs+1:n − ˆµ1:n)²/(2σ²),

where ˆµt:t′ represents the empirical mean of samples {Xt, . . . , Xt′} for any t < t′ ∈N (see Huang et al., 2025; Kaufmann and Koolen, 2021 for derivation). With this change detector D configured, we will subsequently introduce our detection-based restarting algorithm in the next section.

**3 The DAB Algorithm**  
In a stationary bandit framework, a robust algorithm must quickly hone in on near-optimal actions to minimize regret, which leads to infrequent selection of suboptimal actions. However, in a piecewise stationary environment, changes may go unnoticed if they do not influence the actions selected by the stationary bandit algorithm. Detecting such changes requires the forced exploration of suboptimal actions. We accomplish this in our Detection Augmented Bandit (DAB) algorithm, formally recognized in Algorithm 1, by selecting a confined subset of actions, Ae = {ai : i ∈ [da]} ⊆ A, and playing them at regulated intervals to maintain a balance between regret minimization and change detection. To ensure a modular solution for the PS-PB issue, reward samples originating from forced exploration do not affect the stationary bandit algorithm. However, allowing the change detector to utilize samples from the bandit algorithm covering all actions in A (when |A| is finite) while exclusively conducting forced explorations over actions in Ae enhances empirical performance. It’s pertinent to note that this adaptation does not influence order-wise regret calculations, and we implement this variation for our experimental evaluations.

DAB mandates actions in Ae for the initial da time steps, followed by adherence to stationary bandit algorithms for the next ⌈da/αk⌉−da time steps, where αk specifies the forced exploration frequency. A change is declared when any of the da change detectors indicates a shift. Ae must be constructed in such a manner that reward sequences linked to at least one action in Ae disclose a noticeable mean-shift coinciding with potential variations in θt’s. Assuming θt ∈Θ ⊂Rd, we define ∆c := inf θ̸=θ′∈Θ max a∈Ae |µ(⟨θ, a⟩) − µ(⟨θ′, a⟩)|. Then, ∆c plays a crucial role in how effectively the actions in Ae differentiate between candidate governing parameters in Θ. The proof of our regret bound illustrates that ∆c is significantly influential on the performance of the change detectors; enhanced discernibility of changes simplifies detection processes. Given that forced exploration incurs regret, Ae should be judiciously selected to decrease da while maximizing ∆c's measure. If Θ and A are both finite, issue (1) can be resolved to craft Ae requiring the least da. When Θ encompasses vectors spanning Rd, choosing d linearly independent actions with substantial norms from A guarantees a non-zero ∆c. Our concentration is on prior-free algorithm construction, thus we don't presuppose knowledge of Θ, aside from possibly a norm constraint, a common assumption in the literature (e.g., Lattimore and Szepesvári, 2020; Wei and Luo, 2021). Accordingly, the selection of Ae driven by the pursuit of the most linearly independent vectors in A with considerable norms remains resilient to fluctuations in Θ. This strategy results in |Ae| ≤ d, confirming order-optimal regret for DAB in Section 4.

**4 Performance Analysis of DAB**  
To characterize the performance of DAB, we establish a modular regret upper limit by amalgamating the regret examination of the stationary bandit algorithm with the latency of the change detector. Let RB denote the regret upper limit of the stationary bandit algorithm B. Additionally, let ℓD and mD signify the latency and pre-change window periods of the change detector D. As highlighted in Section 1, we presume that the spacing νk − νk−1 should be sufficiently expansive to trigger the change detector, thus prompting DAB to restart prior to the next change event. Without loss of generality, we assume that the maximum regret is bounded as maxa′∈A ft(a′) − ft(a) ≤ C for all a ∈ A and t ∈ [T]. The following result articulates the upper bound for regret:

**Algorithm 1: Detection Augmented Bandit (DAB)**  
**Input:** B, D, T, A, Ae, {αk}∞ k=1  
**Initialization:** da ← |Ae|, τ ← 0, Ha,D ← ∅ ∀ a ∈ Ae, HB ← ∅, k ← 1  

1: for t = 1, 2, …, T do  
2: if (t − τ − 1) mod ⌈da/αk⌉ + 1 = i ≤ da then  
3: At ← ai  
4: Play action At and obtain the reward Xt  
5: HAt,D ← HAt,D ∪ {Xt}  
6: if D(HAt,D) = True then  
7: τ ← t  
8: ∀ a ∈ Ae, Ha,D ← ∅  
9: HB ← ∅  
10: k ← k + 1  
11: end if  
12: else  
13: At ← B(HB)  
14: Play action At and receive the reward Xt  
15: HB ← HB ∪ {(Xt, At)}  
16: end if  
17: end for  

**Theorem 1**: Assume the problem setting described in Section 1. Given Algorithm 1, utilizing a change detector D with parameters δF and δD, a stationary bandit algorithm B, and designated forced exploration frequencies (αk)NT +1 k=1. Suppose that ν1 ≥ ⌈da/αk⌉mD and νk − νk−1 ≥ ⌈da/αk−1⌉ℓD + ⌈da/αk⌉mD for k ∈ [2, NT]. Then, for sufficiently large T, the regret is upper bounded as follows:

RT ≤ CTda(NT + 1)δF + CTNT δD + C NT Σ k=1 ⌈da/αk⌉ℓD + (NT + 1)RB(T/(NT + 1)) + C[¯αT + (NT + 1)da]. 

Where ¯α represents the maximum frequency across k ranging from 1 to NT + 1. Despite the apparent linearity in T of the general regret upper limit in (2), the latter part of the result confirms the existence of order-optimal sublinear growth in regret with suitable selections for δF, δD, and {αk}. We elucidate the components within our upper bound of (2) in the order in which they appear. The first term arises from false alarms, concerning NT + 1, which denotes the number of intervals, each having a false alarm probability δF, culminating in a linear regret of CT for every event. The second term accounts for delayed detections, where NT change points each carry a detection failure probability δD, resulting in similarly incurred CT regret for every event. The third term captures regret incurred due to detection delays. The fourth term emerges from the stationary bandit algorithm, with regret maximized when interval lengths are distributed evenly as T/(NT + 1). The final term encapsulates forced exploration, limited by ¯αT rounds over the horizon and rounding discrepancies C(NT + 1)da.

**Table 1:** Regret Bound Comparison of Algorithms for PS Parametric Bandits.  
“†” denotes finite number of actions, while MASTER, ADA-OPKB, and SCB-WeightUCB also achieve the relevant bounds in this setting. “•” indicates prior-based algorithms.  
**PS Setting | Algorithm | Regret Bound in ˜O(·)**  
PS-LB | MASTER (Wei and Luo, 2021) + LinUCB | d√TNT  
         | ADA-OPKB (Hong et al., 2023) | d√NT T  
         | DAB (ours) + LinUCB (Abbasi-yadkori et al., 2011) | d√NT T  
         | DAB (ours) + LinTS (Agrawal and Goyal, 2013) | d^3/2√NT T  
         | DAB (ours) + PEGE † (Lattimore and Szepesvári, 2020) | √dNT T  
PS-GLB | MASTER (Wei and Luo, 2021) + GLM-UCB | d√NT T  
         | DAB (ours) + GLM-UCB (Filippi et al., 2010) | d√NT T  
         | DAB (ours) + GLM-TSL (Kveton et al., 2020) | d^3/2√NT T  
         | DAB (ours) + SupCB-GLM† (Li et al., 2017) | √dNT T  
PS-SCB | SCB-WeightUCB • (Wang et al., 2023) | d^2/3T^2/3N^1/3 T  
         | DAB (ours) + Logistic-UCB-1 (Faury et al., 2020) | c^−1/2 µ d√NT T  
         | DAB (ours) + OFU-ECOLog (Faury et al., 2022) | d√NT T  
         | DAB (ours) + OFUL-MLogB (Zhang and Sugiyama, 2023) | d√NT T  

PS-PBs encompass PS-LB, PS-GLB, and PS-SCB. Our theoretical analysis summarizes regret upper bounds applicable across these settings with various choices for the stationary bandit algorithm, consistent with the essence of a black-box design. The modular nature of our algorithm renders it straightforward to implement and analyze. Our upper bounds are rooted in standard assumptions regarding the bandit environment, where Θ and A are norm-bounded subsets of Rd. Table 1 illustrates that the DAB algorithm aligns with the theoretically optimal bound of ˜O(√NT T) with specific selections of the stationary bandit algorithms. The dependency of order on d for stationary variants directly translates to its PS variant without alteration. Our results pertaining to PS-SCB in Table 1 utilize the notation cµ = infθ∈Θ,a∈A ˙µ(⟨θ, a⟩) > 0, where ˙h denotes the first derivative of the function h. Furthermore, the variance of the noise εt within SCB is correlated with the mean reward itself, specifically, Var[εt | At] = ˙µ(⟨θt, At⟩). The rewards are assumed to maintain a uniform bound for all actions across A. Given the norm-bounded nature of Θ, the rewards (and the resulting noise) in rewards yield a uniform limit across all θ ∈ Θ and a ∈ A. Zero-mean bounded random variables are categorized as sub-Gaussian, permitting our analysis to encompass PS-SCBs with a uniform bound on variance. Presently, the leading regret upper bound for PS-SCBs is attributed to the WeightUCB method developed in Wang et al. (2023). Alternatively, the MASTER algorithm from Wei and Luo (2021) may be analyzed in the PS-SCB context, yet its regret upper bound remains unspecified. DAB improves the regret upper threshold from ˜O(d^2/3T^2/3N^1/3 T) as shown in Wang et al. (2023) to ˜O(d√NT T) utilizing DAB. This advancement arises from leveraging the black-box mechanisms of DAB to complement an order-optimal stationary SCB algorithm derived from Faury et al. (2022); Zhang and Sugiyama (2023). We align with the findings for PS-SCB presented by Russac et al. (2021), although their analysis mandates an additional requirement unnecessary for our considerations. While the comparisons in this section solely focus on order-optimality, the following section concentrates on evaluating DAB’s empirical performance.

**5 Experimental Results**  
We now present simulation outcomes demonstrating DAB's performance across LB, GLB, and SCB instances within non-stationarity types it was built for (i.e., piecewise stationary environments) in Section 5.1, and those for which it was not tailored (i.e., gradually changing or drifting environments) in Section 5.2. Since no prior research explicitly addresses PS-PB contexts while ensuring order-optimal performance, we lack suitable benchmarks for contrasting DAB. Consequently, we select the following relevant state-of-the-art techniques for comparison, applicable to the PS setting and transferrable to the drifting setup:
- MASTER from Wei and Luo (2021) is the singular existing black-box machinery besides ours achieving the order-optimal regret bound, despite facing certain constraints. Given its function without horizon insight, we configure its block parameter to n = ⌊log2 T⌋−4 to enhance performance. DAB's black-box nature allows for integration with any stationary bandit algorithm. To facilitate a precise comparison, both MASTER and DAB are evaluated with the same stationary algorithm in each PS-PB context: LinUCB (Abbasi-yadkori et al., 2011) for NS-LBs, GLM-UCB (Filippi et al., 2010) for NS-GLBs, and Logistic-UCB-1 (Faury et al., 2020) for NS-SCBs. Although MASTER lacks a theoretical framework regarding SCBs, recent work by Wang et al. (2023) has assessed it using Logistic-UCB-1, which we also adopt. 
- ADA-OPKB from Hong et al. (2023) stands as the only prior-free algorithm obtaining optimal regret for NS-LBs, aside from MASTER. ADA-OPKB necessitates extensive parameter adjustments for robust performance, which cultivates challenges in genuinely prior-free contexts. For equitable comparison, however, we fine-tuned its parameters to optimize its efficacy within our assessments. 
- WeightUCB from Wang et al. (2023) applies to all considered NS-PB contexts, attaining order-optimal regret when faced with drifting non-stationarity, in addition to providing the best-bound for PS-SCBs. Its performance, though notable, remains prior-based and parameterized per recommendations provided in Wang et al. (2023). For DAB's change detectors, we implement the Gaussian GLR test for LBs and GLBs, alongside the Bernoulli GLR version for SCBs. In terms of practical tuning, we follow guidance from Huang et al. (2025) to appropriately set the threshold function β and the parameters δF and δD. 

**5.1 On Piecewise Stationary Environments**  
To assess the algorithms within the PS context, we adopted the geometric change-point model presented in Gerogiannis et al. (2024) and independently sampled the intervals separating change points according to a geometric distribution with a parameter of ρ = T − ξ, with ξ ∈ {0.4, 0.6, 0.8}. The anticipated number of change-points thus became ρT = T^(1 − ξ), which remains sublinear in T based on the selected ξ values. In our experimentation, we avoided imposing restrictions on the interval lengths mandated for our theoretical results outlined in Theorem 1. Throughout, we maintained a fixed d = 5. For LBs and GLBs, we selected 100 actions, while for SCBs, 50 actions were chosen. These actions were independently sampled from N(0, I) and subsequently scaled to reside within the L-ball. Every time θt was initialized or altered, its components were selected uniformly and independently from the range [−1, 1], before scaling to an S-ball. For both LBs and GLBs, we established L = S = 1, while for SCBs, we set S = 3 and L = 4.

For our forced exploration methodology, we implemented the scheme discussed in Section 3, ensuring order-optimal performance. For LB and GLB, we sampled the additive noise according to N(0, 0.01) for each time step, while in the SCB context, we sampled the stochastic reward following Bernoulli(µ(⟨θt, At⟩)) at time t. For both GLB and SCB, we selected µ(x) := (1 + e^−x)−1. We compared the dynamic regret of the methods across respective environments over T = 50000, averaging data over 30 iterations. As evidenced by the results from Figures 1, 2, and 3, DAB distinctly surpassed current leading methodologies for PS-PBs. Beyond achieving a lower mean cumulative regret than benchmarks, DAB also demonstrated the least variance in its regret performance, underscoring its robustness to parameter fluctuations. Predictably, all algorithms exhibited lower growth rates of cumulative regret with reduced change-points (i.e., higher ξ). However, the advantage of DAB over benchmarks significantly escalated with diminishing occurrences of change-points. Note that DAB only disengages the action selections of the stationary bandit algorithm and reinitiates learning when an effective change detector indicates a mean-shift in rewards; thus, it circumvents unnecessary restarts, particularly when intervals between change-points permit detectors to accurately flag the shifts.

**5.2 On Drifting Environments**  
DAB’s design is aimed at PS-PBs; however, numerous practical environments experience gradual drift over time. While DAB isn’t tailored for fluctuating non-stationarity, one can conceive a drifting non-stationary environment as a PS context devoid of a lower threshold on the length of stationary intervals. Thus, it would be logical to assume DAB’s performance might lag behind specific algorithms designed for such conditions. We present a counterintuitive finding that DAB outperformed other algorithms even in drifting scenarios, subsequently probing the reasons behind this occurrence.  

To compare DAB with alternative algorithms, we implemented a drift model where, in each run, θt gradually transitioned over T rounds from θinit to θfinal, defined as θt = (1 − t/T) · θinit + (t/T) · θfinal. These endpoints were determined as described in Section 5.1, with noise and reward structures remaining consistent with those established previously. The performance comparisons across drifting LB, GLB, and SCB are depicted in Figure 4. ADA-OPKB yielded significantly greater cumulative regret when juxtaposed against other methodologies. Thus, for clarity, we opted to exclude its performance from Figure 4. Upon reviewing the graphs, DAB clearly outclassed other methods within the drifting framework. Remarkably, it even performed better than the WeightUCB methodology (Wang et al., 2023), which not only is recognized for achieving the optimal regret threshold in drifting conditions but also boasts strong empirical performance.

The results naturally provoke inquiries concerning the conditions that enable DAB’s efficacy in drifting environments. To initiate our inquiry, we conducted a supplementary experiment with LBs, permitting the governing parameter θt at each time-step to evolve randomly. Specifically, at time t, we set θt+1 := θt + ζt+1, where ζt+1 ∈ Rd was uniformly sampled over a δ-ball. If the resulting θt+1 exceeded the norm-bound on Θ, we dismissed that ζt+1 option and re-sampled. This process was reiterated until a suitable option meeting the norm-bound was derived. Noise was drawn from N(0, 0.1) at every time-step. Our evaluations indicated that the cumulative dynamic regret up to time T for DAB + LinUCB and WeightUCB was optimal over a range of δ values, as illustrated in Figure 5. The other parameters remained consistent with those specified in Section 5.1.  

When δ is minimal, DAB showcases superior performance compared to WeightUCB, a trend that falters with an increase in δ. Further illumination on our hypothesis regarding these observations comes as follows. For an action a ∈ A taken at time t + 1, the ensuing random reward conforms to Xt+1 = ⟨θt, a⟩ + ⟨ζt+1, a⟩ + εt+1. Conversely, if the governing parameter remains consistent, the reward from action a has the form X' t+1 = ⟨θt, a⟩ + ε' t+1, where ε' t+1 represents another iteration of the noise component. Statistically, instances of ⟨ζt+1, a⟩ + εt+1 as well as ε' t+1 closely resemble one another when δ is kept small, despite the resultant (minor) mean-shift arising from the drift in the governing parameter. Accentuating this scenario allows the drift's influence to blend with the noise term εt+1 when δ remains small. Thus, one might anticipate satisfactory performance from an algorithm structured for piecewise stationarity amid slowly drifting conditions. Conversely, a significant δ implies a substantial bias induced by ζt+1, consequently precluding the absorption of this bias within the zero-mean noise term. Across consecutive time-steps, the cumulative effect of this growing bias renders it substantial enough to breach the stationarity premise. With a sufficiently large δ, alterations in θt over a handful of time-steps may be recognized as considerable enough to trigger a restart. DAB, purposed for PS environments where stationary phases endure sufficiently to permit detectors’ responses, is likely to perform sub-optimally; simultaneously, methods crafted for drifting non-stationarity should fare better. 

**6 Summary and Outlook**  
In this research, we unveil DAB as the first practically viable, prior-free, order-optimal black-box strategy tailored for piecewise stationary bandits. Crafted with the intention of addressing piecewise parametric bandit variants, DAB accomplishes order-optimal regret if the stationary bandit algorithm it utilizes comes with similar optimal guarantees. The modular design of DAB renders it not only theoretically interpretable but also easy to execute with assorted stationary bandit algorithms. Most importantly, DAB successfully conserves and modifies the regret attributes of its stationary input algorithm for piecewise-stationary contexts. Consequently, it aligns with the leading existing bounds in PS-LBs and PS-GLBs while substantially enhancing the best-known bounds for PS-SCBs. To evaluate its real-world applicability, we tested DAB across both piecewise stationary and drifting environments. Within the piecewise stationary context, DAB excels beyond the black-box gold standard, MASTER, as well as current leading prior-based and prior-free methods. Remarkably, notwithstanding its original design for piecewise stationary situations, DAB continues to outperform the leading prior-based option, WeightUCB, alongside MASTER and various other prior-free methods in drifting environments. To unpack these unforeseen findings, we articulated key conditions under which DAB excels—an insight corroborated through supplementary experimental work in drifting scenarios. Our findings reinforce a vital takeaway from Gerogiannis et al. (2024): effective detection of non-stationarity plays a foundational role in driving robust practical outcomes. Moreover, they suggest that a well-structured algorithm for piecewise stationarity can extend its utility to a diverse array of drifting scenarios, thereby bridging the gap between these two operational spheres. This paves dedicated avenues for future research in the broader context of non-stationary bandit and reinforcement learning challenges, wherein tapping into piecewise stationarity could remedy a significant slice of the underlying complexities. Ultimately, the modular design of DAB beckons further exploration aimed at expanding its application across diverse piecewise stationary bandit frameworks, aspiring to establish order-optimal bounds universally.

**A note on spontaneous symmetry breaking in the mean-field Bose gas**

Andreas Deuchert, Phan Thành Nam, and Marcin Napiórkowski

February 3, 2025

We examine the homogeneous mean-field Bose gas at positive temperatures. We demonstrate that spontaneous U(1) symmetry breaking occurs if and only if Bose-Einstein condensation is present, defined by the existence of a macroscopic eigenvalue in the one-particle density matrix of the Gibbs state.

1. **Introduction and main results**

1.1. **Spontaneous symmetry breaking and quasi-averages**

Spontaneous symmetry breaking plays a critical role in comprehending intricate phenomena across various sectors of physics, encompassing condensed matter systems and high-energy particle physics. It generally signifies a scenario in which a system's Hamiltonian or Lagrangian shows a symmetry not reflected in the actual state of the system, typically the ground state or a state of thermal equilibrium. Herein, we shall delve into symmetry breaking within a collection of weakly interacting bosons. In the context of non-relativistic quantum many-body systems, the relevant symmetry is the U(1) symmetry associated with the conservation of particle number, reflecting the underlying many-body Hamiltonian (see (1.8)). A cornerstone of statistical physics is the notion that phase transitions are invariably accompanied by symmetry breaking. Since the groundbreaking works by Bose and Einstein [8, 18], it has been established that the ideal (non-interacting) Bose gas undergoes a phase transition known as Bose-Einstein Condensation (BEC) (refer to Sections 1.4 and 1.5 for a succinct overview). This phenomenon is characterized by a significant occupation of a single quantum state and was first observed in practical experiments conducted by Ketterle, Cornell, and Wieman [12, 23]. This behavior has been analytically verified for interacting systems across various scaling regimes, particularly within what is termed the mean-field scaling. The principal conclusion of this paper asserts that the BEC phase transition within the mean-field Bose gas is indeed synonymous with the breaking of the U(1) symmetry related to the respective many-body system. 

While the concept of Bose-Einstein condensation (see (1.16)) is defined in relatively straightforward terms, providing a rigorously mathematical characterization of symmetry breaking is more intricate. To elucidate this concept, let’s focus on a translationally invariant system. In such cases, the macroscopically occupied single-particle quantum state in the condensed phase aligns with the zero momentum mode, whereby the anticipated number of particles with zero momentum, ⟨a∗0a0⟩ (see (1.5) and (1.6) for the definitions of creation and annihilation operators), becomes proportional to the total particle number in the system. This positions the zero momentum mode as paramount, and as proposed by Bogoliubov [5], justifies a classical treatment by replacing the operators a0 and a∗0 with c-numbers, thereby equating ⟨a∗0a0⟩ with |⟨a0⟩|². Since the latter cannot yield a non-zero value in any state with a fixed particle number, it acts as a marker for spontaneous symmetry breaking. To mathematically realize these concepts, Bogoliubov [6, 7] conceived a limiting procedure, commonly referred to as Bogoliubov’s quasi averages, which has since found extensive application across multiple physics domains. This method comprises two primary steps. First, to potentially secure a non-zero expectation for a0, one appends a perturbation λ√V(a∗0 + a0) to the many-body Hamiltonian, disrupting particle number conservation (where V denotes the system's volume). We denote the expectation in such a perturbed state as ⟨·⟩λ. Next, we analyze the double limit given by lim λ→0 lim V→∞ |⟨a0⟩λ|²/V, asserting that a non-zero result indicates symmetry breaking within the system. We emphasize the sequence of limits, stressing that we first take the macroscopic limit, subsequently ‘removing’ the perturbation that breaks symmetry. It should be acknowledged that the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality indicates that |⟨a0⟩λ|²/V ≤ ⟨a∗0a0⟩λ/V, thus establishing that spontaneous symmetry breaking implies BEC within the framework of quasi averages.  

In 2005, Lieb, Seiringer, and Yngvason [28], along with Süt˝o [39] independently, demonstrated that these two phenomena are indeed equivalent. Their studies were influenced by Ginibre’s [20] results, which provided the first rigorous justification for the c-number substitution. In [28], the authors further verified that if BEC occurs in the standard manner, then spontaneous symmetry breaking must also occur, represented by the implication lim V→∞ ⟨a∗0a0⟩λ=0/V ≤ lim λ→0 lim V→∞ |⟨a0⟩λ|²/V. 

It's crucial to highlight that all assertions are conditional, given that the validation of BEC in the thermodynamic limit remains a prominent unresolved issue in mathematical physics. While the thermodynamic limit's challenge persists, one can explore analogous questions within simpler scaling regimes. For this purpose, as previously indicated, we will consider the so-called mean-field scaling (refer to (1.8), which reflects the physical situation of a weakly interacting gas). The characteristics at zero temperature for this model are well understood: the ground state exhibits BEC [9, 24, 30], while the excited states are aptly described by Bogoliubov theory [13, 21, 25, 33, 38]. At positive temperatures, a comprehensive delineation of the Gibbs state associated with the (translationally invariant) mean-field Bose gas is provided in [14], and for a discussion regarding the efficacy of Hartree theory in trapped systems, see [17, Section 1.6]. The remainder of the introduction is devoted to a thorough depiction of the model alongside a precise articulation of the main results.

**Notation**  
We utilize a ≲ b to indicate the existence of a constant C > 0, independent of significant parameters (e.g., the particle number or the inverse temperature), such that a ≤ Cb holds. When both a ≲ b and b ≲ a are true, we denote this relation as a ∼ b, which indicates that the leading orders of a and b balance in the considered limit. If the constant varies depending on a parameter k, we express this as a ≲k b and a ∼k b.  

1.2. **Bosonic Fock space and Hamiltonian**  
We investigate a system composed of bosonic particles confined to the three-dimensional flat torus Λ. The one-particle Hilbert space for the system is denoted as L²(Λ). Our focus is on the grand canonical ensemble, which encompasses systems with a fluctuating particle count. Consequently, the Hilbert space for the entire system can be denoted as the bosonic Fock space F(L²(Λ)) = ∞⨁_{n=0} L² sym(Λⁿ) (1.2) over L²(Λ). Here, L² sym(Λⁿ) signifies the closed linear subspace of L²(Λⁿ) composed of functions Ψ(x₁, ..., xₙ) that are invariant under any permutation of the particle coordinates x₁, ..., xₙ ∈ Λ. Moreover, L² sym(Λ⁰) is designated as C. 

On the n-particle Hilbert space L² sym(Λⁿ), we define the Hamiltonian:
Hₙ(η) = ∑_{i=1}ⁿ −∆ᵢ + 1/η ∑_{1 ≤ i < j ≤ n} v(d(xᵢ, xⱼ)). (1.3) 
Here, ∆ᵢ symbolizes the Laplace-Beltrami operator acting on coordinate xᵢ and reflects the particles' kinetic energy. When representing the unit torus as [0, 1]³, ∆ᵢ corresponds to the standard Laplacian with periodic boundary conditions. Moreover, d(·, ·) signifies the distance on the torus, and the function v: R⁺ → R⁺ describes the particle interactions. The parameter η > 0 will subsequently be shown (see Proposition 1.1) to be proportionate to the anticipated particle count within the system, effectively implementing a mean-field scaling. 

The Hamiltonian for the overall system acts on a suitably dense subset of F(L²(Λ)) and is defined as:
H(η) = ∞⨁_{n=0} Hₙ(η). (1.4) 
To articulate an alternative representation of this Hamiltonian, we introduce the creation and annihilation operators a∗ₚ and aₚ of a particle in the one-particle function ϕₚ(x) = e^{ip·x} with p ∈Λ* = 2πZ³. The annihilation operator aₚ represents a mapping from L² sym(Λⁿ) to L² sym(Λⁿ⁻¹) for n ≥ 1, fulfilling aₚΩ = 0 for Ω = (1, 0, 0, ...) ∈ F. Its action on an n-particle function ψ ∈ L² sym(Λⁿ) is characterized by:
(aₚψ)(x₁, ..., xₙ⁻¹) = √n ∫_{Λ} e^{−ip·x}ψ(x₁, ..., xₙ⁻¹, x) dx, (1.5) and this action extends linearly for general ψ ∈ F. The creation operator a∗ₚ serves as the adjoint of aₚ and acts on ψ ∈ L² sym(Λⁿ) as:
(a∗ₚψ)(x₁, ..., xₙ⁺¹) = √(n + 1) ∑_{j=1}ⁿ e^{ip·x₁}ψ(x₁, ..., x_j⁻¹, x_j⁺¹, ..., xₙ). (1.6)

This family of operators adheres to canonical commutation relations: [aₚ, a∗ₓ] = δₚₓ, [aₚ, aₓ] = 0, [a∗ₚ, a∗ₓ] = 0. (1.7) An alternate representation of the Hamiltonian in (1.4) through these operators is provided by:
H(η) = Σ_{p ∈ Λ*} p²a∗ₚaₚ + 1/2η ∑_{p,u,v ∈ Λ*} ˆv(p)a∗ₖ₊ₚa∗ₜ₋ₖaₜaₖ. (1.8)
The Fourier coefficients ˆv(p) = ∫_{Λ} v(|x|)e^{−ip·x} dx represent the interaction potential v.

1.3. **The grand canonical ensemble**  
We are concerned with a bosonic many-particle system described within a grand canonical ensemble framework. The typical parameters for this ensemble are inverse temperature β > 0 and chemical potential µ ∈ R. The selection of the latter permits achieving any desired expectation of particle number N(β, µ) > 0 in the system. This, in particular, ensures interpreting mean-field scaling consistent with the canonical setup. The family of states on the bosonic Fock space is given by
S = {Γ ∈ B(F) | 0 ≤ Γ, Tr Γ = 1}, (1.9)
where B(F) denotes the set of bounded operators on F(L²(Λ)). For a state Γ ∈ S, the grand potential functional G is defined as:
G(Γ) = Tr[(H(η) − µN)Γ] − (1/β)S(Γ), 
with the von-Neumann entropy S(Γ) = −Tr[Γ ln(Γ)]. (1.10)
Here, µ ∈ R and N = ∞⨁_{n=0} n = ∑_{p ∈ Λ*} a∗ₚaₚ (1.11) represent the chemical potential and number operator, respectively. The minimum of G equals the grand potential
Φ(β, µ) = min Γ ∈ S G(Γ) = −(1/β) ln(Tr exp(−β(H(η) − µN))). (1.12)
The unique minimizer of G within the set S is the grand canonical Gibbs state:
Gβ,µ = exp(−β(H(η) − µN)) / Tr exp(−β(H(η) − µN)). (1.13)
The expected number of particles in the Gibbs state Gβ,µ will be denoted by N(β, µ), specifically:
N(β, µ) = Tr[NGβ,µ]. (1.14)

1.4. **One-particle reduced density matrix and Bose–Einstein condensation**  
Let Γ ∈ S represent a state ensuring that NΓ is trace class. We define the one-particle density matrix (1-pdm) γΓ ∈ B(L²(Λ)) of Γ via its integral kernel in Fourier space:
γΓ(p, q) = Tr[a∗ₖaₚΓ]. (1.15)
It acts as a nonnegative trace-class operator, satisfying tr[γΓ] = Tr[NΓ]. Following [36], we assert that a sequence of states Γₙ ∈ S with Tr[NΓₙ] = N exhibits Bose–Einstein condensation (BEC) if and only if lim inf N → ∞ sup ∥ψ∥ = 1 ⟨ψ, γΓₙψ⟩ / N > 0, (1.16) meaning that the dominant eigenvalue of γΓₙ grows proportionally to N. The largest eigenvalue of γΓₙ compared to N and its corresponding eigenvector are termed the condensate fraction and the condensate wave function, respectively. It is important to note that, aside from the referenced results in the introduction (concerning mean-field scaling), BEC has also been established to hold in additional scaling contexts. For further study, we refer to [1–3,10,19,22,27,31,32] for ground state results and [15–17] for Gibbs state results.

1.5. **The ideal Bose gas on the torus**  
By setting v = 0 in the Hamiltonian definitions provided in (1.8) and the Gibbs state from (1.13), we derive a non-interacting model known as the ideal Bose gas, which can be exactly solved. The 1-pdm of the Gibbs state of the ideal Bose gas is expressed as:
γid = Σ_{p ∈ Λ*} (1 / (exp(β(p² − µ₀)) − 1)) |ϕₚ⟩⟨ϕₚ|, (1.17)
where |ϕₚ⟩⟨ϕₚ| denotes the orthogonal projection onto the one-particle function ϕₚ(x) = e^{ip·x}. In this framework, the chemical potential µ₀(β, N) < 0 can be derived as the unique solution to the equation
N = trL²(Λ)[γid] = Σ_{p ∈ Λ*} (1 / (exp(β(p² − µ₀)) − 1)), (1.18)
where N denotes the expected particle count in the system. As observed by Bose and Einstein [8, 18], the ideal Bose gas undergoes a phase transition (the BEC phase transition) in the large N limit: the largest eigenvalue N₀(β, N) of γid in (1.17) exhibits the behavior given by
N₀(β, N) = (1 / (exp(−βµ₀) − 1)) ≃ N [1 - (βc / β)^(3/2)]⁺, 

where βₜ = βₜ(N) = (1 / (4π)) N ζ(3/2)^(-2/3), (1.19)
as N approaches infinity. It should be noted that β typically depends on the particle count. If we select β such that lim N→∞(βc / β) = 0 (signifying the zero-temperature limit), this leads to N₀(β, N)/N → 1. Generally, however, it is viable to have N₀(β, N)/N → g ∈ [0, 1], suggesting a significant number of particles (on the order of N) occupy p = 0 (indicating the BEC) while simultaneously a macroscopic number of thermally excited particles are also present. Finally, (1.19) suggests the following behavior: if β = κβc with κ > 1, then µ₀ ≃ −(βN₀)⁻¹ ∼ −N^(−1/3), while µ₀ ∼ −β⁻¹ ∼ −N^(−2/3) when β = κβc with κ < 1.

summary: We consider the homogeneous mean-field Bose gas at temperatures proportional to the critical temperature of its Bose--Einstein condensation phase transition. Our main result is a trace-norm approximation of the grand canonical Gibbs state in terms of a reference state, which is given by a convex combination of products of coherent states and Gibbs states associated with certain temperature-dependent Bogoliubov Hamiltonians. The convex combination is expressed as an integral over a Gibbs distribution of a one-mode $\Phi^4$-theory describing the condensate. We interpret this result as a justification of Bogoliubov theory at positive temperature. Further results derived from the norm approximation include various limiting distributions for the number of particles in the condensate, as well as precise formulas for the one- and two-particle density matrices of the Gibbs state. Key ingredients of our proof, which are of independent interest, include two novel abstract correlation inequalities. The proof of one of them is based on an application of an infinite-dimensional version of Stahl's theorem.

# 1. Introduction and Key Findings
## 1.1. Background and Overview
The exploration of Bose gases initiated around a century ago when Bose–Einstein statistics were formulated in the groundbreaking works of Bose and Einstein [23, 45]. Their examination of ideal (non-interacting) gases led them to predict the phenomenon of Bose–Einstein condensation (BEC), where a large number of particles gather in a singular quantum state. They suggested that this phenomenon might extend to interacting bosonic many-particle systems at appropriately low temperatures. In 1947, Bogoliubov [21] discerned that BEC in such systems permits a formal simplification of certain Hamiltonian operators associated with the condensate via a substitution of complex numbers (referred to as the c-number substitution). By disregarding two expectedly minor terms within the Hamiltonian, a solvable model emerged, which forecasts that low-energy excitations manifest as sound waves—indicative of superfluid behavior (flow without resistance). Collectively, this framework is designated Bogoliubov theory. A rigorous demonstration of BEC and a solid foundation for Bogoliubov’s theory through microscopic principles in various parameter contexts remains a significant challenge in contemporary mathematical physics.

In 2002, Lieb and Seiringer [72] provided a proof of BEC under the Gross–Pitaevskii scaling regime, a framework employed for elucidating dilute trapped Bose gases. Additionally, the landmark paper [17] by Boccato, Brennecke, Cenatiempo, and Schlein offered evidence that Bogoliubov theory accurately anticipates the low-energy excitation spectrum of a dilute Bose gas within the same Gross–Pitaevskii limit. Soon after, Fournais and Solovej established the Lee–Huang–Yang formula [64] for the ground-state energy (in the zero-temperature scenario) of dilute Bose gases, confirming Bogoliubov’s predictions within the more complex thermodynamic limit [49, 50]. These advancements wrapped up a remarkable series of contributions over the past six decades [6, 8, 31, 43, 46, 52, 78, 104]. A parallel conjecture regarding low-temperature free energy, where entropy corresponds to the Bogoliubov excitation spectrum, was recently validated in [54, 55]. Earlier insights into the free energy of dilute Bose gases in thermodynamic limits can be found in references [39, 79, 97, 105]. 

Despite these achievements, proving the Bose–Einstein condensation phase transition in the thermodynamic limit remains elusive with existing mathematical techniques—this difficulty extends to detailed explorations of Gibbs state properties. However, an ambitious ongoing project aims to establish BEC in the thermodynamic limit through renormalization group techniques, as discussed in [5].

Conceptually, the thermodynamic limit poses challenges, as it causes the kinetic energy operator to lose its spectral gap, complicating the extraction of state-related insights via coercive energy functionals. Notably, it is still unclear at which point Bogoliubov theory ceases to be applicable and what correction types need to be anticipated.

This paper examines the Gibbs state of a homogeneous Bose gas within the mean-field limit. Although simpler in analysis than the thermodynamic limit, this parameter regime demonstrates substantial mathematical intricacies. BEC and the legitimacy of Bogoliubov theory for the low-energy excitation spectrum were confirmed in Seiringer’s pivotal article [98], which inspired much subsequent research and established the foundational understanding of Bogoliubov theory that eventually led to proving the Lee–Huang–Yang formula.

When the interaction, temperature, and chemical potential parameters are set so that the system approaches the critical point of the BEC phase transition from above, the applicability of Bogoliubov theory diminishes. Independently, studies by Lewin, Nam, and Rougerie [67], along with work from Fröhlich, Knowles, Schlein, and Sohinger [51], indicate that in this parameter range, the correct system depiction can be achieved via a nonlinear classical field theory; observing these effects necessitates stronger interactions than those evaluated by Seiringer.

Current findings regarding the mean-field Bose gas do not furnish insights into the Gibbs state at temperatures aligned with critical temperatures for BEC, where the transition from the condensed to the non-condensed state becomes observable. This paper aims to tackle this inquiry.

We demonstrate that the interacting model's Gibbs state can be precisely characterized as a convex combination of coherent states and Gibbs states linked with certain temperature-dependent Bogoliubov Hamiltonians. Expressing this convex combination requires a specific integral over a Gibbs distribution encompassing a one-mode Φ4-theory that was recently introduced by Boccato, Deuchert, and Stocker [20]. Validating this approximation necessitates the development of overarching techniques that extend significantly beyond basic coerciveness of the Gibbs free energy functional usage. 

Specifically, we commence with a variational problem formulation, leveraging two newly defined abstract correlation inequalities to achieve results for the Gibbs state that differ from approximated energy functional minimizers. We anticipate that the general techniques devised in this study will hold independent significance and ultimately contribute to a more extensive comprehension of the behavior of the Bose gas at positive temperatures across various scaling paradigms.  Additional significant results arising from our norm approximation of the Gibbs state alongside the implementation of our novel correlation inequalities comprise the derivation of several limiting distributions for the number of particles within the condensate, explicit formulations for the one- and two-particle density matrices of the Gibbs state, and an asymptotic expansion for the free energy. The forthcoming sections present our model alongside key results and concepts, with further results necessitating additional notation set to be elaborated in Section 2.

## Notation
We utilize “a ≲b” to indicate the existence of a constant C > 0, independent of relevant parameters (such as particle number or inverse temperature), for which a ≤Cb holds. If a ≲b and b ≲a, we denote this as “a ∼b,” while “a ≃b” signifies that a and b yield equal leading orders under the limit considered. Where needed, if the constant depends on a parameter k, we denote this as “a ≲k b” and “a ∼k b.”

The standard Lp-norm is represented by “∥· ∥p.” All traces of the form Tr[AΓ] involving a positive operator A and a positive trace-class operator Γ are comprehended within the framework of quadratic forms; hence, we define Tr[AΓ] ≔Tr[Γ1/2AΓ1/2]. This definition remains valid even in scenarios where the resultant value approaches +∞, as finiteness of Tr[AΓ] merely necessitates the operator Γ1/2AΓ1/2 being trace-class.

## 1.2. The Many-Body Quantum Model
We consider a system comprised of bosonic particles restricted to the torus Λ = [0, 1]3. The one-particle Hilbert space corresponds to L2(Λ), focusing on a system characterized by a fluctuating particle number (the grand canonical ensemble), leading us to identify the Hilbert space for the complete system as the bosonic Fock space F = F(L2(Λ)) = ∞∑ n=0 L2 sym(Λn) = ℂ ⊕L2(Λ) ⊕L2 sym(Λ2) ⊕· · · (1.1). Here, L2 sym(Λn) denotes the subspace of L2(Λn) containing all functions Ψ(x1, ..., xn) that remain invariant under any permutation of particle coordinates x1, ..., xn ∈Λ. The Hamiltonian governing the system is expressed as 
\[ 
HN = ∞∑ n=0 Hn N = ∞∑ n=0 \left( 
\begin{array}{c}
\sum_{i=1}^n -\Delta_i + \frac{1}{N} \sum_{1 ≤i<j≤n} v(x_i-x_j) 
\end{array} 
\right) (1.2) 
\] 
where the Laplacian \(-\Delta \geq 0\) acts on L2(Λ) under periodic boundary conditions and where \(v: \Lambda → ℝ^+\) is a periodic function meeting the criteria \(0 \leq \hat{v} ∈ ℓ^1(Λ^∗)\), with \(\hat{v}(p) = \langle ϕ_p, v \rangle\) in \(L2(Λ)\) and \(Λ^∗= 2π\mathbb{Z}^3\). In particular, since \(v\) is bounded, \(H_n^N\) becomes a self-adjoint operator on \(L2 sym(Λ^n)\) possessing the same domain as the Laplacian \(\sum_{i=1}^n -\Delta_i\). Additionally, \(H_N\) remains bounded from below on \( \sum_{m \geq 2} L^m \sum_{n=0} H_{2sym}(Λ^n)\) and can be recognized as a self-adjoint operator on \(F(L^2(Λ))\) utilizing Friedrich's extension.

Given parameters \(\beta, N∈(0, ∞)\), we are interested in the grand canonical Gibbs state 
\[
G_{\beta,N} = \frac{\exp\left( -\beta\left( H_N - \mu_{\beta,N} N \right) \right)}{Tr\left[ \exp\left( -\beta\left( H_N - \mu_{\beta,N} N \right) \right) \right]}  (1.3) 
\] 
acting on \(F(L^2(Λ))\). Here, \(N = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} n\) denotes the number operator, and the chemical potential \(\mu_{\beta,N} \in ℝ\) is selected such that \(Tr[NG_{\beta,N}] = N\) holds. In this configuration, the factor \(\frac{1}{N}\) preceding the interaction term within \(H_n^N\) represents a mean-field scaling.

### Second Quantization 
Grand canonical systems are best understood via the lens of second quantization, which we introduce here. The annihilation operator \(a_p\) and creation operator \(a^*_p\) of a particle described by the function \(ϕ_p(x) = e^{ip\cdot x}\) with \(x∈Λ\) and \(p∈Λ^∗\) are defined as 
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
(a_p \psi)(x_1, ..., x_{n-1}) = \sqrt{n}\int_Λ e^{-ip\cdot x}\psi(x_1, ..., x_{n-1}, x) dx ,\\
(a^*_p \psi)(x_1, ..., x_{n+1}) = \sqrt{n+1}\sum_{j=1}^n e^{ip\cdot x_j}\psi(x_1, ..., x_{j-1}, x_j+1, ..., x_n).
\end{array}
\]
The notation suggests that \(a^*(\psi)\) is the Hermitian adjoint of \(a(\psi)\). This operator collection adheres to canonical commutation relations (CCR) 
\[ 
[a_p, a^*_q] = \delta_{p,q}, [a_p, a_q] = 0 = [a^*_p, a^*_q], \quad \forall p, q ∈Λ^∗. (1.6) 
\] 
Utilizing creation and annihilation operators permits a compact representation of numerous operators acting on the Fock space. Notably, if \(h\) denotes a self-adjoint operator on \(L2(Λ)\), its second quantization aligns with 
\[
dΥ(h) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{i=1}^n h_i. 
\] 
For the number operator given in (1.3), this asserts \(N = dΥ(1) = \sum_{p∈Λ^∗} a^*_pa_p\), while the second quantization of the Laplacian \(-\Delta\) is denoted by 
\[
dΥ(-\Delta) =\sum_{p∈Λ^∗}p^2a^*_pa_p. 
\] 
More generally, the grand canonical Hamiltonian \(H_N\) represented in (1.2) can be articulated as 
\[
H_N = \sum_{p∈Λ^∗} p^2a^*_pa_p + \frac{1}{2N} \sum_{p,u,v∈Λ^∗} \hat{v}(p)a^*_ua^*_va_u a_v. 
\] 
The mean-field Hamiltonian within (1.2)-(1.7), alongside its variants such as the canonical version, has garnered considerable investigation over the past six decades. 

Regarding the proofs of BEC for the ground state and low-lying eigenfunctions, references [70, 99] shed light on analyses related to the Lieb–Liniger model, while studies focusing on bosonic atoms, stars, confined systems, and more general frameworks can be explored in [3, 4, 12, 24, 58, 102], [77], or [15, 92, 66]. Subsequent developments within the realm of Bogoliubov excitation spectra have drawn from Seiringer's [98] findings, inspiring advancements seen in [53] for trapped systems and numerous subsequent works.

Thus far, the investigations conducted within the mean-field regime predominantly emphasize the ground state problem or the Gibbs state at approximately unit temperature. Here, the majority of particles tend toward the condensate while a finite число remains within the thermal cloud, supported by credible verification in [80, 84] with exponential estimates. Consequently, assuming a second-order perturbation approach yields predictions regarding thermally excited particle contributions. Conversely, the focal point of this document shifts to realms where the temperature is on the order of \(N^{2/3}\), establishing that the quantity of thermally excited particles remains closely comparable to the entire particle count. Additionally, this phenomenon becomes evident in ideal gas contexts, poised for exploration in subsequent discussions.

## 5.2. Kernel of the 2-pdm 
As we move toward examining pointwise boundaries for the integral kernel of the 2-particle density matrix (2-pdm) of the Gibbs state, we begin by calculating the integral kernels of the state \(\Gamma_{\beta,N}\) as detailed in (9.1). 

While calculating the four-point correlation function of \(\Gamma_{\beta,N}\), we will distinguish between cases where \( N_{0} \geq N^{2/3} \) and \( N_{0} < N^{2/3} \), focusing initially on the former. Using the coherent state notation \( a_{0} |z\rangle = |z\rangle \) presented in (1.14), and considering the Wick theorem (with state \( G(z) \) constructed in (3.2)), we obtain 

\[
\begin{align*} 
\text{Tr}[a^*_0 a^*_0 a_0 a_0 \Gamma_{\beta,N}] & = \int_C \langle z, a^*_0 a^*_0 a_0 a_0 z \rangle g(z) dz \\
& = \int_C |z|^4 g(z) dz, \\
\text{Tr}[a^*_0 a^*_p a_0 a_p \Gamma_{\beta,N}] &= \int_C \langle z, a^*_0 a_0 z \rangle \text{Tr} [a^*_p a_p G(z)] g(z) dz \\
& = \gamma_p \int_C |z|^2 g(z) dz = \gamma_p eN_0(\beta,N), \\ 
\text{Tr}[a^*_0 a^*_0 a_p a_{-p} \Gamma_{\beta,N}] &= \int_C (\text{Tr}[a_p a_{-p} G(z)]) z^2 g(z) dz \\
& = \alpha_p \int_C |z|^2 g(z) dz = \alpha_p eN_0(\beta,N), \\ 
\text{Tr}[a_p a^*_q a_r a_s \Gamma_{\beta,N}] & = \delta_{p,-q} \delta_{r,s} \alpha_p \alpha_r + (\delta_{p,s} \delta_{q,r} + \delta_{p,r} \delta_{q,s}) \gamma_p \gamma_q.
\end{align*}
\]

The corresponding expectations, under the assumption that all terms involving a single creation or annihilation operator with momentum \(0\) vanish, will yield the relationships exhibited above corresponding to the kernel of the 2-dimensional density matrix of \(G_{\beta,N}\).

In subsequent steps, we will analyze the pointwise bounds stated for the 2-pdm, leveraging the established results to categorize the behavior of the condensation characterized by particle distributions given various Bose gas configurations.
In this part, we establish a lemma that will be referenced in Section 9.2 for calculating the one-particle density matrix (1-pdm) of the Gibbs state \( G_{\beta,N} \) in equation (9.3). To maintain the flow of the central argument, we present and prove it here. 

**Lemma D.1.** We analyze the limit as \( N \to \infty \) with \( \beta = \kappa \beta_c(N) \) where \( \kappa \in (0, \infty) \) and \( \beta_c \) is defined in (1.10). The one-particle Hamiltonian \( h \) is set according to Lemma C.1 above. Define \( \gamma_p(\lambda, \mu) \) as in (1.9) with \( p^2 \) replaced by \( h(p) \) and \( \mu_0(\beta, N) \) substituted with \( \mu < 0 \). We find that 

\[
\frac{\partial \gamma_p}{\partial \mu} \lesssim \frac{1}{\beta p^4} \tag{D.1}
\]

and also that 

\[
\frac{\partial \gamma_p(\lambda, \mu)}{\partial \lambda} \lesssim \|f\|_\infty \frac{1}{\beta p^4} 
\]

and 

\[
\frac{\partial^2 \gamma_p}{\partial \lambda^2} \lesssim \|f\|_\infty^2 \frac{1}{\beta p^4}. \tag{D.2}
\]

**Proof.** We reintroduce the definitions of \( \epsilon(p) \), \( u_p \), \( v_p \), \( \gamma_{Bog} \), and \( \gamma_p \) as outlined in (3.11), (3.9), and (1.9), respectively. In each definition, we substitute \( p^2 \) with \( h(p) \) and \( \mu_0(\beta, N) \) with \( \mu \). The first derivative of \( \epsilon(p) \) concerning \( \mu \) yields 

\[
\frac{\partial \epsilon(p)}{\partial \mu} = -\frac{1}{\epsilon(p)} \left( p^2 + \lambda f(p) - \mu + \hat{v}(p) \frac{N_0}{N} \right), \quad \frac{\partial \epsilon(p)}{\partial \mu} \lesssim 1. \tag{D.3}
\]

We also verify 

\[
\frac{\partial \epsilon(p)}{\partial \lambda} = \frac{f(p)}{\epsilon(p)} \left( p^2 + \lambda f(p) - \mu + \hat{v}(p) \frac{N_0}{N} \right), \quad \frac{\partial \epsilon(p)}{\partial \lambda} \lesssim \|f\|_\infty. \tag{D.4}
\]

For the second derivative of the dispersion relation with respect to \( \lambda \), we express 

\[
\frac{\partial^2 \epsilon(p)}{\partial \lambda^2} = \frac{f^2(p)}{\epsilon(p)} \left( 1 - \frac{1}{\epsilon^2(p)} \left( p^2 + \lambda f(p) - \mu + \hat{v}(p) \frac{N_0}{N} \right)^2 \right), \quad \frac{\partial^2 \epsilon(p)}{\partial \lambda^2} \lesssim \|f\|_\infty^2 p^2. \tag{D.5}
\]

The derivative of \( \gamma_{Bog}^p \) concerning \( \mu \) is given by 

\[
\frac{\partial \gamma_{Bog}^p}{\partial \mu} = -\frac{\beta}{8} \text{sinh}^2 \left( \frac{\beta \epsilon(p)}{2} \right) \frac{\partial \epsilon(p)}{\partial \mu}, \quad \frac{\partial \gamma_{Bog}^p}{\partial \mu} \lesssim \frac{1}{\beta p^4}. \tag{D.6}
\]

The bound in (D.6) derives from (D.3). Furthermore, for the derivative concerning \( \lambda \), we find 

\[
\frac{\partial \gamma_{Bog}^p}{\partial \lambda} = -\frac{\beta}{8} \text{sinh}^2 \left( \frac{\beta \epsilon(p)}{2} \right) \frac{\partial \epsilon(p)}{\partial \lambda}, \quad \frac{\partial \gamma_{Bog}^p}{\partial \lambda} \lesssim \|f\|_\infty \frac{1}{\beta p^4}. \tag{D.7}
\]

The second derivative with respect to \( \lambda \) is represented as 

\[
\frac{\partial^2 \gamma_{Bog}^p}{\partial \lambda^2} = -\frac{\beta}{8} \text{sinh}^2 \left( \frac{\beta \epsilon(p)}{2} \right) \frac{\partial^2 \epsilon}{\partial \lambda^2} + \frac{\beta^2}{4} \cosh \left( \frac{\beta \epsilon(p)}{2} \right) \text{sinh}^3 \left( \frac{\beta \epsilon(p)}{2} \right) \left( \frac{\partial \epsilon}{\partial \lambda} \right)^2, 
\]

which simplifies to 

\[
\frac{\partial^2 \gamma_{Bog}^p}{\partial \lambda^2} \lesssim \|f\|_\infty^2 \frac{1}{\beta p^4} \tag{D.8}
\]

where we applied (D.4) and (D.5) for this bound. We also have 

\[
\frac{\partial v_p}{\partial \mu} = u_p \left( p^2 + \lambda f(p) - \mu \right) \frac{1}{p^2 + \lambda f(p) - \mu + 2\hat{v}(p) \frac{N_0}{N}} - 1, \quad \frac{\partial v_p}{\partial \mu} \lesssim \frac{1}{p^2}. \tag{D.9}
\]

Moreover, we establish 

\[
\frac{\partial v_p}{\partial \lambda} = u_p \frac{f(p)}{p^2 + \lambda f(p) - \mu} \left( 1 - \frac{1}{p^2 + \lambda f(p) - \mu + 2\hat{v}(p) \frac{N_0}{N}} \right), \quad \frac{\partial v_p}{\partial \lambda} \lesssim \|f\|_\infty p^2. \tag{D.10}
\]

For the second derivative, we determine 

\[
\frac{\partial^2 v_p}{\partial \lambda^2} = \frac{f^2(p)}{p^2 + \lambda f(p) - \mu} v_p - 1 \left( \frac{1 - 1}{p^2 + \lambda f(p) - \mu + 2\hat{v}(p)N_0/N} \right) + \frac{f^2(p)}{p^2 + \lambda f(p) - \mu} u_p \frac{(p^2 + \lambda f(p) - \mu + 2\hat{v}(p) \frac{N_0}{N})^2}{(p^2 + \lambda f(p) - \mu)^2}, 
\]

leading to 

\[
\frac{\partial^2 v_p}{\partial \lambda^2} \lesssim \|f\|_\infty^2 \frac{1}{p^4}. \tag{D.12}
\]

Finally, analyzing \( \gamma_p \), its first derivative with respect to \( \mu \) gives 

\[
\frac{\partial \gamma_p}{\partial \mu} = 2v_p \frac{\partial v_p}{\partial \mu} \left( 1 + 2\gamma_{Bog}^p \right) + \left( 1 + 2v_p^2 \right) \frac{\partial \gamma_{Bog}^p}{\partial \mu}, \quad \frac{\partial \gamma_p}{\partial \mu} \lesssim \frac{1}{\beta p^4}. \tag{D.13}
\]

This verifies (D.1). From (3.18), (D.6), and (D.9), we confirmed our assessment. For the derivative concerning \( \lambda \), we observe 

\[
\frac{\partial \gamma_p}{\partial \lambda} = 2v_p \frac{\partial v_p}{\partial \lambda} \left( 1 + 2\gamma_{Bog}^p \right) + \left( 1 + 2v_p^2 \right) \frac{\partial \gamma_{Bog}^p}{\partial \lambda}, \quad \frac{\partial \gamma_p}{\partial \lambda} \lesssim \|f\|_\infty \frac{1}{\beta p^4}. \tag{D.14}
\]

The second derivative of \( \gamma_p \) with respect to \( \lambda \) is now defined as 

\[
\frac{\partial^2 \gamma_p}{\partial \lambda^2} = 2 \left[ \left( \frac{\partial v_p}{\partial \lambda} \right)^2 + v_p \frac{\partial^2 v_p}{\partial \lambda^2} \right] \left( 1 + 2\gamma_{Bog}^p \right) + 8v_p \frac{\partial v_p}{\partial \lambda} \frac{\partial \gamma_{Bog}^p}{\partial \lambda} + \left( 1 + 2v_p^2 \right) \frac{\partial^2 \gamma_{Bog}^p}{\partial \lambda^2}. 
\]

We utilize (3.18), (D.7), (D.8), (D.10), and (D.12) to demonstrate that 

\[
\frac{\partial^2 \gamma_p}{\partial \lambda^2} \lesssim \|f\|_\infty^2 \frac{1}{\beta p^4}. \tag{D.16}
\]

The equations (D.14) and (D.16) establish (D.2) and thereby confirm our assertion. □ 

References [1] through [105] remain unchanged.
