**arXiv:2501.19390v1 [math.OC] 31 Jan 2025**

**1 From a Frequency-Domain Willems’ Lemma to Data-Driven Predictive Control**

Tomas J. Meijer, Member, IEEE, Koen J. A. Scheres, Member, IEEE, Sven A. N. Nouwens, Victor S. Dolk, and W. P. M. H. (Maurice) Heemels, Fellow, IEEE 

**Abstract—** Willems’ fundamental lemma has recently garnered a remarkable level of interest within the (data-driven) control community. In this paper, we present a formulation of this well-known result that is based on frequency-domain data. This formulation serves to connect recent advancements in data-driven analysis and control with established methodologies and extensive experience in non-parametric frequency-domain identification prevalent in academia and industry. Furthermore, we extend our findings to facilitate the careful integration of multiple frequency-domain data sets to create a sufficiently comprehensive data set. Building on these findings, we propose a data-driven predictive control strategy that leverages measured frequency-domain data from the plant. This innovative approach offers a frequency-domain variant of the widely recognized data-enabled predictive control method, known as DeePC, which is founded on time-domain data. We establish that, under suitable conditions, our novel frequency-domain data-driven predictive control (FreePC) strategy is equivalent to the corresponding DeePC approach, and we illustrate the advantages of FreePC alongside the use of frequency-domain data through a numerical case study. These advantages include the capability to gather data in a closed-loop setup with a pre-stabilizing controller while addressing data noise, maintaining computational efficiency, and providing an intuitive visualization of uncertainty associated with frequency-domain data. Additionally, we further highlight the potential applications of our frequency-domain Willems’ lemma regarding data-driven simulations and the linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) problem. Lastly, we demonstrate that our results can facilitate the evaluation of the system’s transfer function at a specified frequency utilizing a finite collection of frequency-domain data. 

**Index Terms—** Data-driven control, frequency-response function measurements, model predictive control, DeePC

**I. INTRODUCTION** 

Willems’ (fundamental) lemma (WFL) asserts that for a linear time-invariant (LTI) system, a single sequence of data comprising N input-output points from the time domain with a persistently exciting (PE) input can be utilized to characterize all potential input-output solutions of length L < N for the system [1], [2]. A direct implication of WFL, initially presented in [3], is that a persistently exciting data sequence encompasses the full behavior of the system that generates the data [4]. This finding not only permits the identification of the system using subspace identification approaches [5], but has also positioned WFL as a foundational element of contemporary data-driven control. The quest to extend these groundbreaking results to increasingly diverse and complex systems has spurred a substantial body of work aimed at generalizing WFL for various system types. Examples include non-linear systems [1], [6], linear parameter-varying systems [2], descriptor systems [7], [8], stochastic systems [8], [9], and continuous-time systems [10], among others. For a more comprehensive overview, we refer to [8, Table 1]. 

A particularly influential application of the original time-domain WFL in recent years has emerged as data-enabled predictive control (DeePC), which leverages WFL as a data-driven substitute for the prediction model in predictive control contexts [11]. A recent survey on this vibrant topic can be found in [12]. The success of DeePC has consequently motivated many significant expansions to accommodate systems like descriptor systems [7], linear parameter-varying systems [13], bilinear systems [14], nonlinear systems [15], [16], [17], [18], and stochastic systems [19], [20]. Interestingly, none of the previously mentioned works—whether concerning WFL or the derived data-driven predictive control methods—addresses frequency-domain data. This oversight is somewhat surprising, as classical (loop-shaping) control methodologies typically utilize non-parametric frequency-domain models and data [21], [22]. 

As a result, the historical popularity of these methodologies has led to a multitude of frequency-domain identification techniques, robust datasets, and practical know-how for collecting, interpreting, and leveraging such data for control applications. In contrast to existing formulations, a frequency-domain variant of WLF would not only enable better data exploitation but also allow us to tap into the available expertise and identification techniques without the necessity of converting frequency-domain data into a parametric (state-space) model. Notably, frequency-domain (identification) methods provide considerable advantages, such as the capability to manage data influenced by noise and transient behaviors [23], [24], and the ability to conduct closed-loop frequency-response-function (FRF) measurements for unstable systems [25], [23]. 

The sole known frequency-domain version of WFL, to the authors’ knowledge, is presented in [26]. Unfortunately, this intriguing result is demonstrated only for stable systems and does not accommodate conjugate symmetry in the data, which arises due to the real nature of the data-generating system. A related study connecting WFL to the frequency domain is [27], where time-domain data is employed to compute the system’s frequency response through WFL, complementing the challenge tackled in this paper—utilizing frequency-domain data to characterize the system's dynamics in the time domain. Some connections between predictive control and the frequency domain can be found in references [28], [29], [30], which discuss frequency-domain tuning methods, and in [31] which presents a wavelet-based approach to extract frequency content from time-domain data. 

Despite these contributions, it is essential to recognize that model/data-driven predictive control predominantly relies on time-domain techniques, and direct utilization of frequency-domain data/models of the plant remains largely unexplored without transitioning it into a parametric (state-space) model. To bridge the identified gap, this paper introduces a version of WFL founded on frequency-domain data, thus presenting a frequency-domain counterpart to the traditional time-domain WFL. We account for the conjugate symmetry of the frequency-domain data and, consequently, harness the available information (enabling up to two orders of PE per excited frequency). Compared to the preliminary conference version of this work [32], we not only furnish comprehensive proofs of the frequency-domain WFL but also introduce an extension that accommodates the use of multiple data sets—especially crucial when addressing multi-input multi-output (MIMO) systems. This extension complements a similar one for diverse data sets presented in [4] for the original time-domain WFL. 

In addition, we illustrate several significant applications of our findings—new insights compared to the preliminary version [32]—that include frequency-domain data-driven simulation, linear quadratic regulator (LQR) design, and a method for assessing the transfer function of the unknown system at a targeted complex frequency using a limited amount of frequency-domain data. The latter complements a similar achievement based on time-domain data found in [27]. 

Finally, we employ our findings to propose a frequency-domain data-driven predictive control (FreePC) scheme, which serves as the frequency-domain counterpart to the acclaimed DeePC approach derived from the initial time-domain WFL. In fact, we demonstrate that, under suitable conditions, the new FreePC scheme is equivalent to the associated DeePC method. We also highlight several key advantages of FreePC and generally the use of frequency-domain data in a numerical case study. These advantages encompass the potential for data collection in closed-loop setups with a pre-stabilizing controller—rendering our findings applicable even to unstable systems—effectively handling noisy data while keeping computational burdens low, and presenting intuitive visualizations of the uncertainties present in the data due to noise and transient behaviors. 

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: In Section II, we introduce some relevant preliminaries and establish notation. Section III formally frames the problem context. Sections IV and VI detail our main contributions, presenting the frequency-domain WFL and the frequency-domain data-driven predictive control scheme, respectively. In Section V, we explore several intriguing applications stemming from our frequency-domain WFL results. Finally, Section VII concludes our work, and detailed proofs of the results can be found in the Appendix.

**II. PRELIMINARIES**

A. **Basic Notation** 
Let R denote the field of real numbers, C denote the complex plane, and Z denote the integers. We denote Z[n,m] = {n, n + 1, . . . , m} and Z⩾n = {n, n + 1, . . .}, where n, m ∈Z with n ⩾m. The imaginary unit is denoted by j, i.e., j^2 = −1. For a complex-valued matrix A ∈Cn×m, A⊤, AH, A∗, and A+ refer to its transpose, conjugate transpose, complex conjugate, and pseudo-inverse respectively. ℜA and ℑA represent the real and imaginary parts of A, and A⊥ signifies any matrix whose columns form a basis for ker A. Let (u1, u2, . . . , uq) := col(u1, u2, . . . , uq) for any vectors ui ∈Kni, i ∈{1, 2, . . ., q}. We use ⊗ to indicate the Kronecker product, and ei = (0i−1, 1, 0n−i) ∈Rn to denote the i-th n-dimensional elementary basis vector.

B. **Persistence of Excitation** 
Consider the (time-domain) signal v : Z →Rnv. We denote with v[r,s], r, s ∈Z with r ⩽ s, the vectorized restriction of v to the interval Z[r,s], i.e., v[r,s] := (v⊤ r, v⊤ r+1, ..., v⊤ s)⊤. With slight abuse of notation, we also apply v[r,s] to refer to the real-valued sequence {vk}k∈Z[r,s]. We define the Hankel matrix of depth L ⩽s − r + 1 generated by v[r,s] as 

HL(v[r,s]) := 
\[ 
\begin{bmatrix}
vr & vr+1 & \ldots & vs−L+1 \\
vr+1 & vr+2 & \ldots & vs−L+2 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
vr+L−1 & vr+L & \ldots & vs 
\end{bmatrix}
\]

Next, we recall the definition of persistence of excitation. 

**Definition 1:** The real-valued sequence v[0,N−1] is called persistently exciting (PE) of order L ∈Z[1,N] if the matrix HL(v[0,N−1]) exhibits full row rank. Note that the scope of Definition 1 is explicitly confined to real-valued sequences. This will be significant when we later encounter complex frequency-domain data. 

C. **Willems’ Fundamental Lemma** 
Consider the LTI system Σ characterized by: 

\[
\begin{align*}
x_{k+1} & = Ax_k + Bu_k, \\
y_k & = Cx_k + Du_k,
\end{align*}
\]
where xk ∈Rnx, uk ∈Rnu, and yk ∈Rny denote the state, control input, and measured output signals of Σ at time k ∈Z. Let ℓΣ ∈Z[1,nx] denote the observability index of Σ, i.e., the smallest integer for which the observability matrix OℓΣ := (C⊤, (CA)⊤, \ldots, (CA^{\ellΣ−1})⊤)⊤ satisfies rank OℓΣ = rank Onx. The system Σ, comprising the matrices (A,B,C,D), is unknown. We postulate the following about Σ.

**Assumption 1:** The pair (A, B) is controllable. 

As mentioned earlier, WFL can be employed to characterize the comprehensive behavior of Σ based on a single input-output data sequence produced by Σ, given that the input sequence is PE. The following definitions formalize this concept of data sequences.

**Definition 2:** A pair of real-valued sequences (u[0,N−1], y[0,N−1]) of length N qualifies as an input-output trajectory of Σ in (1) if there exists a state sequence x[0,N−1] fulfilling (1a) for k ∈Z[0,N−2] and (1b) for k ∈Z[0,N−1]. In this case, the triplet (u[0,N−1], x[0,N−1], y[0,N−1]) is termed an input-state-output trajectory of Σ. 

Next, we recall WFL, originally published in [3]. 

**Lemma 1:** Let (ˆu[0,N−1], ˆx[0,N−1], ˆy[0,N−1]) denote an input-state-output trajectory of Σ in (1) compliant with Assumption 1. If ˆu[0,N−1] is PE of order L + nx with L ∈Z⩾1, the following statements hold:

(i) The matrix 
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
H1(x[0,N−L]) & HL(u[0,N−1])
\end{bmatrix}
\]
exhibits full row rank; 

(ii) The real-valued sequences (u[0,L−1], y[0,L−1]) of length L constitute an input-output trajectory of Σ if and only if a g ∈RN−L+1 exists such that 

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
u[0,L−1] \\
y[0,L−1]
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
HL(ˆu[0,L−1]) \\
HL(ˆy[0,L−1])
\end{pmatrix}
g.
\]

Lemma 1 is derived from [3, Corollary 2.(iii)], which corresponds to Lemma 1.(i), and [3, Theorem 1], corresponding to Lemma 1.(ii). Lemma 1.(i) indicates that a powerful rank condition can be attained on a specific matrix comprising both state and input data when Σ is excited with an input exhibiting a PE order high enough, a condition proved valuable in subspace identification [5] and data-driven state-feedback synthesis [33], [4], [34]. Lemma 1.(ii) expresses all viable input-output trajectories of Σ of length L as a linear combination of time-shifted windows of a singular input-output trajectory of length N collected offline via a sufficiently high PE ordered input sequence. This result has found widespread application in system identification, as noted in [5], [35], [36], and remains remarkably impactful in the realm of data-driven predictive control in recent years, as evidenced in [11], [37], [13], [7]. 

Rather than basing the analysis on a single persistently exciting input-output trajectory, Lemma 1 has also been adapted to allow for multiple input-output trajectories, which are collectively but not necessarily independently PE [4]. In the following section, we summarize the application of Lemma 1 in data-driven predictive control.

D. **Data-Driven Predictive Control** 
In DeePC [11], Lemma 1 is utilized to derive a prediction model directly from (time-domain) data. We conclude this preliminary section with a brief overview of the operational principles of DeePC. Let vi,k ∈Rnv, with i ∈Z[m,n] for m, n ∈Z and n ⩾m, denote the predicted sequence vk+i at time k ∈Z. 

We employ the notation v[m,n],k = {vi,k}i∈Z[m,n] to either signify the sequence of such predictions made at time k ∈Z or to refer to the vectorized predicted sequence, i.e., v[m,n],k = (v⊤ m,k, v⊤ m+1,k, \ldots, v⊤ n,k)⊤. Given that DeePC does not rely on a precise realization of Σ, its state is inherently unknown. To guarantee that the initial state of the prediction model aligns with the internal state of Σ, an initial input-output trajectory (u[k−¯T ,k−1], y[k−¯T ,k−1]), for ¯T ∈Z⩾1, is prepended. Notably, since we do not presume the observability of Σ, this internal state may not be uniquely ascertainable from the initial input-output trajectory. However, utilizing an initial trajectory of length ¯T ∈Z⩾ℓΣ uniquely identifies the observable component of the state, thereby ensuring the future output remains unique for any specified input sequence. 

Let T ∈ Z⩾1 denote the prediction horizon, and let (ˆu[0,N−1], ˆy[0,N−1]) constitute an input-output trajectory of Σ, with ˆu[0,N−1] being PE of order ¯T + T + nx ⩾ℓΣ + T + nx. At each k ∈Z⩾0, given the preceding input-output trajectory (u[k−¯T ,k−1], y[k−¯T ,k−1]), DeePC [11] resolves the finite-horizon optimal control problem 

\[
\min_{u[0,T −1],k, y[0,T −1],k, gk, σk} \lambdaσ\|σk\|_1 + \lambda g\|gk\|_1 + \sum_{i=0}^{T-1} \ell(yi,k, ui,k),
\]

subject to 

\[
\begin{bmatrix}
u[k−¯T ,k−1] \\
u[0,T −1],k \\
y[k−¯T ,k−1] + σk \\
y[0,T −1],k
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
H ¯T +T (ˆu[0,N−1])  \\
H ¯T +T (ˆy[0,N−1])
\end{pmatrix} gk,
\]

with ui,k ∈U, yi,k ∈Y applicable for all i ∈Z[0,T −1]. Here, U and Y represent the sets of permissible inputs and outputs, while ℓ: Rny × Rnu →R⩾0 signifies the stage cost. The decision variables in (3) are defined as gk ∈RN−T −¯T +1, σk ∈R ¯T ny, with predicted sequences for the inputs and outputs represented as ui,k and yi,k, i ∈Z[0,T −1], respectively. σk acts as an auxiliary slack variable, while λσ, λg ∈R>0 are regularization parameters [11]. These regularization elements and slack variables are necessary to address noise present in the offline data as well as the initial output trajectory y[k−¯T ,k−1]. In the optimal scenario devoid of noise, λg and σk can both be set to zero. 

To translate (3) into a feedback policy, we denote u∗[0,T −1],k = {u⋆ i,k}i∈Z[0,T −1] as the optimal control action computed at time k by solving (3). DeePC subsequently implements the first element of u⋆[0,T −1],k, meaning uk = u⋆0,k, and reevaluates (3) at time k+1, utilizing the updated initial input-output trajectory (u[k−¯T +1,k], y[k−¯T +1,k]), thereby establishing a receding-horizon feedback policy. 

**III. PROBLEM SETTING**

For the entirety of our study, we consider an LTI system Σ as introduced in (1), fulfilling Assumption 1. We assume the system Σ (comprising A, B, C, D in (1)) is unknown, with frequency-domain data provided instead. To formally define frequency-domain data, we first note that the spectrum V: W →Cnv, with W := (−π, π], of the time-domain sequence {vk}k∈Z, for vk ∈Rnv for all k ∈Z, is computed via the discrete-time Fourier transform (DTFT), i.e., 

\[ 
V(ω) = \sum_{k∈Z} vk e^{-jωk}.
\] 

Recall that since {vk}k∈Z is real-valued, the spectrum V maintains symmetry, i.e., V(ω) = V∗(−ω) for all ω ∈W. 

Consider an equidistant frequency grid consisting of M ∈Z⩾1 frequencies ˆωk = πk/M, k ∈Z[0,M−1]. We denote the frequency sequence as ˆω[0,M−1] := {ˆωk}k∈Z[0,M−1], ensuring that ˆω[0,M−1] ⊂ W. This grid of (normalized) frequencies is often employed in the frequency-domain identification literature [23]. 

We explore frequency-domain data comprised of sequences ˆV[0,M−1] = {ˆVk}k∈Z[0,M−1], with ˆVk = ˆV(ˆωk) for each k ∈Z[0,M−1]. Thanks to the symmetry of ˆV, we need only retain frequencies in [0, π) within ˆω[0,M−1]. Further in this paper, lowercase symbols like v[0,N−1] will reference real-valued time-domain sequences, while uppercase symbols such as V[0,M−1] will indicate complex-valued frequency-domain sequences. Notably, our frequency-domain data may consist of pairs of sequences ( ˆU[0,M−1], ˆY[0,M−1]) or ( ˆU[0,M−1], ˆX[0,M−1]), representing samples of the input alongside the corresponding output or state spectrum of Σ. 

To formalize this notion, we recall that the transfer function H: C →Cny×nu governs Σ as follows: 

\[ 
H(z)= C(zI - A)^{-1}B + D, \quad z ∈C. 
\]

**Definition 3:** A pair of complex-valued sequences ( ˆU[0,M−1], ˆY[0,M−1]) of length M is classified as an input-output spectrum of Σ, provided a state spectrum ˆX[0,M−1] exists that complies with 

\[ 
ejˆωk ˆXk = A ˆXk + B ˆUk, 
\]
for all k ∈ Z[0,M−1], and

\[ 
ˆYk = C ˆXk + D ˆUk. 
\]

In this case, the triplet ( ˆU[0,M−1], ˆX[0,M−1], ˆY[0,M−1]) is referred to as an input-state-output spectrum of Σ, while the pair ( ˆU[0,M−1], ˆX[0,M−1]) is deemed an input-state spectrum of Σ. Interestingly, Definition 3 includes a significant scenario in which we have FRF measurements {H(ejˆωk)}k∈Z[0,M−1], which can be integrated as our frequency-domain data, as elaborated in Example 1 below. 

It is important to note that Definition 3 implicitly restricts the frequency-domain data to observations sourced from steady-state, or periodic, time-domain data due to the absence of transient phenomena in (5). This definition aligns with standard practices in the subspace identification literature, see, e.g., [38], [39], [40]. A straightforward, practical method for obtaining compliant data is illustrated in Example 3, where measurements are taken sufficiently long to allow transients to decline and the initial data segments—where transient effects are significant—are subsequently disregarded. 

We note that ˆXk can be eliminated from (5) so that ( ˆU[0,M−1], ˆY[0,M−1]) constitutes an input-output spectrum of Σ, if and only if 

\[ 
ˆYk = H(ejˆωk) ˆUk, 
\] 

for all k ∈Z[0,M−1]. 

**Example 1 (Incorporating FRF measurements):** Consider that Σ represents a single-input single-output (SISO) system, for which we are given FRF measurements {H(ejˆωk)}k∈Z[0,M−1]. We can integrate this frequency-domain data by setting ˆYk = H(ejˆωk) and ˆUk = 1 for every k ∈Z[0,M−1]. The resulting input-output spectrum { ˆU[0,M−1], ˆY[0,M−1]} will thus constitute our frequency-domain data set. Conversely, in MIMO systems, we can incorporate each input direction rk ∈Cnu for every k ∈Z[0,M−1] in a similar manner, even in scenarios where we possess FRF measurements that include all input directions at each frequency, by setting ˆYk = H(ejˆωk)rk and ˆUk = rk for every k ∈Z[0,M−1]. Consequently, we outline a natural expansion of our findings (see Theorem 2 below) that allows us to work with a collection of multiple input-output spectra, further enabling effective utilization of all available data, particularly in MIMO contexts. 

**Remark 1:** The results presented below are also applicable if the frequencies ˆω[0,M−1] are situated on a non-equidistant grid that does not necessarily contain ˆω0 = 0, as demonstrated in [41]. To meet the conditions outlined in Definition 3, [41] mandates that the frequency-domain data must be derived from periodic time-domain data, thus implying the existence of the greatest common divisor of the excited frequencies. Hence, we can always delineate a grid as in (4) (potentially comprising numerous unexcited frequencies, in which case ˆUk = 0, ˆXk = 0, and ˆYk = 0). 

As highlighted in the introduction, nearly all existing iterations of WFL utilize time-domain data, and less effort has been allocated to formulating data-driven control strategies based on WFL that employ frequency-domain data. This paper seeks to address the resulting literature gaps by establishing a version of WFL grounded on frequency-domain data and subsequently employing it for data-driven (predictive) control. 

**IV. WILLEMS’ LEMMA IN FREQUENCY DOMAIN**

In this section, we will present the concept of persistence of excitation regarding frequency-domain data and utilize such data to articulate a frequency-domain variant of Willems’ fundamental lemma. Similarly to [4], we will extend these findings to leverage multiple frequency-domain datasets. 

**A. Persistence of Excitation in Frequency Domain** 

The original WFL necessitates that the considered time-domain data be sufficiently “rich,” a requirement formalized by the concept of persistence of excitation (refer to Definition 1). It is not surprising that we also require the frequency-domain data to exhibit sufficient “richness,” which we will now formalize by defining PE for the complex-valued sequence V[0,M−1] that was introduced in the previous section. 

Let FL : Cnv(m−n+1) →CnvL×(m−n+1), where m, n ∈Z⩾0 and n ⩾m, denote the matrix-valued function of a length m −n + 1 sequence, described by FL(V[m,n]) = (WL(ejˆωm) ⊗Vm, \ldots, WL(ejˆωn) ⊗Vn). (6) Here, WL(z) := (1, z, \ldots, zL−1)⊤, z ∈C. Utilizing FL and the symmetry of the underlying spectrum, we define PE for the complex-valued sequence V[0,M−1] below.

**Definition 4:** The complex-valued sequence V[0,M−1] ∈ CnvM of length M is declared to be persistently exciting of order L ∈Z[1,2M−1] if the matrix 

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
FL(V[0,M−1]) & F∗L(V[1,M−1])
\end{pmatrix}
\]
exhibits full row rank. 

The following comments are pertinent relative to Definition 4. 

First, it is important to note that Definition 4 harnesses the symmetry inherent in the underlying spectrum by also including F∗L(V[1,M−1]) within the rank condition. This component corresponds to the spectral content at the negative frequencies. It is essential to mention that, as the complex-conjugate data at ˆω0 = 0 contributes no extra information, we exclusively incorporate the complex-conjugate data pertaining to V[1,M−1] (i.e., beginning from V1 and not V0). 

Let Tℜ:= 
\[
\frac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
IM−1 & -jIM−1 & 0 \\
IM−1 & jIM−1 
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

By leveraging the conjugate symmetry, we can express the rank condition in Definition 4 as being equivalent to the real-valued matrix

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
FL(V[0,M−1]) & F∗L(V[1,M−1]) 
\end{pmatrix} Tℜ= 
\begin{pmatrix}
ℜFL(V[0,M−1]) & ℑFL(V[1,M−1])
\end{pmatrix}
\]

exhibiting full row rank. Secondly, the rank condition in Definition 4 implies that 2M −1 ⩾ Lnv. Data at any non-zero frequency, i.e., any frequency in ˆω[1,M−1], provides at most two orders of PE since the complex conjugate also plays a role, while the data at ˆω0 = 0 yields at most one order of PE. 

In Section IV-C, we will extend Definition 4 to facilitate the combination of multiple frequency-domain datasets that, considered individually, do not meet the PE requirement but collectively exhibit sufficient “richness.” 

**B. A Frequency-Domain Willems’ Fundamental Lemma** 

Subsequently, we introduce our frequency-domain interpretation of WFL [3], which provides counterparts to both statements in Lemma 1 based on frequency-domain data. 

**Theorem 1:** Let ( ˆU[0,M−1], ˆX[0,M−1], ˆY[0,M−1]) represent an input-state-output spectrum of Σ in (1) that meets Assumption 1. Assume that ˆU[0,M−1] exhibits PE of order L + nx. The subsequent statements hold:

(i) The matrix 

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
F1( ˆX[0,M−1]) & F∗1( ˆX[1,M−1]) \\
FL( ˆU[0,M−1]) & F∗L( ˆU[1,M−1])
\end{pmatrix}
\]

possesses full row rank; 

(ii) The real-valued sequences (u[0,L−1], y[0,L−1]) of length L constitute an input-output trajectory of Σ if and only if there exists g ∈R(N−L+1) such that 

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
u[0,L−1] \\
y[0,L−1]
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
FL( ˆU[0,M−1]) \\
FL( ˆY[0,M−1])
\end{pmatrix}
g. 
\]

The proof for Theorem 1 can be located in the Appendix. 

Theorem 1.(i) indicates that one can achieve full row rank for a specific matrix containing samples of both the state and input spectrum by introducing an input spectrum whose order of PE equals or exceeds nx + nuL. This result serves as a frequency-domain counterpart of Lemma 1.(i), and has been previously beneficial in various applications, including subspace identification [5] and state-feedback synthesis [33], [4], [34]. 

Conversely, Theorem 1.(ii) provides an analogous counterpart to Lemma 1.(ii) using frequency-domain data, asserting that we can depict all input-output trajectories of length L for Σ employing samples from its input-output spectrum collected offline. Importantly, Theorem 1.(ii) can be applied without requiring measurement of the state spectrum ˆX[0,M−1], as it solely utilizes input-output spectrum data. 

Some additional comments regarding Theorem 1 are warranted. 

• Mirroring the shift theorem of the DTFT [42], the time delays present in the Hankel matrices in Lemma 1 translate into linear phase terms, signified by the increasing powers of ejˆωk in WL(ejˆωk) in Theorem 1; 

• Employing conjugate symmetry, Theorem 1.(i) aligns equivalently with the real-valued matrix 

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
F1( ˆX[0,M−1]) & F∗1( ˆX[1,M−1]) \\
FL( ˆU[0,M−1]) & F∗L( ˆU[1,M−1])
\end{pmatrix} Tℜ=
\begin{pmatrix}
ℜF1( ˆX[0,M−1]) & ℑF1( ˆX[1,M−1]) \\
ℜFL( ˆU[0,M−1]) & ℑFL( ˆU[1,M−1])
\end{pmatrix}
\]

possessing full row rank. Similarly, from Theorem 1.(ii), we observe that the real-valued sequences (u[0,L−1], y[0,L−1]) of length L constitute an input-output trajectory of Σ if, and only if, a g ∈R(2M−1) exists such that 

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
u[0,L−1] \\
y[0,L−1]
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
ℜFL( ˆU[0,M−1]) & ℑFL( ˆU[1,M−1]) \\
ℜFL( ˆY[0,M−1]) & ℑFL( ˆY[1,M−1])
\end{pmatrix}
g.
\]

**C. Extension to Multiple Data Sets** 

We now provide generalizations for Definition 4 and Theorem 1, which represent our frequency-domain versions of PE and WFL, respectively, to facilitate multiple data sets. A similar extension has been proposed for the time-domain WFL in [4], accommodating scenarios like missing data samples and unstable systems. Given that using multiple frequency-domain data sets is both natural and, in fact, essential, this approach allows us to integrate information from multiple input directions at a single frequency. As discussed in Example 1, this flexibility enables the utilization of complete FRF measurements from MIMO transfer functions for our data, i.e., {H(ejˆωk)}k∈Z[0,M−1], while Theorem 1 can only leverage information from H(ejˆωk) for one input direction per frequency. 

**Definition 5:** The collection of complex-valued sequences {V e[0,M−1]}e∈E of length M is termed collectively persistently exciting (CPE) of order L ∈Z[1,E(2M−1)], if 

\[
\left[ 
FL({V e[0,M−1]}e∈E) F∗L({V e [1,M−1]}e∈E)
\right]
\]

exhibits full row rank. 

**Theorem 2:** Let {( ˆU e[0,M−1], ˆXe[0,M−1], ˆY e[0,M−1])}e∈E represent a collection of input-state-output spectra for Σ in (1), satisfying Assumption 1. Should { ˆU e[0,M−1]}e∈E be CPE of order L + nx, then the following statements hold:

(i) The matrix 

\[
\left[
\begin{pmatrix}
F1({ ˆXe e[0,M−1]}e∈E) & F∗1({ ˆXe[1,M−1]}e∈E) \\
FL({ ˆU e[0,M−1]}e∈E) & F∗L({ ˆU e[1,M−1]}e ∈E)
\end{pmatrix}
\right]
\]

has full row rank; 

(ii) The real-valued sequences (u[0,L−1], y[0,L−1]) of length L present an input-output trajectory for Σ if, and only if there exists G0 ∈RE and G1 ∈CE(M−1) such that 

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
u[0,L−1] \\
y[0,L−1]
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
FL({ˆU e[0,M−1]}_{e∈E}) \\
FL({ˆY e[0,M−1]}_{e∈E})
\end{pmatrix}
G.
\]

A sketch of proof for Theorem 2 can be found in the Appendix, detailing how the proof of Theorem 1 can be adapted to extend to multiple sets of frequency-domain data. 

**V. APPLICATIONS**

In this section, several engaging applications of Theorem 1, as well as Theorem 2 in the context of multiple data sets, are showcased. 

**A. FRF-based Simulation** 

It is well established that the steady-state response of an asymptotically stable system (1) can be simulated using FRF measurements. Herein, we leverage our frequency-domain version of WFL to simulate not just the steady-state behavior of Σ, but also its transient response—an advancement which, to our knowledge, is not feasible with existing methods. Moreover, the system's asymptotic stability is not a prerequisite in this instance, although the collected offline data may need to be gathered under closed-loop conditions with a pre-stabilizing controller, as elucidated in Example 3. 

As previously mentioned in Section IV-C, it is sensible to utilize multiple datasets (i.e., various input directions at the same frequency) when dealing with (MIMO) FRF measurements. Thus, we will employ Theorem 2 as the foundation for our FRF-based simulation algorithm. 

**Proposition 1:** Let {( ˆU e[0,M−1], ˆY e [0,M−1])}e∈E stand as a collection of input-output spectra of Σ in (1) that meets Assumption 1. Let L, L0 ∈Z⩾1 and suppose that { ˆU e[0,M−1]}e∈E is CPE of order L+L0+nx. For any historical input-output trajectory of length L0 (u[−L0,−1], y[−L0,−1]) for Σ and a future input sequence u[0,L−1], G0 ∈RE and G1 ∈CE(M−1) exist such that 

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
u[−L0,L−1] \\
y[−L0,L−1]
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
FL0+L({ ˆU e[0,M−1]}e∈E) & F∗L0+L({ ˆU e[1,M−1]}e∈E) \\
FL0({ ˆY e[0,M−1]}e∈E) & F∗L0({ ˆY e[1,M−1]}e∈E)
\end{pmatrix}
G
\]

and 

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
y[0,L−1]
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
FL0+L({ ˆY e[0,M−1]}e∈E) & F∗L0+L({ ˆY e[1,M−1]}e∈E)
\end{pmatrix}
G,
\]

denoting an input-output trajectory for Σ. If, further, L0 ⩾ℓΣ, then the future output y[0,L−1] remains unique. 

Proposition 1 can be utilized to execute data-driven simulations of the unknown system Σ directly based on frequency-domain information regarding the system. To implement this, we ascertain G satisfying 

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
u[−L0,−1] \\
y[−L0,−1]
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
FL0+L({ ˆU e[0,M−1]}e∈E) & F∗ L0+L({ ˆU e[1,M−1]}e∈E) \\
FL0({ ˆY e[0,M−1]}e∈E) & F∗L0({ ˆY e[1,M−1]}e∈E)
\end{pmatrix}
G,
\]

given the past input-output trajectory (u[−L0,−1], y[−L0,−1]) and the future input sequence u[0,L−1]. Subsequently, we leverage the computed G to determine the future output sequence y[0,L−1] from the equations mentioned. Notably, given our non-assumption of observability for Σ, the system's internal state is not guaranteed to be uniquely determined by the initial input-output trajectory. However, the preceding input-output trajectory guarantees that the simulation commences from a consistent initial condition among potential initial conditions compatible with the previous input-output trajectory. With an initial trajectory of length L0 ⩾ℓΣ, the observable aspect of the internal state is uniquely defined, ensuring uniqueness for the future output sequence across any input sequence presented. 

We can also execute an analogous variable transformation as previously discussed in Section IV-B to convert the equations in Proposition 1, which are complex-valued, into a corresponding real-valued formulation. The following sections will elaborate on the use of Proposition 1 for data-driven simulations, exemplifying it through numerical case studies.

All the aforementioned results amalgamate time and frequency domains, in the sense that they utilize frequency-domain offline data to characterize the behavior of Σ in the time domain. For instance, both frequency-domain variants of WFL, i.e., Theorem 1 and 2, present a time-domain response of Σ on the left-hand side of Theorem 1.(ii) and Theorem 2.(ii), respectively, juxtaposed against frequency-domain data on the respective right-hand sides. We leverage Theorem 2 to characterize the frequency response of system Σ at any complex frequency not coinciding with an eigenvalue of A.

**Proposition 2:** Let {( ˆU e[0,M−1], ˆY e[0,M−1])}e∈E be a collection of input-output spectra for Σ in (1), complying with Assumption 1. Assuming that { ˆU e[0,M−1]}e∈E is CPE of order L0 + 1 + nx. For any complex frequency z ∈C that is not an eigenvalue of A and a sample Uz ∈Cnu from the input spectrum at z, the system of linear equations 

\[

\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
Yz \\
G
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
WL0+1(z) ⊗Uz \\
0 
\end{pmatrix},

\[
\text{where } ΨL0+1({ ˆU e[0,M−1]}e∈E) := \left[

\right],
\]

has a unique solution for Yz such that the complex pair (Uz, Yz) corresponds to a sample of the input-output spectrum of Σ evaluated at z (i.e., Yz = H(z)Uz).

**VI. FREQUENCY-DOMAIN DATA-DRIVEN PREDICTIVE CONTROL** 

In Section V, we have previously observed how Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 can be applied for simulating the unknown system Σ defined in (1) based on frequency-domain data. Naturally, these outcomes can also serve as a data-driven, frequency-domain substitute for the predictive model within model predictive control (MPC). The subsequent frequency-domain data-driven predictive control conceptualization (FreePC) is offered as a counterpoint to DeePC [11]. 

**A. FreePC Algorithm** 

Let T ∈Z⩾1 represent the prediction horizon length. As referenced in Section V-A, we are required to utilize a past input-output sequence to ascertain that our simulation—which we define as our prediction in the context of FreePC—originates from the correct initial condition. Suppose we possess frequency-domain data composed of a collection of E input-output spectra {( ˆU e[0,M−1], ˆY e[0,M−1])}e∈E, with { ˆU e[0,M−1]}e∈E being PE of order ¯T + T + nx, thus implying 

\[ 
E(2M −1) ⩾ ¯T + T + nx ⩾ ℓΣ + T + nx. 
\]

At each time k ∈Z, given the prior input-output sequence (u[k−¯T ,k−1], y[k−¯T ,k−1]), the FreePC solution is delineated by the finite-horizon optimal control problem 

\[
\min_{u[0,T−1],k,y[0,T−1],k,G0,k,G1,k,σk} 
\lambdaσ∥σk∥_1 + λG∥Gk∥_1 + \sum_{i=0}^{T−1} \ell(yi,k,ui,k),
\]

subject to 

\[
\begin{bmatrix}
u[k−¯T ,k−1] \\
u[0,T−1],k \\
y[k−¯T ,k−1] + σk \\
y[0,T−1],k
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
F¯T +T ({ ˆU e[0,M−1]}e∈E) & 
F∗¯T +T ({ ˆU e[1,M−1]}e∈E) \\
F¯T +T ({ ˆY e[0,M−1]}e∈E)& 
F∗¯T +T ({ ˆY e[1,M−1]}e∈E)
\end{pmatrix}
Gk,
\]

where Gk = 

\[
\begin{bmatrix}
G0,k \\
G1,k \\
G∗1,k
\end{bmatrix},
\]

ui,k ∈U, yi,k ∈Y for all i ∈Z[0,T−1]. 

Here, we keep in mind that u[0,T−1],k and y[0,T−1],k represent the sequences for predictions of uk+i and yk+i, respectively, as articulated in Section II-D. Analogously to DeePC, ℓ denotes the stage cost; U and Y correspond to the sets of acceptable inputs and outputs, respectively; σk ∈R¯T ny is an auxiliary slack variable, while λσ and λG are regularization parameters constrained to be greater than 0 [11]. These regularization terms and slack variables are essential for managing the noise in the offline data as well as in the initial output trajectory y[k−¯T ,k−1]. In an optimal noiseless scenario, both λG and σk can be set to zero. 

To convert (3) into a feedback policy, we denote u∗[0,T−1],k = {u∗i,k}i∈Z[0,T−1] as the optimal control action computed at time k by solving (16). Thereafter, FreePC executes the foremost element of the optimal control action, identified as u⋆[0,T−1],k, whereby uk = u⋆0,k, and at time k + 1, it again solves (16) using the newly obtained past input-output trajectory (u[k−¯T +1,k], y[k−¯T +1,k]), thereby establishing an iterative optimal control process through a receding-horizon framework.

**B. An Equivalence Result**

Interestingly, when λg = 0 in (3) and λG = 0 in (16), which is feasible in the event that the offline data is noise-free, we can demonstrate that FreePC is equivalent to DeePC. 

**Theorem 3:** Let {( ˆU e[0,M−1], ˆY e[0,M−1])}e∈E and (ˆu[0,N−1], ˆy[0,N−1]) embody a collection of input-output spectra and a corresponding trajectory of Σ in (1) fulfilling Assumption 1. Under the conditions that ¯T ∈Z⩾ℓΣ and T ∈Z⩾1, and given that both { ˆU e[0,M−1]}e∈E and ˆu[0,N−1] are PE of order ¯T + T + nx, we assume that both {( ˆU e[0,M−1], ˆY e[0,M−1])}e∈E and (ˆu[0,N−1], ˆy[0,N−1]) are devoid of noise, thereby establishing λg = 0 in (3) and λG = 0 in (16). 

Consequently, FreePC utilizing (16) equates to DeePC utilizing (3), meaning that, at any k ∈Z, the optimal control problems in (16) and (3) furnish the same optimal control actions and corresponding output trajectories. It follows from Theorem 3 that if (3) produces a unique optimal control action u⋆0,k, then u⋆0,k is also the unique optimal control outcome achieved via (16), and vice versa.

Theorem 3 contemplates FreePC founded on multiple experiments alongside DeePC, which is based on a singular experiment; however, a similar equivalency is valid for DeePC drawing upon multiple experiments.

**C. Numerical Case Study**

Consider the unstable SISO system Σ characterized by (1) and the transfer function denoted as 

\[
H(z) = \frac{0.1164z + 0.1071}{z^2 - 1.891z + 0.7788}.
\] 

Although in this instance we focus on a SISO example—as it permits clearer illustration and interpretation of our results—it is vital to note that the FreePC scheme outlined in Section VI is equally applicable to MIMO systems. 

To incorporate the noise effects in our case study, we adapt the measurement model in (1b) to reflect measurement noise through 

\[
yk = Cxk + Duk + nk.
\] 

Given that (17) is unstable, we procure offline data employing a closed-loop measurement setup [25, Chapter 10], illustrated in Fig. 2, friendlier to the system (17) via the stabilizing controller 

\[
C(z) = \frac{6z - 5.135}{z - 0.1353}.
\] 

The input uk ∈R comprises control feedback coupled with an injected signal {dk}k∈Z. 

To procure offline data, we utilize a multi-sine excitation for the injected signal {dk}k∈Z, encompassing M = 20 frequencies ˆω[0,M−1] in (4), in the presence of zero-mean Gaussian noise nk with a standard deviation of 0.1. We capture p + p0 periods of dk, uk, and yk at the excited frequencies, followed by the discarding of the first p0 periods to minimize transient phenomena. Subsequent computations on a per-period basis produce the DTFT to achieve estimates of { ˆDd ρ(ˆωk)}ρ∈P,k∈Z[0,M−1], { ˆU d ρ (ˆωk)}ρ∈P,k∈Z[0,M−1], and { ˆY d ρ(ˆωk)}ρ∈P,k∈Z[0,M−1] based on collaborative data represented by P := Z[1,p]. 

Instead of directly applying this data, we opt to estimate the transfer function at the frequencies ˆω[0,M−1] to facilitate an illustration of the impact of gradually increasing measurement periods. Utilizing the foundational concepts of transfer function estimation under ideal conditions (assuming absence of transient conditions and noise), we can ascertain 

\[
\begin{align*}
\hat{U} d ρ (ˆωk) & = (1-C(ejˆωk)G(ejˆωk))^{-1} ˆDd ρ (ˆωk), \\
\hat{Y} d ρ (ˆωk) & = G(ejˆωk) ˆU d ρ (ˆωk),
\end{align*}
\]

for every m ∈Z[0,M−1] and ρ ∈P. 

Simultaneously, we estimate the transfer function at the model frequency ˆωk through the expression 

\[
\hat{H} ρ (ˆωk) = \hat{Y} d ρ (ˆωk)( ˆDd ρ(ˆωk))∗ ( ˆU d ρ(ˆωk))∗.
\]

Taking the average across all periods yields our estimated FRF, expressed as the sample mean, which can be represented as 
\[
\hat{H}(ejˆωk) = \frac{1}{p} \sum_{ρ \in P} \hat{H} ρ (ˆωk).
\]

To evaluate the uncertainty in the estimated FRF, we also calculate the sample variance of ˆH(ˆωk), determined via 

\[
\text{var} [\hat{H} (ejˆωk)] = \frac{1}{p(p-1)} \sum_{ρ \in P} | ˆH ρ (ˆωk) - \hat{H}(ˆωk)|^2. 
\]

Figure 4 illustrates the resulting FRF measurements alongside their 99% confidence intervals (developed as per [45, Chapter 6]) for both cases of p = 2 and p = 50 periods. Notably, the capacity to visualize and intuitively interpret confidence intervals, as depicted in Fig. 4, emerges as another significant advantage of employing frequency-domain data. 

Examining Fig. 4, it is clear that confidence intervals for p = 50 contracts (though not at the high frequencies) significantly relative to p = 2, which is corroborated by the lower variance reflected within. This phenomenon is also translated into the precision of FRF estimates, which markedly improves for p = 50 in contrast to p = 2. This pattern aligns naturally with the expectation that gathering additional measurement periods averages out the influence of random noise, leading to enhanced accuracy in estimates. 

Interestingly, in a DeePC scenario, increased periods would result in a higher number of decision variables, thereby elevating (on-line) computational complexity, while the computational complexity of FreePC remains independent of the time-domain experimentation duration and, instead, is defined by the number of excited frequencies. This distinction underscores one of the essential advantages of numerous techniques based on our frequency-domain WFL alongside FreePC compared to time-domain alternatives. 

Next, we implement FreePC corresponding to the FRF measurements obtained from Fig. 4. Given that we are examining a SISO system, we opt for E = 1. Let ˆUk = 1 and ˆYk = ˆH(ejˆωk) for all k ∈Z[0,M−1]. We stipulate a prediction horizon of T = 10, taking the initial input-output trajectory length to be ¯T = 3nx = 6 ⩾ ℓΣ. An inspection verifies that 

\[ 
ˆU[0,M−1] 
\]

is PE of order 

\[ 
2M−1 = 39 ⩾ T + ¯T + nx = 18. 
\]

We construct the stage cost ℓ(y,u) = y⊤Qy + u⊤Ru, where Q = 1 and R = 0.01, applying regularization parameters λG = 0.1 and λσ = 1 · 10^5. The sets of permissible inputs and outputs are assigned as follows: U = [−3, 0.5] and Y = [−0.5, 1.2]. 

We undergo simulation of the FreePC scheme, based on the two sets of FRF measurements delineated in Fig. 4, which were secured through measuring p = 2 and p = 50 periods. The outcomes for input and output trajectories are showcased in Fig. 5. As anticipated, the FreePC approach founded on p = 50 periods surpasses that derived from p = 2. Indeed, it closely aligns with the input-output trajectories achieved via a model-based benchmark that employs a similarly tuned MPC scheme (based on the precise model) also illustrated in Fig. 5. 

To further consolidate the correlations between the number of periods employed and the performance outcomes attained, we execute a Monte Carlo study, conducting FreePC based on datasets structured as described above. We evaluate datasets comprising p = {5, 10, 25, 50} periods (following the discarding of the first 20 periods to lessen transient phenomena), ultimately computing the obtained costs as 

\[ 
J = \sum_{k=0}^{Lsim−1} \ell(yk,uk) \quad \text{over the duration} \, Lsim = 50. 
\] 

The average cost alongside the variance throughout 1000 iterations are recorded in Table II alongside the model-based benchmark costs. 

As expected, as the FRF measurements become increasingly representative of the actual system (17), the average computed cost and its variance exhibit a decrease as the value of p rises, as demonstrated in Table II. This finding confirms that FreePC captures the similar performance attributes as classical MPC employing a parametric state-space prediction model, provided the FRF data secured is sufficiently accurate. 

**VII. CONCLUSIONS**

In this paper, we have introduced a groundbreaking version of Willems’ fundamental lemma rooted in frequency-domain data, aimed at comprehensively characterizing the input-output behavior of an unknown (potentially unstable) system. Through this process, we defined a notion of persistence of excitation applicable to frequency-domain data, in addition to furnishing extensions of our results necessary for managing multiple data sets. To highlight the possible implications of these new findings, we have illustrated their applications in data-driven simulations, frequency-response evaluations (at frequencies other than those found in the offline datasets), and data-driven LQR. We also detailed the frequency-domain fundamental lemma as the foundation for presenting an innovative data-driven predictive control approach, termed FreePC, which utilizes frequency-domain data without the requirement to convert it into a parametric state-space model. Thus, we effectively bridge the divide between recent advancements in data-driven analysis and predictive control and the existing methodologies and expertise surrounding frequency-domain control/identification found in academia and industry. The numerical results presented also showcase a number of benefits associated with leveraging frequency-domain data, particularly when managing challenges associated with noise.

Mathematics Subject Classification 2020: 11B37 1 1 Introduction The exponential local-global principle, commonly referred to as the Skolem conjecture, states (see [2]): Conjecture 1.1 (Exponential local-global principle). Let a1, . . . , ad ∈ Q such that ad ≠ 0 and all roots of the polynomial f(x) = xd − a1xd−1 − a2xd−2 − · · · − ad are simple. Suppose b is a positive integer, and let the sequence u = (un)∞n=−∞ be such that each term is in Z[1/b] and, for all n ∈ Z, un+d = a1un+d−1 + · · · + adun. There is no zero term un if and only if, for some integer m ≥ 2, we have gcd(b, m) = 1 and every term un is not in mZ[1/b]. □ If there is a zero term in u, it is evident that the condition concerning m must fail. The most compelling aspect of the conjecture is in its contrapositive—a statement asserting that if no zero term exists in u, then the condition regarding m must hold. The conjecture remains open in its entirety. The requirement that the roots of f(x) are simple is vital, as illustrated by the following example. Example 1.2. (See [2].) Consider the sequence u in Z[1/2] defined by un = (2n + 1)2n for n ∈ Z. We have un+2 = 4un+1 − 4un for n ∈ Z, and f(x) = x2 − 4x + 4 = (x − 2)². None of the terms of u are zero. However, for each odd positive integer m, m divides un for every integer n of the form n = km + (m − 1)/2 with k ∈ Z. □ For any prime p, define vp(x) as the p-adic valuation of a nonzero rational number x (for example, vp(pn) = n for n ∈ Z). We say that a prime p is coprime to a nonzero rational number x if and only if vp(x) = 0. Proving the exponential local-global principle in the linear case, specifically when d = 1, is rather straightforward. Proposition 1.3. The exponential local-global principle holds in the case when d = 1. Proof. Consider a sequence u of numbers in Z[1/b] where, for some a1 ∈ Q \ {0}, we have un+1 = a1un for n ∈ Z. It follows that un = u0a1n for all n ∈ Z. If u0 = 0, then every term in u is zero, and the conjecture is satisfied. If u0 ≠ 0, then no term of u is zero, and each prime p that is coprime to both a1 and u0 satisfies un ≠ 0 (mod p) for all n ∈ Z, confirming the conjecture (and virtually all primes work as valid choices for m). 2 The primary objective of this paper is to demonstrate a stronger version of the exponential local-global principle in multiple instances where d = 2 and f(x) has two distinct rational roots. Following that, certain degenerate cases for d = 3 will swiftly arise. This work was showcased at the Stellenbosch Number Theory Conference 2025 in January 2025 at Stellenbosch University; a significant portion was also presented at the 67th Annual Congress of the South African Mathematical Society in December 2024 at the University of Pretoria. This paper discusses the first year of a planned three-year research initiative linked to the University of Pretoria’s Research Development Programme; in the second and third years, the goal is to establish the exponential local-global principle in additional cases (including families where f(x) is cubic or quartic) and to explore whether and under what conditions the principle holds when considering algebraic number fields beyond Q. In this article, until the section on degenerate cubic cases, we assume d = 2, that the numbers a1, a2 in Q comply such that a2 ≠ 0 and a2 1 + 4a2 ≠ 0, let b be a positive integer, consider the sequence u = (un)∞n=−∞ of numbers in Z[1/b] such that un+2 = a1un+1 + a2un for all n ∈ Z, and assume that the roots c1 and c2 of f(x) = x² − a1x − a2 are rational. According to Vieta’s formulas, c1c2 = −a2 ≠ 0. The condition a2 1 + 4a2 ≠ 0 ensures c1 ≠ c2, thus according to a well-known result, there are b1, b2 ∈ Q such that for n ∈ Z, we have un = b1c n 1 + b2c n 2. If 0 is included in {b1, b2}, then u ≡ 0 or we are in a d = 1 scenario; for the time being, let us assume b1 ≠ 0 and b2 ≠ 0. We define B = −b2/b1 and C = c1/c2. Under these assumptions, we will prove the following main theorem. Theorem 1.4. Assume the following conditions: (1) Cm = B for some m ∈ Z, or (2) (C, B) = (1, −1), or (3) BkCℓ/∉{±1} for all k ∈ Z \ {0} and all ℓ ∈ Z. Then there is no zero term in u if and only if for infinitely many primes p, we have gcd(b, p) = 1 and every term un is not divisible by p. □ To establish Theorem 1.4, we will utilize a result resembling Chebotarev density by Schinzel [4] regarding power residue symbols. Unlike some articles by Schinzel [4, 5] that tackled specific quadratic instances of the exponential local-global principle, here a2 is not necessarily ±1; thus, Theorem 1.4 appears to be a novel result. 3 2 Initial Results We have B = −b2/b1 ∈ Q \ {0} and C = c1/c2 ∈ Q \ {0}. For each n ∈ Z, we find un = 0 ⇔ b1c n 1 = −b2c n 2 ⇔  c1 c2  n = −b2/b1 ⇔ Cn = B, and for every prime p coprime to all of b, b1, b2, c1, and c2 at the same time, it follows that un ≡ 0 (mod p) ⇔ b1c n 1 ≡ −b2c n 2 (mod p) ⇔  c1 c2  n ≡ −b2/b1 (mod p) ⇔ Cn ≡ B (mod p). Cases (1) and (2) of Theorem 1.4 are straightforward. In case (1), with Cm = B for some m ∈ Z, it follows that um = 0, hence Theorem 1.4 holds. In case (2), having (C, B) = (1, −1) implies Cn ≠ B for all n ∈ Z, and for every odd prime p, Cn ≢ B (mod p), thus Theorem 1.4 also holds. From here on, we assume we are in case (3); that is, we assume that BkCℓ/∉{±1} for all k ∈ Z \ {0} and all ℓ ∈ Z. We must show that Cn ≢ B (mod p) for infinitely many primes p. To set the stage for this proof, we will revisit some foundational information on power residue symbols. 3 Power Residue Symbols (See [3, pp. 244–248] and [1, exercise 2, pp. 351–354].) Consider a number field K and a positive integer n with K ⊇ μn. Definition 3.1 (Power residue symbols). Let a ∈ K \ {0}. Let S(a) denote the set of archimedean places and prime ideals p such that ordp(n) ≠ 0 or ordp(a) ≠ 0. (2) Let  a Q j p c j  n = Q j  a p j  c j n for integers c j (for finite products). (3) For b ∈ K \ {0}, let � a b  n =  a ⟨b⟩S(a)  n, where ⟨b⟩S(a) stands for the ideal derived from the prime-ideal factorization of ⟨b⟩ by excluding all powers of prime ideals p such that p ∈ S(a). □ The subsequent result by Schinzel indicates that we can, in some sense, select the values of finitely many power residue symbols. Theorem 3.2. [4, Theorem 4, p. 246] Let n be an odd prime. Let a1, . . . , ak denote some numbers in Q fulfilling the condition: For x1, . . . , xk ∈ Z and r ∈ Q, if a x1 1 · · · a xk k = rn, then n divides each of x1, . . . , xk. This holds especially true if a1, . . . , ak are distinct primes. □ Schinzel's paper [4] extends this inquiry to all algebraic number fields; however, we only utilize the scenario incorporating Q. Schinzel's proof employs the Chebotarev density theorem. 4 Proof of Remaining Part of Main Theorem We now revert to proving Theorem 1.4. What still requires proof is case (3): Under the assumptions that C ∈ Q \ {0}, B ∈ Q \ {0, 1}, (C, B) ≠ (1, −1), and BkCℓ/∉{±1} for every k ∈ Z \ {0} and every ℓ ∈ Z, we need to confirm the existence of an infinite set S of primes, each coprime to both B and C simultaneously, such that for all r in S and all k in Z, we find Ck ≢ B (mod r). Let P be the comprehensive set of primes. Define T = {p1, . . . , pm} as the set of primes p fulfilling (vp(b), vp(b1), vp(b2), vp(c1), vp(c2)) ≠ (0, 0, 0, 0, 0). Let M be the matrix  vp1(C) vp2(C) · · · vpm(C) vp1(B) vp2(B) · · · vpm(B)  =  vp(C) vp(B)  p∈T . Considering that BkCℓ/∉{±1} across all k ∈ Z \ {0} and ℓ ∈ Z, it follows that (1) The upper row of M is a zero row, or (2) The matrix M retains rank 2. Consequently, at least one of the two conditions must hold: (1) There exists a prime p′ such that vp′(C) = 0 while vp′(B) ≠ 0. (2) There exist primes p′ and q′ such that d := det  vp′(C) vq′(C) vp′(B) vq′(B)  does not equal zero. In the following discussion, wherever a list featuring items (1) and (2) appears, each item relates to the case where the corresponding condition prevails. Choose a prime n such that 5 (1) gcd(n, 2vp′(B)) = 1. (2) gcd(n, 2d) = 1. We will evaluate the nth power residue symbol for Q(ζn). Let S signify the collection of primes r in P \ T \ {n} matching the following criteria: (1) For p ∈ T \ {p′}, we have � p r  n = 1 and  p′ r  n = ζn. (2) For p ∈ T \ {p′, q′}, � p r  n = 1,  p′ r  n = ζa n, and  q′ r  n = ζb n, where the numbers a, b ∈ {0, 1, . . ., n − 1} are established such that avp′(C) + bvq′(C) ≡ 0 (mod n) and avp′(B) + bvq′(B) ≡ 1 (mod n) (such a and b can be found under the previous conditions). The set S is infinite as noted in Schinzel’s findings. Because n is odd, it follows that (−ζn)n = (−1)n = −1 implies that −1 is an nth power in Q(ζn), hence each r ∈ S satisfies � −1 r  n = 1. This infers that for each r ∈ S, the number � B r  n is a primitive nth root of unity, but we have � C r  n = 1, thus  Ck r  n = 1 for all k ∈ Z, leading us to deduce that for every k ∈ Z, we find Ck ≢ B (mod r). This finalizes the proof of Theorem 1.4. 5 Corollary: Some Degenerate Cubic Cases Theorem 1.4 readily yields certain degenerate cubic instances of the exponential local-global principle. Corollary 5.1. Let c1 and c2 be nonzero rational numbers such that c1 /∈ {c2, −c2}. Let b1, b2, and b3 be nonzero rational numbers. Analyze the sequence u = (un)∞ n=−∞ defined such that un = b1c n 1 + (b2 + (−1)nb3)c n 2 for n ∈ Z. (Note that if we define rational numbers a1, a2, and a3 such that (x − c1)(x − c2)(x + c2) = x³ − a1x² − a2x − a3 identically, then un+3 = a1un+2 + a2un+1 + a3un for all n ∈ Z.) Let C = c1/c2, B+ = −(b2 + b3)/b1, and B− = −(b2 − b3)/b1. The exponential local-global principle holds for u if for each B ∈ {B+, B−}, at least one of the following is valid: (1) (C, B) = (1, −1).
